This is a big subject. The US situations shown here definitely does not apply in the UK, in which home AirCon (AC) is unknown. AC takes lots of power; the US grid (in hot areas) is built to deliver about 10-14 kW per home continuous. But in UK home power need is for "lighting+"... the peak load per home is c. 800W, which is in winter (no summer need for AC).

So the built UK grid (well, the distribution system) is good for 1 to 1.5 kW per home. Alas, EVs charge often @ 7 kW... thus to stay within design limits, about 5 houses can take nothing (oops) whilst 1 EV charges. Today, charging the occasional EV is OK... but as numbers rise, the UK networks will be discovered as inadequate. We can make the power, but cannot deliver it as transformers and cables to c. 80% of UK homes are very inadequate. Heat Pumps add to the problem (often being bigger net loads than EVs).

Variations of this situation likely also apply to European nations traditionally without home AirCon or electric heating.

Also, in the US the distribution systems are overhead - but in the UK these are buried. So lots of digging to upgrade cables etc.

If anyone wants to look more into this, check out the DNO's ED2 proposals (for 2022..2027) of what they are going to do about this. Papers on this issue include a ENA/EATL report (DS2030 WP3) from 2012, and the Session 3 slides by Nikolas Hill, Ricardo Energy 2019 "Impact analysis of mass EV adoption and low carbon intensity fuels scenarios", 13th Concawe Symposium 2019, Antwerp (especially slide 12).

I think this is the biggest issue in the way of grid expansion and reconfiguration to better support distribution generation.

This video misrepresents this issue hard and I fear will hurt peoples perception of EVs as a result.

First off a 25% increase is a HUGE increase in energy consumption its not 'just' a trillion kwhs thats a lot of energy. The video throws out ideas like reduced oil refinery energy consumption and using EVs as grid battery storage but it fails to address where the rest of that 25% comes from. That being said people being incentivised to charge off peak will be a big help. The reality is that the grid will need serious investment to accomdate electric cars and charge them at the speeds people desire. This does not mean electric cars are not useful or an inferior technology, after all oil requires a seperate hugely expensive energy network to provide you will reliable gas(and only is cheap due to gas subsidies). Unlike gas powered cars EVs don't need an energy distribution system built from the ground up, they can use an energy distribution system that already exists, it will simply need upgrades. The amount of electricity EVs demand is no small fraction of what your home consumes so your neighborhood with already at capacity lines may need their power transfer capacity increased by more than just 25%. After all that 25% is the average, not maximum, energy consumption increase evenly spread over a year so on average people will demand 25% more electricity. What if everyone tries charging their car at the same time? Anything more than average will require more than a 25% increase in capacity. That is a lot of transformers, substations, power lines, etc that need to be built.

Now don't get me wrong this is very solveable problem but a problem all the same. Serious investment will need to be made and measures will need to be put in place so we don't blow transformers left and right like we did when AC came around. EV owners could have smart chargers that monitor grid capacity and only charge when the grid has energy to provide, in exchange the consumer pays a lower price similiar to the charging at night idea but this would be at all periods. This could become a regulatory standard for all EVs while the grid catches up. EV owners could notify the state utility commision of their purchase so they could better track and project EV growth and predict capacity issues in their neighborhood. These are just some ideas, all in all EVs will demand a lot of energy, enough to cause a disturbance but that will be temporary growing pains. The same way we have to deal with the construction of bigger highways as more people move in or buy cars we will need more electric infrastructure and like those roads it wont be cheap. My greatest fear is that people will see electic cars as the enemy and cities will start banning them to save power rather than spending money on upgrades. Its important that people have explained to them that yes this is going to cost hundreds of billions if not trillions but that this is an investment in the economy. The cost of transportation will all EVs will halve with current effciency and america will have total control over the energy needed to run its economy, the benefits are huge enough to justify the spending.

The skeptics think of this as battery capacity that needs to be charged, the smarter people see this as potential energy ready to be discharged, as mosttly cars spent most of their time not being driven around. They spend far more time being parked than being driven. 

If you use 50kwh as the average battery capacity of an EV, you can do some fun math. 2 million vehicles would be 100M kwh, or about 100 gwh or  0.1 twh. Going from 2 to 20 million vehicles, you get to a twh of battery capacity added every year. These batteries have about 1500 cycles so that is about 1.5pwh of energy that can be absorbed and released back to the grid over their lifetime when they are charging and discharging,  That's a huge buffer in other words.

We have unlimited access to cheap solar energy during the day. All we need is a place to put that energy so we can use it at night. Vehicle to grid is just part of the equation here. At scale, using lithium ion for the grid doesn't make sense from a cost point of view as there are cheaper ways of storing and releasing energy. But even so, having a fleet of tens or hundreds of millions of EVs represents a huge amount of storage. The challenge isn't how to charge these batteries but how to leverage the charged potential energy in a way that makes sense economically, 

All this is before you consider improvements that are likely to come to batteries. They are going to be cheaper, last longer (more cycles) etc. Also, a lot of car batteries enjoy a second life as grid storage. So, all that battery capacity is going to end up trickling down to that kind of thing,. We're deploying grid storage by the gwh currently. Soon that will be by the twh.

Remember this is demand at any one time an increased national demand of 966Gw. Where is that capacity coming from? Is it sat unused now on the Grid?

The estimated average daily output of an average power plant is therefore calculated as 6,384 MW x 90% x 24 hours, which gives us approximately 138,000 MWh per day. But only 5,745MW demand at any one time allowing for the 90% safety... You have to build hundreds of power stations to supply the additional demand, and even if you have that capacity can the Grid physically support an increased demand of 966Gw constant draw?

That's at 50% of people charging at the same time, what happens when 75% do it? Has anyone actually though through just how much electrical power is actually required.

Looking at the other end fitting a higher capacity charging unit at home means significantly increased amperage draw and potentially new wiring and distribution units, it's not like a cooker it shower unless you limit yourself to the slow 7Kw units. Even then 7,000,000W @ 230V is 30Amps double that for 110V. Can your house support a draw of another 30Amps consistently for several hours with wiring overheating or safety breakers tripping? That's an entire electrical ring main (UK term) at fully capacity sustained over hours.

For a high capacity 27Kw unit that 117Amps well above the maximum capacity for the entire house.

The one thing that wasnt mentioned but is very exciting is the maturation of the idea of microgrids. The idea of a microgrid is basically that instead of a centralized power station servicing 100 miles of customers, every community would have its own solar and/or wind and most importantly, its own stable storage. Stable storage is really THE key to making renewables work, but also solves the problems of demand peaks and virtually eliminates brown outs. Microgrids can even operate wholly with stable storage and not even produce their own power, by buying cheap power from utilities during off-peak hours and then selling it to their customers. The goal of these systems isnt nessecarily to eliminate big powerstations, but to transform the energy use curve at the power plant level away from the duck-curve and towards a totally flat baseline. 

There are also programs like energy co-ops that allow communities to actually OWN their own local energy production that have been succesful in Europe. Those schemes usually have a third-party investor who buys the equipment and land, and takes a fraction of the profits, while the community investors sit on the board and make decisions. Especially for people who live in small rural communities who are most vulnerable to aging power infrastructure, they could produce their own power and reduce their reliance on that aging grid. These schemes also tend to be able to sell power for cheaper than the big utilities and without the seasonal price swings.

OK let's counter the points made - I've had discussions with experts in this field in the past and they had major concerns which are not properly or correctly tackled in this video:

The thing is, right now there's a massive over capacity in many residential areas where solar panels are used. The net has no batteries - it needs to use the electricity - but the power usage of companies & factories in many areas is far lower than that of the solar panels (we've had large adoption of solar panels here in Belgium).

The thing is that by the time people come home, the solar panels are hours behind peak performance. The energy suppliers have to kick in with gas, coal, nuclear or wind energy with wind not even being a reliable option on all days (and nowhere near enough to account for all power usage). So you lose the green aspect of EVs - saying "just charge them at night" to me is utterly ridiculous. What's the point of driving EV if you STILL rely on fossil fuels?

Also, the nodes are not only a bottleneck for Solar Panels but also for EVs for the exact same reason. It's estimated that if everyone charges at least one EV at the same time in a single residential area, that the peak power usage would triple. It seems that most people that comment on the Tesla semi may have never sat in a semi let alone have driven one. I am all for EV's but until their battery charging times are similar to refuelling time for an ICE vehicle they will be for local use only.  ON a coast to coast run, it would take an extra day and a half to charge the battery. Tesla claimed it to have “built it around the driver,” but that is just nonsense. Starting by how much space it just wastes with its central seating position. While that is the one the McLaren F1 adopted, it works better on hypercars than on trucks. The central driving position makes it more challenging to look ahead and overtake. That happens because a truck is a wide vehicle. If you are in the middle of the cabin, you are far from the edge of the lane, where you have a better view of the traffic ahead. On a two-way road, that’s also where you can see oncoming traffic. Truck drivers have to pay tolls, talk to people in gatehouses, and handle the paperwork while entering a factory or delivering anything. The Semi does not give access to a window. In fact, it has no windows that can be opened: the driver will have to get up from their seat, open the door and deal with whatever they need – even in the winter. Talking about cold weather,  having the doors in the back of the cabin will force the driver to walk a bit to reach their seats. In the winter, with muddy boots, doing that will mess up the cabin interior. A truck with doors that give direct access to the driver’s seat prevents that from happening: they can take off their boots and just walk barefoot in the cabin.
That would be especially useful for trucks with a bed. The Semi apparently does not offer one, which is another flaw in the electric truck’s concept. If you think it through, it also speaks a bunch about the limited use the truck will have, almost like a Class 8 last-mile truck, if that even exists. A hypothetical bed could be in the back, but it is not there because that’s where the Semi has its doors. Another option would be to put a bed above the windscreen. Even if the Semi was not conceived for long trips – as the lack of a bed suggests –  people driving at night often find it useful to take a quick nap to keep driving safely. 
The massive screens inside the Semi are dangerous. The “tablets" are simply not designed for use in moving vehicles. Drivers need physical buttons that they can reach without taking their eyes off the road. They reflect stuff and glow too much, even in dark mode, which makes them terrible for night driving.
I am also not happy about the rear-view mirrors. Thanks to the central driving position (again) and the cabin being narrower in the front, Tesla had to place them in really long arms. If they get dirty (and they eventually will), the driver will not reach them easily to clean them.
Tesla seems particularly proud of: the bullet shape of the cabin, which imposes an angled windscreen. As aerodynamic as that is,  it would only help snow build up on top of it. People who find it difficult to clean a passenger car's windscreen in the winter should have fun doing so on a glass surface sitting ten feet above the ground. Vertical windscreens do not have that issue. In the summer, the angled windscreen will turn the cabin into a glasshouse.
So there you have a semi driver's view of this foolish waste of engineering talent.

​At least in the USA, rail transport (freight, not passenger!) costs LESS per ton than any truck freight regardless of distance— long haul, regional, or "last mile". A tremendous amount of freight is transported by rail in America ...AND THEN 72% of all freight is STILL loaded onto tractor-trailer rigs (semi trucks) for regional distribution. 

The admittedly enormous long-haul trucking market exists IN ADDITION TO the huge long-haul rail freight market for at least three reasons: 
1. small to medium-sized companies who don't have the economies of scale to merit rail freight, consolidating enough of their freight to merit a truck of any size. Semi trucks offer the best rate per pallet, or per ton (per pound, for very small companies). So if you can consolidate enough freight to move by semi rather than a smaller truck, you do that. 
(Notice how many trucking companies use the word CONSOLIDATED in their names!)

2. refrigerated freight, or anything that needs to be delivered as quickly as possible. Rail freight takes a while, not because trains travel slowly (they don't, considering all the factors involved) but because the loading, transferring, etc. takes a while... and it will all wind up on some sort of truck anyway at the end of the rail line. A semi can deliver a significant load from one end of the USA to the other in less than 24 hours. If you have a lot of expedited cargo, hire more semis. There's a lot of flexibility here— and when you're at the point of purchasing your own fleet of semis and hiring your own drivers, you reconsider rail freight, as refrigerated or expedited rail might cost less and serve you almost as well (of course, you'll still hire trucks for that "last mile" or "last thirty miles" delivery). 

3. "on-demand" expedited cargo. Not only does the customer want it ASAP, but the customer just called you today to arrange it. All sorts of emergencies fall into this category, not to mention things like moving companies, and ALL OF THEM go by truck, because they CAN'T plan shipments weeks or months in advance. You can argue about refrigerated rail vs. refrigerated semis, but trains can't touch this "sudden need" freight market. In fact, trucking's only competitor in this market is air freight, and only for long-haul cargo. (Although *IF* low-cost small electric air-cargo planes operating from small regional airports really make a go of it, they'll be able to compete with consolidated semi trucks and smaller trucks in the regional-delivery market, but that's an awfully big "if".)

And FWIW, as many others also pointed out, American freight trains are already super-efficient diesel-electric hybrids. 

Because of this and many other efficiencies developed over the past 175 years, rail cargo does NOT cost more than road-carried cargo... but rail is an option only if you organize your own supply chain and measure your annual cargo in the tens or hundreds of tons.

It's a shame that the Semi would fail to meet European and U.K. truck dimension regulations. There's a very good reason why our trucks have much flatter fronts than US ones; that's to stay within maximum length laws whilst maximising cargo volume. The cab is also shorter to minimise the room needed for manoeuvring in comparatively small spaces. 
In addition, that long  bonnet makes a signigicant blind area around each side of the front of the vehicle. A pedestrian or bicycle could be close to the front of the truck, and in that blind area. That can be a very dangerous flaw. 
Also, the Semi has two 'blind sides', from the dricer's seating position, meaning that neither side has a clear direct line of sight down to the rear of the rig. That clear line of sight makes for much easier reversing and turning into loading bays or tipping areas. Sure, a driver can work around that one, to some extent, but any experienced truck driver will tell you how important that line of eight can be. 
Furthermore, if you've ever driven a well-designed articulated truck, you'll notice that you almost wear the vehicle, rather than just sit in it. It effectively becomes an extension of your body, once you've driven it for a short distance. The central seating position is going to be very strange for a seasoned driver to adapt to. That said, I would expect that  the driver's seating position should be adjustable to the right or left without too much redesign.

8:50 - The reason for leaving a diesel truck to idle when getting out to hand over paperwork or grab a coffee (or whatever the driver needs to do) is to allow some of the components that run particularly hot, such as the turbo, enough time to cool down slowly... In the same way that you 'warm up' an engine, you also have to let it cool down the same way for the same reasons, but in reverse.
Additionally, it costs extra fuel and wear & tear to start a stopped engine. If you are going to be a couple of minutes, then leaving the truck to idle saves on both fuel and wear & tear.

Regenerative braking will be a bit more complicated than it is on an all-wheel drive Tesla sedan that can use regenerative braking on all four wheels. Normally these tractor/trailer configurations have five axles. Regenerative braking applies only to the driven axles on the tractor. Light braking can be achieved by using regenerative braking the active (cruise) axle. For more aggressive deceleration, it will be necessary to engage the other drive motors so they can contribute to the regenerative braking that is available which means clever software control for engaging those motors when needed for braking. The front axle on the tractor and the trailer axles only have service brakes, so when quick stops are required, the service brakes will need to supplement the regen braking and hence the wear on the service brakes will be more than negligible.

Americans do more than just drive to work, so that is only a valid point if customers can afford to buy a single use vehicle. Especially for families. Most need the capacity possible in a four wheeled vehicle. This is mainly because owning multiple vehicles for specific needs is not an option for most people. Most people need a multi-purpose transport. The four door sedan form factor meets the greatest number of applications for an urban or suburban driver. From one person commuting to needing to take kids to school or food shopping for a family of four. The other concern is the price, you are not getting enough functionality for $15K. The limited use of this vehicle has it overpriced by at least one third. All of which adds up to a reduced market potential. There are many design elements here that are right-on what is needed, some very welcome positives. Simplicity, limitations of the non-optional extras so many EV makers stuff into their designs, greatly inflating the price. I replaced my 2004 Mustang with a red Solo in October, just hit 1700 miles coming home today.  It's my daily driver, commuting about 21 miles/day and also going shopping and to restaurants around town.  It is a blast to drive, and I get thumbs up, photos and videos everywhere, folks always saying they like it.  The styling is very eye-catching.

My biggest complaint is also the loud and enthusiastic fan.  The first increment should be half or a third what it is.

As to the range, I get somewhere near 1 mile/% commuting by keeping my maximum speed down to 45-50 for about half my route where I could go faster.  I'm not in a big hurry, just going to work!  Keep in mind that aerodynamic drag goes by the square of the speed; 60 mph has nearly twice the drag as 45.  You spend any time at 80 and the range will go down significantly.  This car is intended as a city commuter and not optimized for a lot of high speed travel.  Of course, if you charge it every night back up to nearly full it won't matter that much anyhow.

As a single person, this is ideal for me.  Plenty of room for me and my groceries (if you need more space, you have a family and another larger vehicle anyway).  Plenty of performance to get the job done.  Inexpensive to charge.  Appealing and easy to live with.

A Canadian man is calling electric vehicles the "biggest scam of modern times" after his frustrating experience with an electric truck. 

Dalbir Bala, who lives in the Winnipeg area, bought a Ford F150 Lightning EV in January for $115,000, plus tax. He told FOX Business he needed the vehicle for his work, but also wanted something suitable for recreational activities such as driving to his cabin or going fishing. He also wanted an environmentally friendly vehicle as owning one is "responsible citizenship these days." 

But Bala was quickly hit with the reality of owning and operating an EV soon after the purchase. The vehicle compelled him to install two charges – one at work and one at home – for $10,000. To accommodate the charger, he had to upgrade his home’s electric panel for $6,000. 

In all, Bala spent more than $130,000 – plus tax. 

Not long after the purchase, Bala got into a minor accident which, he said, required "light assembly" on the front bumper. Bala took the vehicle to the body shop and did not get it back for six months. He said no one from Ford answered his email or phone calls for help. 

The limitations of the EV truck became even more apparent when Bala embarked on a chaotic 1,400-mile road trip to Chicago. 

Fast charging stations – which only charge EV’s up to 90% – cost more than gas for the same mileage. On the family’s first stop in Fargo, North Dakota, it took two hours and $56 to charge his vehicle from 10% to 90%. The charge was good for another 215 miles. 

On the second stop, in Albertville, Minnesota, the free charger was faulty and the phone number on the charging station was of no help, he said. The family drove to another charging station in Elk River, Minnesota, but the charger was faulty there as well. 

"This sheer helplessness was mind-boggling," Bala wrote in an online post. "My kids and wife were really worried and stressed at this point." 

There were no other fast charging stations within range of Elk River and his vehicle only had 12 miles left. 

"By now it was late afternoon. We were really stuck, hungry, and heartbroken," Bala said. 

Bala ultimately had the vehicle towed to a Ford dealership in Elk River and rented a regular gas vehicle to complete the family’s trip to Chicago. The family picked up the F150 on their way back to Winnipeg. 

"It was in [the] shop for 6 months. I can’t take it to my lake cabin. I cannot take it for off-grid camping. I cannot take for even a road trip," Bala wrote. "I can only drive in city – biggest scam of modern times." 

Bala told FOX Business he believes the government needs to do more to "provide consumers with the right information." 

"People have to make the right choices. I want to tell everybody to read my story," he said. "Do your research before even thinking about it and make a wiser choice." 

"The actual thing they promised is not even close. Not even 50%. And once you buy it, you're stuck with it and you have to carry huge losses to get rid of that. And nobody is there to help you."

I wish you would do your homework before swallowing and regurgitating the hype. Axial flux motors are NOT new. They have been around as long as electric motors have existed. They haven't been developed for the same reason hydrogen as an energy source wasn't ubiquitous decades ago even though the technology was already there. While there are applications that are a good fit, they are much less flexible and adaptable and the number of suitable applications is severely limited.

Axial flux motors are much more limited in their RPM range than the more common radial flux motors because... SURPRISE! PHYSICS, not technology. In order to get as high RPMs as a radial flux motor, you would have to stack multiple rotors of the same diameter as the radial flux rotor, completely negating all the benefits of axial flux by increasing complexity, mass and cost. If you tried to spin an axial flux motor as fast as an equivalent power radial flux motor, the axial flux motor would explode because it would have a much larger diameter rotor. Much shorter/thinner (hence the term "pancake motor", but much wider across. The combination of short but wide and relatively low RPMs make them fairly ideal for some applications (like aviation), but the packaging (along with literally ALL performance characteristics) actually is detrimental for automotive applications.

As with any technology, billion-dollar concept vehicles can appear to make them attractive, but the reality is that it's not a good fit for mass adoption.

The Electrom is impractical and unsafe.  For secure storage, you really need to live in a house with a garage.  Most condos or apartments don’t have street-level storage for such a long bike.  It’s also too heavy for stairs.  If you use the Electrom to shop or go to work, you’re restricted to street parking.  It’s too big to bring into your workplace or store.  Even with a strong lock, I wouldn’t leave a $12,000 bike un-attended for several hours.

The cover or fairing is a safety hazard because it’s at head level.  In a collision or sudden stop, your face or throat will likely hit the edge of the fairing.  With a conventional bike, the same situation will cause a endo.  An endo may injure the rider, but it will be much less severe than the fairing hitting your face or throat.  Has Electrom done any collision testing with the fairing?  

The fairing’s aero advantage is not important because most conventional e-bike can easily reach the 45km/h limit in USA & Canada.  The fairing also doesn’t provide any rain protection.  The fairing is gimmicky without any real benefit.

There are so many problems with this. I live in Budapest and I work as a bike delivery man. So I know how biking in cities are like. 
First: this is huge. The best part in cycling in cities is that it's practical. You can easily fit through very tiny spaces. You can slalom between cars in a traffic jam. You can easily turn it around if you have to and you can park anywhere. This "bike" is just too long and too heavy to do any of these. Especially too long in european cities where there are narrow streets. 
Second: the aerodynamics just doesnt make sense. I can easily do a 20-25 km/h average speed for a day with a regular bike. With an electric it's an easy 30 even 35. Maybe it's more aerodynamic but it's heavy af and the wheels are too thick and the diameter of theme is too small. You have to add more energy to make a wheel go if it's smaller. 
Third: it's bigger than a haul bike but it doesn't have the capacity. So a deliveryman cannot use it. 
So it's too big for cities, i'm pretty sure it almost has the same range and speed as a better ebike. So the only people who could use it are people in the country side who use it once or twice a year for a trip. But it's too expensive for a hobby like this.

I really hope Aptera succeeds, but I'm concerned about its viability in the EV space. By the time this autocycle is available, the market will be further saturated with new and used EVs of every stripe. The use case of a large rolling two-seat teardrop essentially appeals to only a few hardcore tech geeks. Yes, preorders seem strong but will that translate into actual sales? Is that enough to sustain the company? Once the early adopters are satiated, will demand remain? 

This reminds me of Arcimoto's story with an incredibly long development phase followed by production difficulties, missed deadlines, cost inflation and ultimately waning demand. The Aptera is a much more advanced vehicle, but is that enough? Three-wheelers struggle for acceptance unless they're highly focused on recreation. I'm also concerned it won't be as affordable as some think. Initial investor types will happily purchase the costly first production runs, but it's unclear whether the autocycle will achieve any economies of scale to be profitable. 

My advice for potential buyers? Get one as soon as you can.

SMC is not what the Aptera guy described at 5:32, so either they are not using SMC, or he doesn't understand the process. SMC comes as a sheet which is then moulded to shape; it does not start with bulk fibre ("goo") and resin. Given the use of the term "goo" he may be referring to Bulk Moulding Compound (BMC) (bulk moulding composite, dough moulding compound (DMC))... but even that does not use both the dough and additional resin. The shape of the first part shown suggests BMC to me, while the hatch shown is likely SMC, but that's only a guess.

It's a strange mix. From the point of view of focusing on aerodynamics, low mass, and lower battery size and weight requirement, it's a huge step in the right direction away from the heavy, aerodynamically poor designs everywhere else. But the size of the vehicle, carrying maximum two passengers does nothing to deal with the basic problem with personal vehicles, which is the density of passengers per highway or road mile. This is what makes cars a long-term losing main component of transportation strategies.

Related: I've recently moved to Kuala Lumpur, and I'm convinced that some (but not all) of the larger balances in transportation are being worked out here. It's a fantastically vertical city, and it has very good, clean, efficient and available public transportation. almost all large centres like malls have large stacked parking indoors, but all the prestige malls and many of the others have train connections which can take you anywhere; and in the weather here, not driving in heat or torrential rain and being taken there makes much more sense. 

You can see how this city would electrify cars easily, because those stacked garages are ideal charging infrastructure points. That's much more meaningful than solar panels on the hood, roof and deck. But in cities like those in the US that don't have the governance and financing to do the kinds of transformations now common elsewhere, the self-charging Aptera gives the illusion of being sensible.

 But you can also see that KL, in the rush to integrate the car, from a small traditional asian city, has created a nightmare of freeways, flyovers, multilane divided urban roads that pedestrians have to have bridges to cross. The Aptera, like all cars, would tend to reinforce this negative side of KL. And there are dozens of cities around the world, perhaps hundreds, where the wholesale rebuilding of the entire urban infrastructure is happening. Those that learn from KL won't build the road infrastructure that SoCal assumes is the way to go. But in the meantime, the Aptera is very cool.

Aptera has what they need to build at least the first 4-8 hand-built Production Intent (PI) Launch Edition (LE) test vehicles. Aptera is in the process of working with US Capital Global (USCG) to raise $60M to construct the additional PI vehicles needed for crash and durability testing (and public and press demos!), and to build-out the prototype factory in Carlsbad, plus start initial low-rate production, which will not only serve to debug the prototype production system but will also get the first vehicles into customer hands. If all goes well, the USCG raise could conclude this year, though I expect it will continue so long as investor demand exists.

After that comes production ramp-up, where the existence of even a small amount of initial revenue from sales will make fundraising easier, particularly if Aptera is able to use affordable debt, such as in combination with possible Federal loan guarantees. Once "enough" vehicles are on the road and revenues rise with production, Aptera will quickly execute their IPO to finance construction of their first true mass-production facilities (likely outside of California) which will consist of making many copies of the Carlsbad prototype subassembly and final assembly lines.

This is what will enable Aptera to become profitable while keeping prices affordable. Many EV startups, including Rivian and Lucid, still aren't profitable despite having scaled production and having introduced additional models. Essentially, these companies are stuck in quicksand, like Fisker was for so long, needing continued investment (and debt) despite increased production. Aptera hopes to bypass that swamp by making the Carlsbad prototype assembly line itself become profitable (excluding the rest of Aptera, such as R&D and other non-factory staff and expenses), before 10K vehicles have been produced.

Like everything else Aptera does, those goals are extremely ambitious and strictly depend on the timing of funds arriving, so expect the schedule, as always, to be "flexible".

A factor one must never forget is that, whether the car is good or not (and our Ioniq 5 is the best car we've ever had), there is more to owning a particular brand than what the reviewers tell you in YouTube videos. For instance, our experience as Hyundai customers in the UK has been abysmal. Dealership franchises seem unable (and sometimes unwilling) to address issues with EV cars such as our Ioniq, especially relating to manufacturer recalls. Communication with Hyundai is often terrible or nonexistent. Hyundai garages don't know how to diagnose or fix problems, and we've been to many, many dealerships to hopefully find the best service but were sadly disappointed. These hard-to-ignore factors have really put us off from buying the 2025 Ioniq 5. So we recommend that reviewers add this angle to the excellent videos they make to create a bigger picture of what it means to be a customer of a specific brand.

You cast aspersion on somebody creating a hybrid model Y,  but I don't quite understand why. I currently own a 2018 Chevy Volt plug-in hybrid and I think it is absolutely brilliant! I get about 65 miles of battery-only range when driving around town which is about 90% of the total miles that I drive and where I average about 110-120 mpge. This is more than enough electrical range that I very very seldom need to call on the gasoline engine. 

Maybe one day high speed chargers will be as common as gasoline refueling stations are now. But here in the US that day isn't today. So when driving cross country, having a gasoline engine means that I don't need to do careful route planning to make sure I can always reach a high speed charging station. 

And while it might seem inefficient to carry around a ICE engine and associated generator all the time for the infrequent times I need it, the same could be said for the battery pack in the long range Tesla 3. The average miles per year is around 12,000. That works out to 33 miles per day. Even bumping that up to 50 miles per day, the Tesla is only using 20% of charge in the 1000 lb (454 kg) battery pack. That means that 800 lbs of batteries are carried around unused for those rare days when you need to drive cross country. 

So I get an electric car with enough range that the gas engine doesn't get used for months at a time, and yet for the relatively few percentage of my total miles where I need to drive long distances as efficiently as possible, I can use a small amount of gasoline to get me where I need to go TODAY without the careful route planning needed to make sure I am never out of range of a high speed charging station. 

Research is currently underway to use renewable energy to manufacture fuel starting with CO2 (from captured CO2 from concrete plants or from atmospheric CO2 capture) and H2 (from splitting water), adds electrical energy through an electro-catalyst and you end up with methane and methanol. Go through a second step to combine those and you get butanol, which is a 4 carbon chain alcohol and is a drop-in replacement for gasoline. So even the fuel used for the longer trips could eventually be carbon neutral.

The front window is flat as f$$$ allegedly because of the efficiency, but the side windows are bizarly curved as f$$$... because of what??? All that tripe about aerodynamics not being important if the vehicle is light is extremely disingenuous. It may be fine for a "city car" that never goes above 60 kmph, but the second you hit the highway the range will evaporate like a drop of water in the Mojave. In fact, aero is FAR more important than weight for efficiency. Especially because of regenerative braking and things like crosswinds. The lighter the vehicle, the more likely it is to get blown right off the highway or sucked right into the pressure trough of a passing truck. The more a car weighs, the more it wants to keep going in spite of the wind and the less energy you spend fighting the wind. A heavy but highly aerodynamic car is *always* far more efficient than a light but high drag car. The heavier car is also far more stable and safer in every way.

PLEASE: Stop talking this bullshit of lighter battery electric cars being more efficient! This claim just doesn't hold up in reality! 
Doubling the weight of any car increases the consumption on acceleration and holding speed by barely anything (<5%) on the motorway and maximum of 30% on really slow city driving. 
This is simple mathematics and high-school level physics. Weight only has an impact on rolling resistance. And rolling resistance is a force independent of speed. So lower speed -> higher weight impact, higher speed -> lower weight impact.
*BUT* : Heavier EVs have bigger motors and batteries ... so they have the potential to regen at way higher rates and thus make up for the higher rolling resistance. A Kona 64kWh can be driven without using ANY friction brake, everywhere, and this while driving far from slow. This is, what up to 150kW of regenerative breaking gives you. Brakes electrically almost as quickly as it accelerates. Good luck trying to do this in a Fiat 500e or Dacia Spring!

Example: compare these 6 cars and their real energy consumption according to ev-database:
Dacia Spring 25kWh: weight: 1T consumption: 156Wh/km
Fiat 500e 42kWh: weight: 1.4T consumption: 159Wh/km
Kona 64kWh: weight: 1.8T consumption: 162Wh/km
Ioniq 6 RWD 77kWh: weight: 2T consumption: 156Wh/km
Zoe ZE50: weight: 1.55T consumption: 165Wh/km
Model 3 SR: weight: 1.85T consumption: 151Wh/km

So now tell me, where you see the correlation between weight and consumption!!!

In fact due to the Spring having no heat pump or seat heating leads to the user using the PTC heater way more in winter and thus having a way higher consumption on their commute compared to the Kona! So being way more efficient in winter plus having the same consumption in mild weather *_makes the Kona overall more efficient, despite being 80% heavier._*

In fact this is all a question of overall system design. 
For example: Halving the battery size from e.g. 60kWh to 30kWh only lowers the weight of the car by 150 to 180kg, let's say around 10% of weight reduction. So you save 10% of rolling resistance (nothing more is saved when reducing weight), which in turn only makes up around 10 to 50% of resisting forces (depending on the speeds on your commute). So all you can save is 1 to 5% of consumption on acceleration and holding the speed, but you loose 50% of your regen capability and thus have to use your brakes way more often, wasting energy! This is break-even!

-> EV get the most efficient, when you cram in a battery and motor size, that allows you to drive completely without friction brakes. And this causes a bit of weight!

An Ioniq 6 weighing 2T manages to consume only 145Wh/km on country roads in winter around freezing from tests I've seen. Make that 130Wh/km in warm weather.
A Dacia Spring needs around 115Wh/km in the same conditions. That is a *_difference in consumption of around 15% for a weight difference of 100%_* !!!
What does that mean? The weight only has a share of 30% on the resisting forces at speeds driven on country roads (about 80km/h / 50mph).

I would also greatly appreciate presenters being less breathless about structural batteries. It doesn’t look like that’s what’s actually happening here, because the battery samples they showed were still cylindrical, cell batteries, but structural batteries are going to be a big problem for consumers eventually. Probably not for the buyers of this vehicle, I’m sure this is going to be hundreds of thousands if not $1 million for this vehicle. so if they get into some kind of a crash or fender, bender and I have to buy a whole new car, it’s not even going to register for them.

But structural batteries, if they are not designed in a way to plan for repairs, are going to be the bane of the average consumers life, even if they have a six-figure income. Right now, Tesla is going this direction and it stayed if they wanted to, and their resistance to allowing repairs of their vehicles is very similar to the way Apple and other phone manufacturers have treated their phones.

Once car motive, batteries are integrated into the structure of the vehicle, if you get into any kind of an accent, even if it’s a minor, one, then dance, part of your frame, you’re basically going to have to spend between 25 to 50% of the vehicles original cost to get it up and running again. Right now it’s about 10 to 30% of the vehicles, original cost, which is still too expensive. But just imagine what will happen. If you bend your frame, it causes your batteries to be unusable safely, and you have to essentially replace the entire structural internals of a vehicle. You’re going to just simply buy a new one because that’s how much it’s going to cost.

We should be encouraging manufactures to make batteries easily replaceable. Maybe not go as far as Neo goes, but certainly your local repair shop or be able to drop the battery out of the vehicle and then you can purchase a replacement battery, getting a significant return on the component parts of the removed battery. It should be no more expensive than replacing the transmission of an engine from a gasoline car. But structural batteries will be significantly more expensive, and some instances may be more expensive than a brand new car.

I love the practicality of bringing the cabin forward. But what I want to know is how this changes front impact safety?  The bits of the vehicle in front of the passenger compartment needs to absorb as much energy from the impact as possible, as SLOWLY as possible, in order stretch out the time between impact and the meat scak coming to a complete stop. More milliseconds means fewer Gs of decelleration, and a better chance of not scrambling your organs.  And the more the distance between the front of the car and the driver/front passenger, the more options there are for reducing the impact to the occupants.  Maybe this is a topic for a future video interview with someone involved in this aspect of car design.

Talking about Kei EVs, you forgot the Mitsubish i-Miev (it's actually your channel's 1st video)... which actually hit the market earlier than the Leaf. Also worth noting the Kei department of Nissan is mostly done by Mitsubishi instead of Nissan (hence the Sakura also has the Mitsubish eK X EV equivalent - Nissan provided the drive train while it's built on a Mitsubishi platform). That's said on your point on Kei cars electrification (pronounced 'kei-ji-dou-sha'), Honda and Suzuki-Daihatsu-Toyota partnership already presented their plans and prototypes, they'll start with Kei-Vans first next year then move on to passenger models. Essentially now for mainstream Kei cars (not counting likes of Caterham which also qualifies) only Suzuki, Daihatsu, Mitsubishi, and Honda (which now discontinued Kei-trucks) do Kei cars themselves, all others are rebranded models of the above manufactures (ie. Subaru, Mazda, Nissan, Toyota). This one is an exception as it's more of a concept car project of Toyota made into production for Tokyo Olympics and Paralympics, and NOT available for public to purchase (only for lease - Toyota also does not classify it as a car, but 'micro-mobility') - I think these info should've been communicated by the reviewer, instead of all these imaginations of this being a 'car' (and yes even for Japanese safety standards these would've feared much worse than an ordinary Kei car nowadays so can't blame ENCAP). And as to EV strategy of Toyota and other Japanese manufacturers, if you've done your research you would have known they actually started taking them seriously quite a few years ago (with Honda - a engine manufacturer - planning to discontinue all internal combustion engines by 2040 - yes they do not want hybrid in long-run and are very committed on EVs with 5 partnerships in liquid batteries, one in semi-solid state and a in-house solid state programme) - yes they (excl. Nissan) are later than the others, but they wanted to have more things done inhouse, unlike many others in the market that barely bought whole package of the solution from the others (which is fine for short-term but not sustainable business-wise), and obviously these results won't come in at least a few years time so everything out are essentially interim to bridge gaps. I predict that in 70 years, hydrogen fuel cell car as well actually makes sense. That’s not today, but today hydrogen is in the same place that battery electric vehicles were in the 1900s. A seemingly good idea, but with a lot of practical problems.

The question then is, when that 70 years comes around, will the hydrogen fuel cell vehicle solve a problem that battery electric vehicles can’t solve?

Maybe?

While there is a lot of downplaying of the problems of charging battery electric vehicles with the current grid, there are a lot of forces that are at play that may actually make that be a real problem. It’s an open question whether the public monopolies of power generation companies, which are both public utilities and for-profit companies in most cases, will allow all the continued proliferation of solar power generation for individuals. they are making moves to try and charge people for services. They don’t need if they have sufficient solar and other generative on site power and don’t need power from the grid. So far in California, they haven’t succeeded, but they’re not going to stop.

Additionally, there are several sources which suggest that if everyone who drives a gas car now drove an electric vehicle, that it is actually true that the grid wouldn’t be able to handle it. That is another problem that needs to be solved, it could be solved by nuclear power plants, but environmental advocates still haven’t come to grips with the fact that nuclear power is the second safest power generation technology behind solar. Even taking into account the handful of meltdowns that have occurred over the last hundred years. And new nuclear power plants are going to be even safer. Not to mention less expensive to build. That said, power companies are going to want to build the big more expensive plants as was laid out by John Oliver’s very good peace on the subject.

On the other hand, it is possible that better electric vehicles will get more efficient, and therefore use less overall power. But the likelihood that they’ll get significantly more efficient is very small.

The other issue with battery electric vehicles is powered density. it’s still not comparable to gasoline or hydrogen. As a result, you have to have very large vehicles in order to get the usable range that most people are used to. And you can make the argument that people only drive under 30 miles every day and can charge at home so your blue in the face, but there is going to be time to make the transition from where we are to where we want to go. I would imagine it’s going to be at least 20 years before the vast majority of Americans in any case can charge an electric vehicle at home. Now in that timeframe, is it likely that we’re going to get battery technology that charges faster and has better storage density? Sure, it’s very possible.

But at the same time, it seems like it’s about the same lift to figure out a way to effectively generate and store hydrogen for use with fuel cell vehicles. and to me, it’s worth the research because there are other factors involved as well.

The biggest factor that’s of concern is how are we going to make enough batteries of any chemistry to satisfy the requirements that are coming? We’re not just talking about electric automobiles, but trucks, big, rigs, potentially transport ships, and even airplanes. Not to mention trains, and continuing to make batteries for all the electronics that we become so fond of. It turns out that while they don’t have an exclusive on materials, China is at the forefront of providing the materials necessary to make the batteries that we use in electric vehicles. but China is making moves to leverage that to give them control of global politics. It will not surprise me if in the next few years, China will finally make a move to re-incorporate Taijuan in the way that they did with Hong Kong. When they make this effort, there will be opposition, but then China will cut off, the materials for better electric vehicles. If we are all still dependent on China, at that time, we will be hard-pressed not to cave-in to their demands. And then, like a big, economic chess match, China will have Taijuan, which is basically the only place currently with large production of the micro chips that make all these things work.

For better or worse, the development of hydrogen fuel cell technology is crucial, along with the development of other sources of materials, necessary for batteries, as well as coming up with chemistry’s, that don’t require exotic materials that China currently has a stranglehold on, for our transportation needs.

Well, I agree that it’s far more likely that we will as an international community develop battery technology that is more efficient and uses other materials than the ones that China is currently supplying, I also believe that we need to not put all our eggs in the one basket of battery electric vehicles. And I still failed to see why it’s beneficial to denigrate the efforts in Japan, especially to develop an alternative to better electric vehicles. We are going to need hydrogen for many different technologies in the near future. Not just for vehicles, but also potentially for fusion power, plants, and for alternatives to petroleum materials that we would become dependent on for medical devices, and many of the products that we need for our day-to-day lives. Hydrocarbons are extremely important to the current technological and economic boom that we are at the tail end of. When plastic goes away, a lot of other things are going to go away. But, it’s very possible that developing ways of extracting hydrogen combined with carbon dioxide sequestration will actually allow us to continue to make those products, but in better ways, while ceasing the need to extract petroleum from the ground.

I just find it truly shortsighted and not constructive to denigrate the pursuit of hydrogen for fuel cells. Our market is dominated and basically controlled by American car companies that are focused on providing expensive EVs for a niche market. If the Chinese vehicles were allowed into our market I would seriously consider a small EV for a city car and keep my larger gas powered vehicle for winter and long distance travels. That’s why SUVs are so inefficient. No matter how “slippery” they make them, the fact that they’re larger always ends up resulting in less efficient vehicles.

Given that high drag the major range killer in EVs, a lower and slipperier hatchback and especially saloon (or sedan for those of us here in the States) just makes sense over a large boxy SUV with the aerodynamics of a barn door. And if Kia and the other manufacturers offered towing packages that were fully designed in and factory installed, then the lack of interior cargo space isn't so much an issue since a small utility trailer can add far more cargo hauling capability than the interior cargo capacity of even the biggest draggiest SUV. 

When in Sweden in 2011 I noticed that nearly every car was a saloon with a fewer number of hatchbacks and nearly every car had a trailer hitch. To go along with this just about every petrol station had 4 or 5 small trailers for rent. With this infrastructure, there is little need to make larger cargo capacity a permanent part of the vehicle resulting in a steep efficiency penalty every time you drive the vehicle in order to have that extra interior cargo capacity for the small percentage of trips where it is actually needed. Instead when you need to get a new mega sized television home or many bags of soil and plants to remake a corner of the garden, the Swedes just pop over to the local petrol station and rent one of their trailers for a couple of hours.

Of course the cost of having your own trailer is modest if you have space to store it. I have even seen trailers that fold up and store vertically against the wall of the garage (either inside or outside with a weather cover). The size when folded is only about 45 cm deep with the width and height of about 1.5 m. When unfolded they have a bed of about 1.2 x 2.4 meters

You are better off getting a decent push-bike with a good group set and use the gears up the hills. The new bikes are so light, that peddling is a doddle. If you are looking for a way back into cycling and you are maybe older and need a city bike with some EV range, perhaps. All-in-all though, you will save more money and get more exercise with a normal bike. They're more of a fad. I sold mine in the end and wouldn't buy one again. Now if a really lightweight battery came to market with really good density and a really lightweight motor printed in 3D carbon-fibre came to be, then maybe, just maybe I'd look again.

I wouldn't consider anything other than an e-bike with a bottom bracket (ie. mid-drive) motor (ie. Bosch, Shimano, Impulse), not a hub motor. The mid-drive motors are always operating in their peak torque range which is especially good with slow climbs, whereas hub motors are hopeless at the slow end. Mid-drive motors also allow you to have a proper hub gearbox in the rear & a full chain case, rather than a messy derailleur setup. The former is far better for an all-round transport bicycle, using normal clothes, etc. It also reduces maintenance a LOT.

I wrote to Cambridge Council with an idea I called "City Link" which is a form of multi-model transport, combining two forms of transport to complete one journey. By adding special quick loading bike trailers to busses and creating special point to point bus (link) routes for them, commuters could cycle 2-3 miles to a city-link station from home, then 2-3 miles to work after getting off the city-link bus. Yay, nice to see e-bikes getting some attention in the UK (they are totally normal in many parts of Europe). When not in "lock down" I would cycle 30-40km per day on mine, barely slower than the train (in terms of door-to-door time).

My recommendation for beginners is (a) always test ride the bikes over a couple of km including a hill or two (b) consider choices like "chain vs belt" or "center vs wheel motor" carefully (there's a bunch of trade-offs there as regards maintenance and ease of use). Since e-bikes are a bit of an investment, don't make a quick decision and make sure you get what works for you.

When riding on roads, also be very aware that pedestrians and other road users will not expect a bicycle to be going at that speed (up to 30mph for my bike), so be extra careful of things like people waiting to cross, or cars waiting to pull out from junctions.

My bike is currently a Kalkhoff Integrale (no idea if that's available in the UK). It's a belt drive with hub gearing (so no oil or chain maintenance) and a centered motor at the pedals (so I get the benefit of gearing for hills, and a more balanced weight distribution). It has a range of 110km (70 miles) which means no range anxiety. However it doesn't do regenerative braking, which is a minor negative on super long, hilly rides. Not cheap, but since I've never owned a car, it's great for mid-distance riding.

I must admit I'm amazed at the vitriol being poured on Swytch in these comments. Firstly on the "...you can get a complete ebike for less..." comments, I'm sure you can but you're going to get a gas-pipe framed bike. If you need to spend at least £500 to get a half-decent quality bike, how exactly are you going to get the same but with an electric motor and Li-Ion battery for the same price? With a kit you can take your quality bike and update it to electric (and back again) for the same price as your gas-pipe monstrosity.

As to alternative kits you may be right, but the sort of price I'm seeing at a cursory look is around £6-700 for an (illegal) 500W motor and 500Wh battery. Now I don't know what your experience is of cheap Chinese Li-Ion batteries is, but mine certainly isn't good. Quality batteries are expensive and if  Swytch provide a reasonable warranty on theirs it will certainly be worth paying £100 or so more for something that lasts.

The point I'm making is that it's horses for courses. You want the absolute cheapest kit, go to eBay. If you want something that might be rather higher quality then you might consider Swytch. Be reasonable guys!

A lot of Ebikes are built like this with the motor in the hub but that approach means you cannot use gears to allow a trade-off between speed and hill-climbing ability. Any cyclist will know that life is easier when climbing an incline if you change to a lower gear. To allow the Ebike to provide more "help" on hills you need a mid-mounted motor that assists the pedal crank which feeds effort through the gear system to the wheel and this approach is recommended for you in hilly areas. Also, the UK legal limit for Ebikes is 250w before you have to fit a number plate and register your bike as a moped. Almost all cheaper imported conversion kits provide options with higher output motors if you are prepared to flout the law and 750w is common -  3 times the power of this conversion kit.

I paid 800€ for my first ebike with a 250W hub motor and a 557Wh battery (brandnew) 4 years ago. What we see here is an ultra cheap conversion kit, that you can buy everywhere at ebay or Amazon but those offerings incl. a more than 500Wh battery and a display for under 600€. To pay a 1000 bucks for this, is bullsh*t. They don't have it in stock and you should preorder and wait 12weeks? Just go and buy it somewhere else. 

Second thing, a 250W hubmotor with a peak performance of 400-500W is not enough, to get you up on every hill - just look at Robert. If you're not that lightweight, dont buy a hubmotor, go for a mid drive. You can climb even alpine roads with a 250W mid drive, but not with a hubmotor. Even some smaller hills can be the end of your journey. 

Why you should not buy a 250Wh battery? Just because it is too small to last. Like in every car the capacity will shrink down to 80% within some years. This battery is enough for maybe 25-30km so it will shrink down to 20-24km and when you need the peak power from an older battery, a small batterie will break down like your smartphone when it gets old. So get everything from 500Wh upwards and you will be future proof, or buy cheap small shit that gets hazardous waste within some years. 

And just one safety thing, hubmotors in the frontwheel are the most dangerous position for a motor. This is not like you would think with cars. When the surface gets slippy and you drive with a motor in the front into a corner, your chances are very high that your front wheel loses tracktion and you get wheelspin with the high chance to taste the tarmac.

E-bikes only make sense if you've never ridden a proper bike. My advice to anyone willing to shell out stupid money on an e-bike or a conversion is to first ride a proper bike for a couple of weeks.

I'm asthmatic, have a herniated disc and knees that barely hold together but I ride a proper good bike and because of that I fly past all e-bikes. Even up most long steep hills such as the one shown in this video. Truth is that if you use your bike for commuting several times a week you will soon get fit enough that you will be faster and happier with a proper bike.

A proper bike weighs less than 9 kilos and have low rotational mass. That last point is very important. Even expensive bikes usually come with stupidly heavy wheels and tires that completely ruin the ride. You want a bike that's easy to get up to speed because once you're rolling it's also easy to maintain that speed.
Having slim clothes also helps massively if you want to maintain a high average speed. A slim body is easily achieved if you commute on a proper bike so you will feel right at home in those slim clothes in no time.

I wouldn't touch any bike you can't change the saddle on with a sh*tty stick, having checked on their website though and it turns out you can change the saddle - but you need to swap out the seatpost to a conventional one.
Great video. Please if you can, test the specialized turbo vado sl 5.0 eq. Thanks

Great review, well presented. I am 4 months into riding an Electrified S2 and really enjoying it for my commute as I can ride in ready to go without shower/changing.  Re. The accessories (pannier rack, splash guards) I bought  mine from VanMoof afterwards and fitted myself without issue, so no need to order with the bike. Also it is possible to swap the seat and pedals...see the VanMoof support site.

Interesting as the tech is, I would like to see the opposite end of the scale: can e-bikes be stripped down to a level of simplicity where it will only cost a few hundred dollars? Is there gadgetry that can be discarded, more basic bike builds that can be used, etc? I want to see dirt cheap, very simple e-bikes in KMart, Target, and so on.
Best of both worlds (assisted & non-assisted): Pendix
Helen absolutely nailed it. Brilliant!
So van Moof is the Apple or AOL of ebikes. You are stuck within their walled garden. The idea that you are stuck within the range of accessories that they offer (down to the saddle) is a dealbreaker.

I use my electric bike mostly for distance. Where I life there are some hills but most of it is flat lands. So besides a little bridge over some water you really don't require climbing support. 
But I tell you, an electric bike will get you from A to B, against the wind, in the rain. And you'll be decently okay! 
The bike I have is mid drive so yeah, slightly more expensive in ways, and designed to get you up to speed and keep you at certain speeds. That is where the motor likes to be!
Cost wise my e bike will cost me about 200-250 euro a year, there is after all upkeep, repairs done by the shop [don't worry I have a warrantee package in what some of it already is paid for] and in the end, yes the battery! That battery will have to be replaced at a point!
It's good to see the Legalities Explained at 2:45 there are far too many unregistered electric motorcycles on our roads already..

I'm intrigued by the saddle problem. Why exactly can the owner not just buy a wider saddle and fit that as they would to a non-E-bike ?  It's not just ladies that have a problem with narrow bike saddles, it took me awhile to find a nice wide, soft and comfortable saddle for my male human powered push bike.

Looking at your riding position and leg extension, I’d suggest your saddle was too high which would have caused more saddle discomfort than would have been expected from the wide, supportive saddle Van Moof use.

I've had an ebike for years mine are built from ebike kit's to meet my needs, I live in London and would never go back to daily commuting on a normal bike, like one of the other comments I'd wouldn't buy a ebike that I couldn't remove the battery especially in very cold weather and to would let the battery get up to room temperature before charging, ebikes are a great way to get from a to b and I'm looking forward to when the energy density and cycle life of batteries improves so I can go on longer ride's with out the need to carry a spare battery, looking forward for the cargo bike video, fully charged why not have a chat with John from velo-ads proper dapper chap from London who does some great reviews on bikes
Do one for OAP's that don't use smart phones please.
10 times better than any of the car reviews

I think electric bikes are an amazing device and will definitely replace many shorter car journey's . I do, however think that the legislation is a little too restrictive though, in terms of power output and top speed and if they allowed bikes of say 500w and 25mph, think of how many thousands of additional daily commutes would suddenly become viable on a bike.

Good review, I had looked at the Van Moof 3 but after many reviews pointed out that although you can take it to 15mph if you try to go faster under your own steam the bike seems to hold you back making this increase almost impossible. I cycle a normal mountain bike and can easily get into the high 20mph range so was concerned that the benefits of this motor could be negated by this hold back other reviewers have commented on.

There are terrible reviews about vanmoofs customer Support out there. Bikes have random errors and vanmoof is unable  to repair them and charges customers high prices for the repair if something happens out of warranty. Consider this before buying.

All very nice with the high tech bikes. Here in Denmark, most people ride a more traditional style cycle. They are dressed for their destination, not the journey. Maybe show a few of these electric bikes, they are comfortable, easy to ride and very efficient. The Co-op in Denmark has a couple of e-bikes (Mustang-SCO) in the lower price range 500-650. Batavas, Kildemoes, Winther are available for a slightly higher price. I have a Batavas which reeks of high quality (still have my old Batavas bought 18 years ago and done really good mileage). Have a look at what the Dutch and the Danes are riding.
Absolutely brilliant video. I love your delivery, Helen. So composed and professional whilst also friendly and compelling. Also, such a level headed review. Wonderful!

I don't understand electric bikes as a way to exercise. If you are commuting on one great, but isn't exercise about challenging yourself? The problem that I have found as a walker, is that people on electric bikes use all the speed they can at every time. So you have people going way to fast that have little control, even to the point where they are way out of control on shared walking and bike paths.
You might want to check out the Cowboy Ebike. It's made by another European company and it's incredible.
Well I'd rather buy a nice little car and sit in traffic with the heater on CD playing and dry, watching ebikers struggling against the wind and rain for 4000k..... good presentation thou.
Amazed there didn’t seem to be any mention of the bikes party piece... the turbo button. Helps me getting away from traffic lights by pulling all the motors power at once. It’s also a bit addictive.

Superb review. More excellent content from FC. Maybe it’s not perfect, but the v3 really looks like one of the best around atm. I love the look. I assume you must be able to swap the saddle for one you prefer?
I thought you are not allowed to ride the bike on pavement
Excellent review as usual
At that price point would an option to select the saddle geometry best suited to the purchaser have been so difficult?
Thank you for a very straight forward, unhyped review

She said they are getting better.. Of course they are and as they getting better they getting more expensive and they are already far too pricey now!   £1000 upwards.. They can stick that.  The only people whom really are buying these rip off's are the very lazy fat rich buggers who think £1000 upwards for a bicycle which can do most of the hard pedaling for them is a cheap price since they can throw money at any problem Unlike the rest of us who can't.  I have a normal mountain bicycle and it is only my 4th bicycle in my over 52 years of cycling. And I use also now a trailer. I can't afford to spend £1000 upwards on one item. my whole system cost me only £200 Far better than over a £1000.  E-Bikes are only for the lazy rich or rich media lovers who wish to brag.
Nice long advert for the Apple of Ebikes

This has really made me think about investing in a Van Moof. Thanks :)
The price tag is a little scary if I don't use it enough, but certainly cheaper than a 2nd car for our household.

As an x3 owner the range is great for my wife to use it... whereas me and my heft struggle for range... 28km ride, liberal use of boost and hills took 73% of battery. 

It’s probably down to how you use the boost and what speed you sit at.

Strange that they don't allow replacement saddles.

Because, sure, for the other stuff, you can see why, as they're integrating the circuitry, battery, motors and such into the frame. But, for the saddle, it just sits atop the frame and I can't really see why you wouldn't allow for it to be removed and replaced, as it doesn't really make a sodding bit of difference to the rest of the bike and its operation.

Also, at 13:15, that dude behind you is totally checking you out. Just saying.
Excellent review, more like this please. I'm more likely to be in the market for a new e-bike than an expensive new e-car. Stick with km, we're in the 21st century after all.
In my town it is clearly the old lady brigade that made ebikes visible. Constantly getting overtaken by wee 70+ year old ladies on the hilly streets
Id prefer a 1000w from alibaba and set a 15mph and 30mph limiter.
Not sure it would take my gigantic frame. Sad really- seems like a great idea to get fit.

I got a second hand ebike with dead battery. Replaced all the control electrinics with a kit, made my own battery, and hooked it up to the motor that was still good. less than 300 euro, and a few hiurs work! after a year, still very much enjoying my ebike. And if the battery runs dead in a few years, I can replace it for 100 euros.
Much cheaper than replacing the branded battery that is very expensive. 600 euro!
Really professional review, great uploaded
Looks like you were in Kingston! :D
For 3000£ there are a lot of great motorcycles. So... what's the point of a ebicycle?
Good you like the bike. Here in Holland they peddel alot
Until e-bikes have a realistic price point (sub £500) they will just be the plaything of people who shop at Waitrose.
I wish the assist wasn't limited to 15mph. There should be a road mode and a pedestrian route mode, so when you're on busy roads you're assisted up to at least 30.
We're in UK! Miles not km plz!
In S.E.A almost all E-Bikes are prohibitively expensive and out of reach for most of us who could really use this tech....go figure?..

LIKE if you'd like to see more e-bikes, less cars & SHARE if you know someone that you'd like to get into cycling!

E-bikes are no passing phase. We asked Helen to investigate and gave her one of the slick Van Moof S3 electric bikes to help her along the way. The brand new Van Moof S3 has a minimalistic, but clever, design with everything integrated into the frame. It comes with some swanky features and is bursting with cool tech, but what will Helen think when she takes it for a ride around the streets, and up one of the most challenging climbs in the Surrey Hills?

*Timestamps*
00:00 The Rise of E-Bikes
02:31 History of the Humble Bicycle
02:46 What is an E-Bike?
03:21 Cycling in a Post-Pandemic World
05:14 The Van Moof S3
05:45 Swanky Modes
07:13 Bike Hunters 
08:21 Time for a Ride
09:21 What's the but?
11:19 Helen's Hill Challenge
12:59 Not out of Breath!
13:44 In Summary
15:00 Helping People Enjoy Cycling
15:42 A Developing Technology
16:50 No Threat to Conventional Cycling

From a Dutch perspective I would say getting up hills is not the main reason to go for an e-bike.  ;-)
Here, cycling is just a part of life and not necessarily a hobby or a sport. It's just the most convenient way to commute. And an E-bike, regardless of your age or stamina, makes it even more convenient.

Very much appreciate the comment that "e-bikes are a replacement for cars, not a threat to pedal bikes". It gives them a better context. I'm not a cyclist and TBH hate the idea, but I want a potential commuting alternative even to public transport. Who knows, an e-bike introduction could get me fit and experienced *enough* to then explore cycling proper, but until then, I need some confidence that I will actually make it into the office in a fit state! Thanks Helen

The non-removable battery is kind of a dealbreaker on this one though. I've had an e-bike for about three  years now that I use during the winter season. I have no possibility to charge it where I park it, and there's usually subzero temperatures there, which aren't good either when charging it. I usually bring the battery indoors and let it sit for a couple of hours first to let it reach room temperature before charging. 
 I have studded tires on it, which makes it even heavier, so thats when the helper motor really is convenient. The weight of it also make it push down through slush and such, giving it better grip than a conventional bicycle.

Good review peppered with lots of legitimate concerns about the bike.
Good to see the strengths of eBikes prioritised.
The future is here.
Thanks Helen.

LIKE if you're excited by Electric Motorbikes & SHARE if you want to see more electric two-wheelers. See description below...

Fast, light and fun. We sent Andy Torbet to Stockholm to try out the beautifully designed Kalk OR, the flagship electric motorbike from innovative company CAKE. As this comes in both an off road and street legal version, we thought it only fair that Andy try out both versions!  Sitting somewhere between an electric bike and an electric motorbike, these bikes are built from scratch to make them powerful but also light in weight and can run for 3 hours on one charge. With 6 models of bikes now available, CAKE are definitely a company to watch...

Head to CAKE's website for more info: https://ridecake.com/

I've no great interest in e-bikes (or modern life in general), but I watched the video to see how far EVs might have progressed since my last Elli-rant appeared in the corner of a Fully Charged Comment section. Look away now if you're easily bored.

It turns out that things haven't progressed very far, really. Quel surprise. It's those darned Lithium batteries again, isn't it. Lithium technology is rubbish. Try again in 70 years.

Cake? As in: have it and eat it, too? Guys, it's cool, but then so is a surfboard. Surfing's a great leisure activity, but that's about it.

Market-wise I think this idea nestles in the same sort of place as one of those absurd enclosed recumbent e-trike-cars that has a tiny pedal-assisted motor and costs between £25,000 and £46,000 (yes, really). Very chic. This bike is neat and tidy and modern. But impractical. It's like an off-road surfboard. Or an on-road skateboard.

So... it's another toy for the boys. Yay. Earnestly and lovingly developed, yes; carefully detailed, yes; but still a toy. Load it up with racks and panniers and you've got a short-ish range, underpowered e-bike (without pedals) wilting under the weight of umpteen bags of flour and spuds and sacks of rice and four-dozen tins of kidney beans. So... not exactly a practical mule/ workhorse. An electric wheelbarrow would do a better job. But this is certainly a cool toy. 

There's nothing wrong with making toys. People should be free to buy, rent, hire, or lease Segways or fancy EVs or whatever they please with their hard-earned second mortgages - but I've still yet to see any cheap alternatives to these stylish 'premium' products, whether on two wheels, three wheels, or four.

Angry traditional bikers will hate everything about the Cake because it's not an angry off-road angry bike that lets them be angry bikers (angrily), and angry TT riders will hate it because its gentle image emasculates their high-octane (angry) machismo.

Fully Charged viewers who are also (angry) bikers will hate the fact that Andy didn't smash it to bits to expose its many flaws and prove that he was an experienced ex-World Champion angry off-roader trials rider, and everyone else will ask, "Was this trip really necessary?"

Clive Sinclair might have made something less cool, more accessible, and a bit cheaper (by using stock parts), and the Chinese would have made something even less cool, even more accessible, and for only 1/8 the price, but it would have been assembled by malnourished baby pandas in secret government 'Correctional Facilities'.

I spend far too much time whining about the expense of EVs on Fully Charged, so I'll shut up now.

But wait. Um...  mentioning Apple at the end was a mistake, Andy.  ;-)

It might have been meant as a compliment, but some of us loathe all-things Mac - including those smug people who love all-things Mac.

Ooh, look: Cake! More lovely, aspirational, shiny, overpriced futuristic products for rich people! So... this bike's all about cachet, snob value, scum-shaming, Trumphole bragging rights, over-specced 'added value' features, badge awareness, and HUGE profits, eh?
