Here’s why renewable energy such as solar panels with battery back up is a fantasy.
When Crossrail opens fully in London the new class 345 Bombardier trains will be 12 carriages long and carry 1500 people. There will be 24 an hour at peak times running in each direction amounting to around 200 journeys over say 4 hours of peak journey time and another 14 hours at a reduced rate amounting to say 600 journeys over the 60 mile track per day. To move that train down a mile of track would need a battery the size of a garden shed. It would make more sense to have the battery at the trackside than to transport it down the track. Therefore there would need to be 600 garden shed sized batteries along each mile of track to provide power for the days journeys. Now imagine the size of the solar array you would need to charge all those batteries. Bear in mind that on a foggy winters day in London there won’t be any power generation so you probably need back up batteries to cover at least 7 days of inclement weather which would not be unusual in London. So now you have 4200 garden shed sized batteries per mile of track at say £50,000 each and where are you going to put the solar array which is also now 7 times bigger. There are thousands of train journeys per day across London and many thousands more across the rest of the country. Now you can imagine that your solar array is much bigger than the city itself and that’s just for the trains. Someone could fine tune my rough calculations but I think I can rest my case.

There are MANY comments here about price, IE that it is too high compared to a mass-produced high volume bike.
Some things should perhaps be taken into account:
QUALITY: You can get relatively 'low' priced aftermarket motors, if you look around. From China. You get what you pay for: they may break down after a fairly low mileage, the 'support' does not speak English as a first language, and you will have to send it back to China for repair. (No, I am not talking about Bafang here).
The bikes themselves have to be more robust, as you have the weight of the motor, plus the weight of the battery, and then the massive increase in torque from a motor that can put strain on a frame in ways it was not designed for.
If you want a 'seamless' take-up of the drive, that feeds the power in smoothly, that comes at a cost. You can get a drive that gives lots of power, but as soon as you put pressure on the pedal, you take off like a jack rabbit! Life just might get quite exciting if that happens at the wrong time.
To repeat: You get what you pay for.

Helen heads to the London village of Barnes to find out how local independent shops are partnering with Ginger Town to use Tern e-cargo bikes for local deliveries. As more and more villages, towns and cities look for ways to reduce the number of vehicles on their streets, could the E-Cargo Bike offer the perfect solution to small scale cargo transport? These electro assist bikes might be small and nimble, but can also hold a fair amount of delivery stock and could be part of the answer to making high street shops more accessible.

One potential issue is simply the size of it, it'll take up the entire cycling lanes in a lot of places. That might not seem like a big issue in countries where commuting by bicycle isn't much of a thing but if these things were to block all commuting in places like Amsterdam, Copenhagen etc. they'd end up wanting them banned entirely from cycling paths.. And for good reason. Those kinds of cities are entirely dependent on people commuting by bicycles, it's way more useful for them (traffic wise, pollution wise etc) to have a large part of their commuting done by bicycle than to not have a (relatively) few delivery trucks in their city. There's far more people commuting than there are delivery trucks after all. Even the more "normal" cargo bikes are becoming a problem on cycling paths in several places, the cycling paths simply aren't designed for "unlimited" width of bicycles, they're designed around "normal" bicycle width.

I wonder if it'd be possible to up their speed a bit so they don't need the cycling paths at all, it's not like traffic in the center of larger cities tend to move all that fast anyway so it's not like they'd need to go 100 km/h or whatever to follow traffic around city centers.

The more I watch this video the more annoyed I become. 

I have always adored electric vehicles and am impatient for the full switch from combustion engines. 

But the pedalling part of this product is just enforced virtue signalling by proxy on the part of the company. 

You have the operators pedalling like trained monkeys instead of stepping on an accelerator or twisting a throttle. They designed it this way not for efficacy but in order to create the image of the load movement being part human assisted. 

That's bullshit. It works for bikes where the only added weight to the electric bikes is the human body so the pedalling part can contribute a significant portion of the energy needed. But with a van full of Ocado produce, the human pedalling will contribute only a very small percentage of the energy needed for transport. 

So instead of having the operator sit on a comfortable seat all day long and reserve their energy for humping the produce to the customer's door or perhaps even up several flights of stairs, they make them sit on a bike seat for eight to ten hours a day over miles and miles of rough road with very little suspension and have them pedalling like fools with almost no contribution to the range just so the company's product image can tickle the Flintstone hippy types and give it some faux credibility.

There is no reason at all why this can't just be an all electric vehicle

Almost zero consideration was given to aerodynamic drag.
First of all, it cuts a huge hole in the air, far bigger than it needs to.  Secondly, they could improve the shape to cut the air as it moves forward.  And finally, they could round the corners at the roof to help with crosswinds.  The old VW bus had a surprisingly low coefficient of drag, and a rig like this would be significantly improved if the designers took some ideas from the bus.

One other thing, this is the third electric assist velomobile I've seen that does not connect the rider's power output directly to the wheels.  That's the wrong direction to take, and I would never touch a vehicle with that design.  The operator needs to sense the amount of power needed for any given condition, and being directly connected in the power train gives him that sensitivity.  With that information, he can add the amount of extra electrical assist that he feels is needed.

With those comments, I think you can see that I give this a failing grade.
It may appeal to executives of major delivery corporations, but only for a while.  Those huge companies don't need some little manufacturer like this guy to build them such simple vehicles.  They'll buy a few, run them for a while, gather feedback from their drivers, and then they'll have better versions built buy a subdivision of their own. "50% of the costs are in the final mile of delivery".

We need to be really careful about what is being said here. There are a different costs involved with deliveries - environmental and economic (fuel, maintenance, labour) - and vehicles like this will only reduce some of them. And being smaller vehicles, may even increase others.

Whatever we are talking about, the costs are loaded towards the final mile. It takes fewer vehicles and drivers to move large lorries between depots. Having multiple smaller vehicles out doing the final mile (in order to get everything delivered in one day), spending a lot of time idling, pushes the environmental cost to the final mile. Having more vehicles and drivers push the economic costs to the final mile. And that's where we need to be careful - if you would need two or three of these to replace each traditional delivery van, and therefore need 2 or 3 times the staff, financially that's going to increase the costs.

Companies can have a desire to improve environmentally, but they still need to be price competitive. I've owned a Zero SR/F since Nov 2019 and have utterly loved it. Use it for my daily commute (30 miles each way) which is a mixture of urban and dual carriageway riding.
I've got charge points at work so I can charge there if needed although the SR/F easily gets me to work and back on a single charge even if I'm in sport mode the whole way.
A few things I've learned. 
1) For taller riders you can get a higher seat and also the SR/S footpegs fit the SR/F, these sit lower than the SR/F's which give you more legroom. I'm 6 foot (1m84cm) and I'd recommend those changes for anyone my height (or taller).
2) The best I've ever managed is 109 miles on a charge but that was ECO mode the whole time and very little over 50mph (80kmh) - realistically you're looking at between 70-90 miles.
3) I know Charlie recommended getting the extra charge tank for the SR/F but think hard about that option as the storage area is really really useful (which you lose if you add the charge tank). I can fit my charging cable, a bike lock, my pack lunch, and a thin waterproof top in there. Obviously the decision will be if you need the extra range the charge tank gives you but don't just add it by default if you're ordering one.
4) Zero should fit LED indicators by default on this bike. It's a + £20,000 cool futuristic bike and I'm still using old school bulbs in my turn signals!! You can buy LED indicators as an optional extra but I think they should be standard on a bike of this price level
5) The rear hugger is utterly useless. It needs to be longer as it does very little to protect the rear section of the bike. A longer one wouldn't look as cool but once you've owned it a few months and you realise how much dirt is getting flicked up you'd prefer a better hugger
6) I disagree with Charlie on throttle response, I find mine absolutely as smooth as silk. Sure, in Sport mode it is very responsive and if you're not ready it will really snap your head back but I haven't found it an issue at all. I will add that I haven't had the pleasure of riding a LiveWire so maybe that's smoother still?
7) Cruise control implementation on the SR/F is really poor. The button to activate and set cruise is on the right-hand side and just a littttle bit too far away so you have to streeetch your thumb to reach it. It's a small issue but I notice it daily as a section of my commute is average speed camera so cruise control is useful for those bits.
8) Traction control is really good on the SR/F. It has 100% saved me on two occasions when I was overzealous in slightly damp conditions. Without TC i would have certainly been in a hedge. 
9) Filtering is really easy, the low down weight makes it a doddle to handle at slow speeds as you thread through a traffic jam.
10) They're still too expensive. The LiveWire is still waaaay out of my reach and the SR/F was only just in reach after a lot of saving and tweaking of budgets. I hope they get cheaper soon as it is a true barrier to many riders.
11) I've had ICE bikes all my life (am 42 now) but when I test rode the SR/F I knew it was the bike for me. I love it. Even if you're not thinking of buying one I really recommend getting a test ride just to experience the torque and smoothness of power delivery.

A version of the Wuling mini, upgraded to EU safety standards, is being assembled in Lithuania by a company called Nikrob and branded as the Freze for the EU market. They advertise a price of 14,000 Euros. just over £12,000 at current exchange rates before import duty 10%, UK VAT 20% and registration  about £800. (around £16400)plus agent fees and delivery.

In response to an email I sent asking if they will be producing a version for the UK market or if a left hand drive version could be imported into the UK I got this reply.

"We can technically make a right-hand drive car - model. With a partner in England who can  invest money in buying of  cars, we could be refit  the steering wheel to the right side".

Sadly, to be available in the UK market will a) require a dealership prepared to import a volume of cars to justify the modification and b) require the car to be added to the UK government list of cars for which they are prepared to give the £2,500 ev grant. This is paid to the dealer to pass on to the customer. A bit opaque really as all listed cars could have their prices inflated by £2,500 prior to the deduction of the grant.

With the cheapest new ev on the road prices in the UK at around £28,000 upwards the Wuling/Freze L/H drive ev might still appeal to those happy to organise a one off import, find someone to service it and import spares if needed.

I personally wouldn't want a car like this because I do have some concerns about it. I think these cars are a great idea for city driving. I mean, in places like norway, these types of cars were a regular sight before those bigger electric cars came along. In my opinion it makes sense to buy an ev that has just enough energystorage for the amount of driving you'll actually do. So a small battery in a car that isn't going much futher than a few kilometers a day is perfect and doesn't use up unnecessary ressources. 

But I could imagine some downsides to this ev that aren't talked about in this review, first of all, it's a very small and simple built car so I think it will be classified as a light electric vehicle, meaning that the safety regulations won't be as strict but what I really don't like about this concept is that if it's "that" cheap, its probably something that looks good at first but deteriorates quite quickly and falls apart. Also since it's extremely cheap, people in richer countries will probably don't take it seriously, buy it for fun and dump it once it's "not so good anymore". I mean, do you really expect anyone to buy this afterwards? So it just ends up on the scrap yard and pollutes the environment whereas "regular" cars tend to keep their resale value better so they can be passed on to the next owner who would actually bother to repair it or have it repaired or have the battery serviced. 

As an example, I've seen super cheap electric scooters being imported from china shipped to Germany in huge numbers just because they're currently cool and hip among teens and kids and because they sell well. Once the owner looses interest it probably just ends up on the dump. While I agree that there should be cheap alternatives to our current big cars for those who just want to travel from point a to point b, I feel like there has to be a limit to how cheaply those cheaper alternatives are allowed to be produced at. Because at some point you "will" have to cut corners where you can't just eliminate stuff out of pragmatic reasons and instead reduce the quality of the parts used as well and with anything that is cheap here in richer countries, it's too cheap to repair so you'd just throw it on the dumpster and get a new one. That's not how I imagine a clean enviroment friendly future.

I've shared this video with other people, and I think I've spotted the flaw for the Western market.

It's too compact. Folks were talking about "bubble cars" and seeing it in that light, as it's so squashed up.

If they made a model where instead of the "back seats or boot space" conversion thing, it's slightly longer with permanent back seats and a proper boot.

It can still be a small city runabout car. Just more the proportions of a Mini. Just a metre or two longer for putting an actual boot space behind the back seats (and maybe making more leg room for those back seats - Westerners are generally taller, as you know from banging your head).

Yes, such a model would cost more. But if it's £3,400 like this, then even if it went up to £5,000 for a "proper length" version, that's still stupidly cheap and would sell like hot cakes.

But I think making it that "super compact" as they have might be a mistake, perception-wise, to a Western market. As I say, I shared this video and the responses were talking about "bubble cars" and being unsafe on the roads.

The first thing people see is its size and I fear this is instantly colouring perceptions. That it's "not a real car", a silly "concept car", comparisons to the bubble car, etc.

But make a Mini-esque version of this - so still small, but not super-compact - and then it'll get a good reception in the West.

I don't want to be the gremlin.  But I have had lots of three- wheel experience, and there are two good reasons to put the two wheels up front, as Solo, Aptera and Arcimoto have done, and Corbin did 20 years ago.

A trike with one wheel in the front is unstable going around turns, the faster the turn, the more unstable; if the brakes are applied, the harder the braking, the more unstable it is.  Turning and braking can be hazardous, even if the trike is leaning into the curve.

When braking in a straight line, there is only half as much rubber on the road, which increases any instability and likelihood of a skid, putting the trike out of control.  Even a toy trike like I had as a toddler had a tendency to tip when going around a corner.

Building complex, eye- catching, leaning hardware into the trike is not the answer: as Elon Musk says: "the best part is no part; the best process is no process".

Another problem with trikes with a single wheel up front is that you cannot use the front to judge how closely you can get to other vehicles and objects when trying to make a tight pass--- when you have two wheels up front, you don't need to look back to see if the rear end is making a safe clearing.

This is a bit of a disappointment, when you know about the Lynx Lean Electric, also called the Lynx e Carver. 

It was a project that started all the way back in 2011 that was set to deliver a next generation electric Carver with a top speed of 156 km/h and an estimated city range of around 150 km from a innovative 12kWh Lithium Manganese battery pack(no cobalt needed) that could be recharged from 0-100 % in 30 minutes on a 22 kW ChaDeMo charger or less than four hours with a European 230 volt 13 amp plug.

The price was significantly higher, at 35.995 Euro excl. VAT., however that was with a deluxe leather interior and a decent sound system. They got to develop most of it, however in 2014 the project hit a roadblock due to not being able to find investors and despite several attempts and postponed launches all the way to 2018 it newer came to market. 

The lack of investors willing to invest in EVs, because Tesla Motors showed that even the claimed market leader wasn't able to make a profit at the time, killed a lot of interesting projects. 

Lynx cars was an interesting company. Based in Denmark they started their business making electric bicycles, but knew from the start that the goal was to build electric cars and used the bicycles to develop technology needed to make a good electric car. In 2009 they launched their Lynx GT, an electric roadster capable of 0-60 Mph in less than 3 seconds due to a revolutionary Lithium Polymer battery design. The buyer could choose between a 16 kWh and a 32 kWh battery pack, with the last having a claimed range of up to 350 km(~220 miles). It was priced slightly lower than the Tesla Roadster of the time, which needed around 4 seconds to get from 0-60 Mph. It was also capable of charging faster than the Tesla. The issue was that it was a very limited production run, due to the fact that they were not able to get more than around 20 chassis from Opel(it was based on the Speedster).  
 

The idea was not to make performance sports cars, but instead to use the developed technology to build an EV for ordinary people. 
 
This lead to the development of the Lynx Nanoq, an electrified Geely Panda, that got a 22 kWh LiPo battery pack giving it a range of around 120 miles(200 km) and a top speed of 80 miles(130 kph) set to launch for the at the time, it was planned to go on sale for around US$38,000 in early 2010. The battery could be charged to 100 % with a European 230 volt 13 amp plug in six hours or charge to 80 % in around an hour on the Strömpil Public charger. The cooperation sadly did not result in any Lynx Nanoq being launched, but it does seem that Geely later did electrify the Panda with some success. 

After that disappointment Lynx ended up with the Lynx Lean project that they fought for but sadly had to drop due to lack of investors, and they seem to have dropped the idea of trying to launch EVs since. The battery tech developed did end up making them some money though.

A great insight - and shows how China didn’t just ‘accidentally’ become the manufactory of the world overnight for no reason.  It’s hard work and in some cases, hard labour.  However, on the positive side, even as people took the p!$$ out of the Japanese motorcycles in the 1980’s I knew that the British and American machines were now having a real competitor in the ‘big four’ as Yamaha, Honda, Kawasaki and Suzuki were known.  And the big four made motorcycles that same exact way, for maybe 3 decades.  1980 to 2010, no change really, except more valves became the norm, and big ‘adventure’ bikes became a thing.  From 2010 to now, the Japanese electronics and software-driven dials and traction control, have picked up, but if that was meant to stave off the electrification of motorcycles and scooters, it failed.

Now, the Chinese have come along, and after 15 years or so of people slagging off the Chinese bike-in-a-crate business, the Chinese are into territory that the Japanese were around 1980.  We will shift very quickly from being sceptical about Chinese quality, into being properly appreciative of that same quality - and Electric Vehicles turn out to be the thing that will usher China into the consciousness of the bulk of car-owners and drivers, and scooters and motorcycles.  In other words, is it fair to say, EVs are the catalyst that will assert Chinese strength and even prowess, in manufacturing worldwide?

This ‘big’ bike ridden at the end, looks like the 400 to 600cc equivalence.  A multi (usually 4-cylinder) of this size, is pretty heavy, and a compact single-cylinder can be quite light but ‘thumpy’, and you cannot see a thing out the mirrors at certain roadspeeds on a single-cylinder!  In ‘old money’ ie the tax system and licensing of riders, 400cc and a certain power is a demarcation line for example, so lots of 600cc bikes, had lower-capacity versions made for the Japanese market specifically, that were 400cc.  The obvious issue being, either the 400 was too heavy (think two disk brakes up front) or the 600 was too light (think skinny bendy front forks that ‘twist’ too much).

In other words, this bike is in the sweet spot.  Somewhere in the old size of a middleweight from say 250cc to 600cc, there is a ‘general purpose’ bike that will suit many people.  If it is the new electrically-propelled technology, it stands to reason it will last longer, and has a future.  Plus, you can start this thing at 2am without waking the neighbours/wife/cat/dog etc, which means that as often happens, wheeling it down the alley-way or path is not an issue any longer.  These are great times, strides are being made and I thank Fully Charged for bringing it to us, and I agree with other contributors that the presentation is a lot better now, but we were all happy to stick with it, unlike some shows, it’s not a personality cult!  Noticed the bigger bike uses a chain not an in-wheel or hub motor?  Perhaps hub motors are not quite fettled yet, for this power range and maybe there’s a smidgeon of marketing there too - it’s a REAL motorcycle, it’s got to have a chain, as it were?

Another great episode anyway and having a presenter in China is frankly, an obvious need in the world of EVs, so well done for not doing a UK Govt thing, of missing the flaming obvious and choosing a complex, twisted, and hardly-likely-to-work method instead (Coronavirus testing labs that never really worked and now we find they are often giving wrong results - I’m looking at you, because the government could have availed itself of many university labs and other private labs instead. It's an important message, but insulation of houses is *at least* as important. It's of course good that you can change the source of energy you use, but there should be as much focus on not needing energy.
In addition, insulating a house also reduces the need to cool it, as insulation not only shields the house from leaking heat, but also shields it from heat creeping in (when proper consideration is given to areas such as windows). I've seen many newer buildings in warmer countries, being built basically without insulation, but with lots of air conditioning. This needs to be as much of a focus as everything else! Insulation reduces the need for heating and cooling!
I know that most homes are not really candidates to becoming zero energy/passive, but you can do so much by insulating roofs, removing cold-bridges, and insulating/heating floors (warm feet, and an even heat, makes a room feel much more comfortable at lower temperatures), whenever possible.
Most heat pumps are also much more efficient, when they don't need to reach a high difference in temperature (delta T), therefore it's much less efficient to have centralized heating, such as radiators. In a house that's not well insulated, this also makes air-to-air heat pumps more efficient at heating a room to a comfortable temperature (as they actively circulate the air that it heats, and the transfer of heat is more direct), than installing earth-to-water heat, and using the heated water to heat through radiators. If a house is renovated and floor heating is added, then the earth-to-water heat will likely be more efficient.
These are all things that are really important to know/consider if one wants to renovate, or upgrade heating, or whatever the case may be, because by considering these things, you can balance your investment to get a more comfortable temperature, at much less energy input. 

So in stead of spending 100% of your budget on switching to an expensive heating solution, you could maybe save an additional 50% on heating, by investing less in the heating solution, and a large portion on insulating floors, adding in-floor-heating, and insulating roof, and spending a smaller amount on the heating source. Then down the line, you could replace windows to triple layer, and have a relatively energy efficient house.

I think the reason you are getting too much battery heat is that the internal resistance of the cells increases with age; 
and therefore when you increase current through the cells (during both charging and discharging) more heat is generated inside the cells.
Of course the BMS is programmed for new cells which heat up much slower, and can't detect the excess heat until it's too late. 
It would be interesting to repeat this test at a maximum of 100kmh because the much lower power draw, improved efficiency and less rapid gating may result in a similar trip time.

Just made a trip Riga - Zakopane (around 1100 km) with the classic Ioniq and it was flawless. I was scared of autobahn consumption and driving, but driving 120-130 kmh is pretty comfortable even with frequent charging stops. The main problem is polish charging infrastructure, which is not yet developed enough comparing to Baltic states. I think I would not notice that if I drove a car with a large battery, but driving my ioniq I could clearly see that sometimes there were situations where I could not get to the next charger if something goes wrong with the one that I was aiming for 💀 (luckily everything went perfect). For example, there is one 90 km gap between two chargers. And chargers are old 50 kw and with only one charging spot. Other than that, everything went perfect. I did not do 1100 km in one day - I stayed in Warsaw and then moved on to Krakow - Zakopane. It was my first really long trip with my ioniq in more than 2 years of ownership. Before that maximum I drove was 550 km. Thanks to this car, Bjorn to recommend it in his old videos and Polish people for the warm welcome! 😊

comments.Comment: I did the same thing a few years ago during a 1,600km summer road trip, I found the best thermal management was to drive at 90km/h and keep the A/C at max. The battery is too big of a thermal load for the A/C at any other speed from what I found

Another thing - driving 120 km/h drains battery = more energy to recharge = more time at the charger = more stops for recharging
On the other side, if we would have "non standard" driving at a speed below 110 km/h = less energy used = less energy to recharge = shorter stops/longer distances = fewer stops for recharging. 
I've driven my should for 240k km half Norway and Sweden around. It's works. 
And no need for the additional fan then.

Did the same on my ioniq 28, same results. Small note , charging at more than 90% gets really bad with that delta of temps because the bms try to equalize the cells but can't much with the temp
BTW Vacuum makes even better temperature insulation. Where no air is left, nothing can transfer heat 😃
Lessons from late 90s cpu over clocking and cooling coming to mind
Good idea to rent adapter. I was one of who bought first from china and I do not use it as the leaf is now second car and rarely used DC charging... I am going to offer it someone to use.

This was a good test. It might still be worth having another go to learn more, and you what your learning now.. how about
   • locating and targeting the hottest battery cells
   • venting the air outside when it leaves the battery - might also help with quieter running
   • trying with the Aircon on
   • checking the battery for degradation, even though it's new

40KWH Nissan Leaf 500km challenge please 😎
I had an 120a i3s and the charging curve was like a ninja 50kW to 90% before throttling.
e-Golf for the win😊

A CPU has thermal paste, but still uses air to cool the heatsink unless you have a water cooled system. The issues with the Soul seem to be that 1. the pack design doesn’t have good airflow to all cells so you get the big delta, and 2. if the battery fan is on 9 but the HVAC fan is on medium then it will suck in air from the cabin which is warmer. If you could fully seal the connection from HVAC to battery inlet and adjust the emergency box to use the same fan speed as the HVAC outlet you might improve this (and then it might be worth using AC as you’d get closer to 5 degrees at the inlet), but still wouldn’t fix the cell layout/airflow
Great series 👍
And the same question: why not a full fan speed on HVAC?
If you dropped your speed to 90km it may not overheat

I wonder if you had switched on AC the inlet temperature should be far lower than 15 degrees and since the cabin temperature (which the AC responds to) would hardly go down the AC will probably keep running full blast.
haha nothing change but it costs more. 😆
battery shape is probably bad too, those max temp cells are probably so bad positioned that everything you try has little to no effect...

the battery must be around 100 to 200kg. Air-cooling such a big block of mass... hm... is much more useless, than water cooling (also between the cells). Valdemar did a great job, good work of you booth for developing and testing 👍

Would it help putting the cabin fan speed to max (when feeding air into the battery), to get more air through the battery? Looks like you have set it to +15, but fan at step 5 of 8. Is it too noisy to run it at max?

The more tests I'm watching the more i understand that charging faster or driving way faster is not giving a good amount of faster travalling. Even weightreduction like in the i3 is not really doin a big difference (i.m.O.).
By watching the test, I thought there would be a way bigger time gap to the unmodified run. Maybe the two runs are not 100% compatible but I really thought it would turn out like 30 mins faster or so...really interesting.

You should definitely have tried at least one charging session with        
A/C running, just to see what would happen - increased loss from charging vs possible increased cooling.
Just to appreciate....it's good to see mjurson (sry for not knowing the right writing) again.
Leaf test with 5/12 or 6/12 battery? How it will do in reality. Feels like those are like 4 seater e-scoots at that point 🤔 And how quickly the battery would finally die from 6/12 bars (SOH not SOC)

The Chinese company making the adapters has recently lowered their 1000 unit price to below £400; however none of the European distributors has lowered their price.

I have spoken to the people making the CATL battery replacement kits for the Leaf, and sadly, they have no plans for a Soul kit right now; I am hoping that, by the time my battery starts degrading, they will have something on offer (holding steady at 96.8% SOH and 26.1 KWh useable).
Add an extra ventilator to remove hot air out of the trunk to outside the car 😊
Bmw i3 120 Ah next?

wasn't the cooling problem with the kias mainly related to the uneven heat extraction from the modules? increasing the capacity somewhat shouldnt really be expected to help much with that problem, also indicated in the video yesterday where the max temp of the battery did not go down as quickly as the min. liquid cooling and proper metal heat pipes in packs showed up for a reason...

Big difference in battery min-max temps, 35C-50C. Cells that are on the edge are cooling better, cells that are sandwiched in the middle does not get any cool air, need to transfer heat to adjacent cells first.
If the battery cooling exhaust is into the trunk, probably taking the floor out of the trunk would help a bit. The Ioniq has the exhaust outside the car, which is a better solution.
What about hooking up the ecoflow AC unit and pump cold air straight into the battery

comments.Comment: We've just bought an ID5 and have a new one on the way soon. Thank you for the video, so incredibly useful! Any other baby-related videos on the ID5 will be most welcome 😀
The ID.6 is great for these tasks. It's a more spacious version of the ID.4. We own one. It's superb.

I love it! You may need to add air to the tires though. https://www.youtube.com/post/UgkxCaFvSVryLTkivIF4hk3BmXD6n1GX8i8F  It was easy to assemble. I am 5’8 and the height of the handle is perfect for me. Great amount of storage underneath. Can’t beat the price and quality on tu is one. I bought it because I Liv in Florida. There is sand, grass and rocks all over. It was important for us to have wheels that is all terrain.
Thank you. It was in time for guests.
The trunk is way to small in my opinion. With that stroller there is no room for other things like suitcase or grocerys

Does it have heated backseats? Suppose you do not need that while you have kids in the baby seats but once they grow out of those and sit in the backseat it is a really good feature. Then when you have older kids with drivers license you often find yourself in the backseat, and then it becomes a mandatory feature, at least for us that live here up north :)
The ID.3 actually also has isofix in the front.
I thought you aren't supposed to have a baby in the front
“Always bring protection” - The guy putting baby things in a car 😂
I believe ID.4 also has isofix in th front. At least the Enyaq has it.

yeas this is exactly family type of car I am enjoying Enyaq iV 80 over a year now with two kids and never had an issue with the space so far also had all the gears and gadgets from Cybex great products as well.
Nice video. I still see no sensible reason to take this over the Enyaq, though.
I saw a video where some guys made a Frunk for ID4 from a recycle bin ^^

Hey. About the kick sensor just do one straight forward kick in the middle(like you would kick a football)step back and count to 3... don't wave your leg under multiple times it confuses it. Try next time works every time!
"It's soo easy! it's almost like stealing candy from a baby... Oh, that came out wrong!" 😂
I was watching that whilst hunting round for where the beeps were coming from. I thought I had left my freezer door open.

I am a decade+ out from needing this stuff (my youngest is 12), but it’s cool to see the advancements in baby transporting made in that time! 

But you gotta do full-on baby gear for a full test: diaper bags, portable bassinet, accoutrements (clothing changes, changing pad, breast pump, baby food [in cooler], toys, bottles, etc…). Plus do on the road in-car diaper changes, from simple diaper swap to full-on, bio haz-mat blow out, with complete wardrobe change and seat cleaning! A road trip with baby is never just the stroller. (Oh yeah and how about Mom and Dad’s gear, too?) Our car of choice back then with two babies was the Toyota Sienna minivan - minivan for the win!

Great fun watching these videos. Brings back a lot of memories!
Comparing price vs range and space and tech features and safety, I'd rather have a Tesla.
Husk at airbaggen kan løse ut og treffe babystolen. Isåfall må den kobles ut. Kanskje best i baksetet

Here is a very simple video on how to use the kick sensor. Basically, you just have to put your leg forward and the backward again, no left/right swing needed. This is actually the way it works on most of the cars that I know. So no Capoeira motion needed in most of the cars :D

Great review, Bjørn. How would you compare the backseat of id5 vs model y? Width? Is there more space in the middle seat in one of them?
'always bring protection' bit late now, mate..😁
Excellent review! Love the family with child viewpoint.
I have a Clek Foonf, and it fits really well in my ID4 in the back seat, which is a convertible seat.
I love this review category. Good work!
Great test for parents! Could you also do it for other cars? I did it before ordering an ID.3. And to my surprice all baby stuff fitted in the booth :-)
Boy, have those child seats changed since I had kids.
it’s illegal to mount a child seat in the front seat of the car in Australia.

I have a Passat GTE Estate, the reason I bought the car is that is has one of the largest boots in the hybrid market. I have a Emmaljunga stoller and lie flat seat in the back tied down on top of each other and I can still fit my 2 dogs in the back, Or I can take the wheels off and but the stroller behind the seat and have the more space in the boot. There needs to be more EV Wagons/Variant/Estates, they are smaller outside but just as big inside if not bigger

Wow - time changes....now we are back to compare cars how good and practical they are for your daily life, the fact that it's an EV doesn't matter anymore. Great review mate, all of these are so relevant at this stage of my life 😂 it's the only reason why I've got a model y on order, I need the space for a +1 arriving soon and to lug around the other half's 4 wheeled walker due to mobility issues

I just have a few small suggestion/requests for you if you plan on doing these kinds of vids for different cars in the future, which might be useful to us parents. For example, you could look at how much space maybe one or two different industry standard baby seats (both forward and backwards facing) take up in the back seats, e.g. to see if it is comfortable for a parent travelling in the back with kids when there is more than 1 baby seat. Another is to see what kind of leg space is available for both the driver and front seat passenger when the baby seats are in place are fully extended/tilted. For example, I spent many hours trying to find which toddler seat (up to ca. 4-6 years or 115 cm) would take up the least amount of space behind the driver seat, because I am quite tall with long legs, and need to push the driver seat almost all the way back to drive comfortably (this way my poor wife can sit on the other side beside the baby and still have OK leg room instead of being squeezed behind me). There were no decent youtube videos that talked about this kind of thing so I had to spend hours looking at ADAC reviews (in the end, I found that the Nuna Prym apparently took up less space than other baby seats, scoring high on 'ergonomics'). It still isn't ideal, as I can't push my driver seat as back as I wish I could (for a not so small crossover, the Model Y has disappointingly little leg room for tall drivers!), but it works OK. This kind of problem/question is probably not something an Asian ninja like you has to deal with, but tall followers like myself would appreciate it a lot! Keep on truckin!

The Model S is a great car. But then I may be a little biased. My 2016 85D has done 267,000 miles and is still a great drive. Firstly re the tyres I use the Hankooks iON Evo EV tyres. A rated for grip, A rated for efficiency, quieter than the Michelins and wear very well. I'm thinking of trying their new iON FlexClimate all season tyres, as I'm off back down to southern Italy next month, and you need winter tyres after 15th November in Italy. The wiper linkage is £155.00 from Tesla and comes complete with a new motor, but it's the spindles that wear, as I'm sure you already know. It's pretty straight forward to replace, once you have removed the frunk and surrounding panels. There are numerous YouTube videos on the subject, which will save you some time if you do the repair yourself. I don't know when the charge flaps closed themselves on the S but my year they don't close, it's manual. A long press on the section of the key where you double press for the tailgate opens the charge flap or the button on the supercharger connector, of cause. My car had the CCS upgrade when I bought it but I paid for the MCU2 upgrade myself. Which i feel has been worth the cost, especially on long European trips. Probably worth making sure the brakes are serviced, so they don't drag and reduce efficiency. And get the battery seal tested. By 6 to 8 years, they can start letting moisture in, which is the main cause of battery problems on the older S and X. If the battery seal is replaced, then the batteries are considered good for 600,000. I could keep waffling on, but enjoy the S, they are brilliant cars.

Interesting discussion, but doesn't really apply to me. I recently added my own solar. We have load shedding (6hrs on, 12hrs off) so I needed batteries too. Batteries are about half the cost (no labor because I did it myself). Although panel placement is important, and I could get more power by tilting them and placing them better, it makes more sense for me to just add a few more panels, as they are relatively cheap. Right now my problem is I get too much power and am throwing it away because I don't yet have enough batteries. That will change once I have more batteries and I will need more power in the summer (air conditioning will be most of my usage).

I installed my 13 panels 430 bifacial panels for £12.5k, heatable quote is £14,500, panels are oriented NW and SE, not ideal location but that is where my roof faces, I have a GivEnergy AIO battery plus inverter. In March I generated 688, whereas the guys got around 400KWh, I have a single inverter with a startup voltage of 80v, this is typical for an inverter not 200V as previously mentioned. I appreciate my location is further south, but the weather has been appalling. I would prefer since the guys have one of each panel, to do a side by side comparison rather than comparing two roofs at two different locations, with one using very cheap panels, you can get a bifacial panel for less than £90, . Any solar company worth their salt will give you the right advice for your location, and you will save yourself the best part of £2k. Heatable may not do the hard sell by knocking on doors but they make it sound like rocket science when there are also lots of disadvantages when using optimisers and locally installed inverters per panel, the more electronics the higher the risk of failure and installing a scaffold would wipe any suggested savings for years, whereas statistically failure rate of panels is extremely low, and while there is an argument that optimisers may give you a few extra watts, the cost and risk is probably not worth it unless you have major issues with shading

As a solar expert with 15 years of experience in installations, I have a 10.8kW system composed of 47 south-facing 13 year old panels with an efficiency of 15%. Here are some performance metrics:
- In March, the highest yield was on the 9th with 43kWh, compared to 24kWh on the 30th.
- In June, the peak yield was on the 29th with 56kWh, closely followed by 55kWh on the 22nd.
- The total yield for June was 1140kWh.
9.473 kWh per Watt for the Month of June.

As a matter of wording, electric cars often have 2 batteries. a main, and an auxiliary battery. The high voltage main battery to power the car down the road, the auxiliary is the 12 volt battery, used to power the windows, head lights, fans or anything that uses the normal 12 volts. A "Battery" is 2 or more CELLS in a series circuit, to provide a voltage higher than an individual cell. Both examples in this video are cells. It IS, however, proper to call a cell a "battery", if only one is necessary to provide the system voltage. A wall clock may use only one 1.5 volt alkaline 'AA' cell, therefore, its the clock's battery. A Cell phone usually runs on the 3.7 volt Lithium Ion cell, thus, it's the phone's battery.

I like the video as a whole. However, there are some minor ad some bigger issues. Firstly, what you are holding as 'your typical battery' is a non-rechargeable alkaline battery. MY typical battery is a 18650 Li-ion cell from Panasonic or a Li-po pack for a racing drone. The 18650 is exactly what is used in a Tesla car. A Panasonic one. They degrade more with time-temperature than they do with charge cycles.  Secondly, degradation is not only capacity but performance. Specifically, internal resistance goes up. That results in less maximum power and more heating of the battery, further degrading performance. And while I wish the data form model S were true, I am very skeptical. There are no failed batteries shown for one thing. Secondly, number of Teslas from early years is very small and they are mostly enthusiasts. We don't really know what happens after 10-15 years, especially in cold conditions. Also batteries don't degrade endlessly, they start to fail, cell by cell. And no, you can't just replace failed cells with new ones because they will not be matched properly. You have to make-buy a complete refurbished pack, but most of these will go into power walls. You really don't want to drive a car with unreliable packs without Tesla support. After battery goes, you either replace with new battery or scrap the car. The only question is, how long will they really last. More than 8 years, sure. 15 years? Not so sure. It is an expensive car to scrap after just 10 years. It is an open question. One important point needs making: The EV contains two main batteries. There is one traction battery. That battery is made from many cells. Each cell needs protecting by the BMS. So in terms of refurbishment just because of degradation over age, the battery is better off used as a stationary power station. Replacing individual cells will not increase the usable SOC that much. How ever, there are differences again (like you already said) between manufacturers. A Leaf uses series battery system with ~200 cells. If one fails, the battery is dead. In a Tesla, you have about 2000-2500 cells. They are arranged in both series (more voltage) and in parallel (more range, SOC). Now in a Tesla, you can actually "revive" some degraded batteries. This only applies to a small amount of cases, though. OTOH if you’d been holding up a Panasonic 18650B you could have said this is very similar to the individual cells in a Tesla Model S. Bottom line - the chemistries we are using in EVs, aren’t that different from the chemistry in your cell phone (less cobalt in cars) - sure you have better thermal and capacity management in a car than you do in a cell phone.. But all lithium ion cells are rated in cycles. You do a lot more cycles in your cell phone than most people would ever do in a car. You do a lot more cycles in a Nissan LEAF than you do in a Model S - which is the main reason that they degrade a lot faster. 30kWh pack v 85kWh pack. So to do the same number of K’s you’re doing at least twice as many cycles. Thermal management is important particularly in hot climates, but in the UK, unless you’re charging a lot below freezing or rapidgating frequently, it shouldn’t have a major impact. Panasonic 18650Bs are good for around 1500 cycles to 70% and Tesla claims they are on track to achieve twice that. Let’s say Tesla get around 7kms to the kWh. Semantics are important.  Most electric cars possess two batteries, not many.  A battery is a group of cells hooked together to provide power.  The two batteries in an electric car are the drive battery, which is many volts and lots of amps, and the instrumentation battery, which is simply a conventional 12 volt car battery with six cells.  No matter the size, there is only one drive battery which is comprised of however many cells it takes to provide the required amount of power.

7Kw chargers are not for everyone. Hmm lets assume the wiring is just fine. I use a 13A socket for 1 reason I get 50% cheaper electric. Now I'll set the scene before anyone runs off with EV night tariff advice. I charge my i3 once every 2 weeks as I don't drive more than 150 miles and it works fine. Therefore if I was on a EV tariff my volume electic consumption (house) would be much more than it should be. I also have a 2.2Kw Solar array that most clear days produces 1.6Kw which means the excess of around (1.3Kw) is available to be consumed by my Immersion heater via the SOLIC 200 or used to offset the charging of the car on a 2.4KW 10A charger.  So 10Amps gives 2.3Kw and less the 1.3kw means I am paying for only 1Kwh to charge the car a 56% discount. Now if I had a 7Kw home charger unless it was intelligent costing more it would push more than 2.3Kw meaning the % saving by augmenting with my solar would not be as beneficial. You may shout that intelligent EV chargers can export only the solar export into the car but for me that's not practical as the sun goes in and out the car will start and stop charging. But then there's the conflict of energy being grabbed by the SOLIC 200 which measures the export current and dumps ALL excess amps into the immersion heater. I am not sure an EV intelligent charger would cope well fighting the SOLIC for export amps. Summary I am happy to charge my 40Kwh battery when down to 75% for  approx 4 hours using half price electric. p.s I do have a 7Kw charger at my other house I drive 90 miles too for a fast charge to top up.  Using this method I get electric for the car at around 11p and free hot water meaning no use of GAS which has increased by almost 200%

The problem is the missing equation as a civilization as opposed to a singular driver thinking about themselves.. Where does the electricity come from? How does it operate? What is the electric grid dependant on? Where do all the materials for a Tesla/EV engine come from? What is the logistics of these things combined? Electric grids are dependant on other energy factors, infrastructure, logistics, transportation, labour, top-down managements etc etc.. all to give you one car to plug in.
If majority of a civilization is running on EVs, the electric grid becomes overloaded, thus energy output must be choked/throttled for conservation and costs. So all the individual drivers are now dependant on each other as a civilization that is dependant on that which allows the electric grid to function (see first paragraph).
It's a nice marketing scheme, but it's not logical and realistic for entire civilizations. This will lead to shrinking the oil/gas industries, which will lead to throttles on the electric grid, which will lead to people having less freedoms as they are dependant on the entirety of the system to support their individual travels/life styles.

I can add another dimension to this discussion - visiting from abroad. Some UK charge networks are actually unavailable to those of us visiting from abroad with an EV:
- Chargeplace Scotland and CYC require you to have a UK bank account, as they only accept payment via direct debit. Meaning you probably need to be a UK resident. CYC confirmed this via email. 
- The BP Pulse app is geofenced, so i at least can't install it in Norway. It's predecessor Polar Instant was available though. BP Chargemaster haven't replied to my email about this yet (after 2 weeks). 

Geniepoint is just unwelcoming: The Geniepoint App is also geofenced, but the support people tell me that i can use the webpage instead. Not really ideal. And why exactly do geniepoint have 2 different web domains anyway? (geniepoint.co.uk and evsolutions.engie.co.uk)

I would also recommend https://abetterrouteplanner.com/ in addition to zap map. It doesn't have the live data, but it does so excellent route planning and displays info for most public chargers (across europe) from level 2 up.

All companies only put points in areas of high population density, so there are large areas of the coast with little or no charge resource . If you then add to that the poor quality internet connection it pretty much comes to - Buy a Tesla or an hybrid. It is not worth the cost of commercial charging for a plug in hybrid as you only get 80% of a small distance capacity and the cost / connection charges are designed for full EV with higher ranges . So with a plug in hybrid charge at home or at your destination and forget the on route situation. Leave the chargers for the full EV's.

The 80/20 rule exists in lots of electrical items, in safety critical industries, like the nuclear industry, if incandescent bulbs were used a special circuit is used, off is 20% brightness and on is (you guessed it) 80% on. This 80/20 rule means that components are not running at extremes, heating and cooling, pulling larger start up currents etc. As a real world example, critical (or hard to access) incandescent bulbs, in an 80/20 circuit can last many many years, never "blowing" as they  never get the shock of a 0 to 100% power up. (Why use incandescent? Many years ago there was no choice, today they are still used in situations where a strobe effect of cheap LEDs or Fluorescents could be dangerous)

Hi Andy,  Interesting report, thank you.  Your recommendation regarding charge cycling when not in use doesn’t agree with what Nissan advise for the 30 kWh LEAF so as you’ve asked for comments for each EV model, I offer the following:

For my early 2017 30kWh LEAF, page EV-23 of the Owner’s Manual states:

To maximise the battery’s useful life, use the following driving and charging habits where possible:

* Recharge fully, from 10% or less to 100% using AC Normal Charge. (My comment for clarification: Normal charge is when plugged into a non-rapid charger such as at home).
* If the vehicle will not be used for an extended period of time allow the battery charge level to drop below 6 bars (My comment for clarification:  This equates to 50% charge or less) before parking and disconnect the charge cable.  Check the charge level every 3 months and recharge (if necessary) to maintain 2 bars minimum.   (My comment for clarification:  The bottom 2 bars are those in the red zine on the dashboard state if charge indicator).
* Avoid leaving the vehicle for over 14 days with a very low state of charge.
etc.

Note the 24 kWh LEAFs allowed the user to set a maximum charge limit of 80% even when slow or normal charging at home.  At the time, Nissan claimed this would reduce the rate of battery degradation, but when the 30 kWh LEAF was introduced with its improved battery technology, this feature was no longer provided.  My local Nissan dealer was unaware of this or the reason for the change so I e-mailed Nissan Customer Services to ask why.  They replied (eventually) to say that the feature was discontinued because analysis of data from a large number of LEAFs showed no benefit, and the recommendation as quoted above, to charge to 100%, was substituted instead.

Hope this helps, and keep up the good work.

The Tesla is unique in that you can configure the charge level of the traction battery. Most EVs display a virtual battery to the user, my BMW i3 included. When the i3 shows 100% charged, the traction battery is not at 100%, probably closer to 85-90%. This is because the battery management software prevents the traction battery from ever being fully charged, or fully depleted. In my i3 120Ah, this means the 42kWh traction battery, has about 37 to 39kWh of usable charge - this is hidden from the owner/user of the vehicle by the battery management system, which displays information about the virtual battery state of charge, not the 'real' battery. All of which means for us non-Tesla owners, charging to 100% as shown on the dashboard is perfectly safe for the long term health of your traction batteries.

I think that there is an issue that you have neglected to factor in your presentation. If I have a 400 mile journey and I'm driving an EV with 200 mile range, clearly I will need to recharge during the journey. If the publicly available chargers provide approximately 100 miles of range per 1 hour of charge (because in any random 400 mile route, there is very little chance of finding a 350Kwh charger), then to do that 400 mile journey, will require that the journey time will be increased by the essential recharge time - in this case, ... an additional 2 hours. Obviously that compares badly with the time it takes enough petrol / diesel into an ICE car to add 200 miles of range.

This possibly explains why the popular EV in the UK for business lease is the Tesla Mocdel 3 Long Range. It has a good range AND access to a network of well maintained, high performance public rechargers that minimise the recharge time.

If Tesla open up their recharger network to other EVs, that will (potentially) be useful ... but, unless the government intervenes to ensure that, before 2030, when all new ICE car sales will be banned, a high performance, affordable, well maintained network of chargers is installed, ... the only EVs that will be really useable for long trips will be Tesla.

There are some excellent EVs being launched now but if they are all doomed to the frankly appalling, mainly slow, often broken, mosaic of multiple charger networks, then  long distance travel in the UK for the general public will become increasingly problematic.

I would love for this prediction to be proved wrong ... but I'm not holding my breath.

Greetings from the U.S.  This is an interesting video on how vehicles are used, and yes, even in our large geographic area, daily uses are actually quite similar.  Now, I do agree that we don't need 600 plus mile range batteries.  Still, range is king for a few reasons.  First, you aren't cycling the battery through a charge cycle as often.  We have a 2012 LEAF, had a 2019 LEAF E+ (as it's called for other markets - ours was called the SL Plus as it was top trim) for a year, before just this last weekend trading it in on a 2020 Chevy Bolt Premier.  The LEAF in particular hates rapid charging cycles.  The Rapidgate issue in your markets underscores this.  Our 62kw model still suffered from rapidgate as it couldn't evaporate its heat, hence why it was replaced.  Outside of this, a larger battery means more time between charge cycles.  Every time you charge the battery on an EV, especially a DCFC, you "age" it a little more.  All batteries have a lifespan rated in the number of cycles.  The farther you travel between those charges, the longer your lifespan.  Even when I commute, I only charge when I need to, or in advance of a period of days off to allow for the freedom of get up and go as we see fit.  In effect, we're still using the extended range.  In comparison, our 2012 LEAF, has lost three of it's capacity bars.  It has only 48k miles on it.  This is of course due to Nissan's getting the chemistry wrong, and also due to the fact that the very short range, combined with heat, have caused them to degrade rapidly with their frequent cycling.  We're "OK" with this as it's used as a neighborhood car, while the 2019 LEAF (we actually bought it first) had distance duty.  Our Bolt now covers distance driving, and yes, we do regularly cover longer distances.  We also have a driving style that is allowing us to stretch the Bolt's range a little past the 300 mile mark, vs. the 259 it's rated for.  Finally, in the U.S. anyway, the infrastructure is pretty sketchy even in areas where it's shown to be pretty built up.  Added range in most cases allows us to choose stopping points where backup stations are available, due to the very real issue of broken charging stations - especially from Electrify America.  Finally, especially in the midwestern stretches of the U.S., the infrastructure in of itself is still quite limited.  Longer range allows for more of a buffer in the case of a DCFC station not functioning, forcing us to a L2 station to charge just enough to get to a working DCFC station, and to not push the limits altogether just as a matter of course given the distance between some of the stations (150 - 200 miles in a few cases).  Hopefully this helps with getting a feel of the mindset of wanting the bigger battery, vs. a smaller one. You're correct... mostly.  When I talk to people about range who have never driven an EV, they generally just extrapolate that their current car does 600km so they need an EV that does 600km.  They fail to understand that in an EV (which charges at home overnight) you're always starting out with your full range.  In a gas car you end up going out periodically to replenish your range.  Unless you've just filled up, at any given time your actual range is much lower.  HOWEVER, for those folks who do not have access to home charging, for whatever reason, this does not hold.  It no longer matters how much you drive per day, it matters how many days you can drive that car before you need to make a trip to somewhere to to recharge.  Yes, as infrastructure catches up this may change, but for now this is a valid reason why you may need more range. 

Towing is another.  For those people who tow on a regular basis, then you might as well chop your range by 75% and recalculate.

The final reason is not really a big concern in the UK, but in other areas of the world (like Canada) there are quite a few common drives though mountainous regions which see vehicles needing to cover hundreds of kms with no services (even gas) and half the time you're doing it in very cold temperatures along with the possibility of being stuck for hours in the middle of nowhere if a road is suddenly becomes impassible when you're on it due to weather or avalanche.  You need to be able to wait it out till they get that thing open, or have enough reserve capacity to follow a major detour.  Another example: Thousands of people work in the oil sands, north of Edmonton, they commute 6-9 hours (each way) every other weekend to see their families.  Are they stopping for breaks?  No.  In fact they do this drive after a full shift at 2x the posted speed limit wherever they can get away with it.  And no, it's in no way safe, there's a ton of accidents.  Regardless, this is still the use case.  Of course, I'm not trying to claim that this is the majority use case.  All I'm trying to get across is that this kind of thing is not as rare as EV boosters would like to imagine. 

At the end of the day, we need a range of ranges.  I have no problem if someone tells me that a car with 300 miles of range is more than sufficient for 80% of the population, in fact I could agree that a car with 200 miles of range is probably workable for nearly 80%, especially as infrastructure expands.  But I also don't think we should lose sight of the fact that we will need BEVs that have these crazy long ranges if we want to get more than that 80% of the population into them.

Sort of Correct...  the 240 mile number is roughly the median value and you don't really want to design (a system) for the median.  That would mean that half of the people wouldn't be satisfied.  This gets complicated when discussing cars.  Once you get about 200 miles of range, you've probably covered the daily needs for 99% (or more) of the people.  Nightly recharging at home (for those who can charge at home) essentially eliminates the whole refueling issue on a daily basis (A very nice feature of EVs).  So we are really only talking about longer "road" trips.  For most people this is only a few times a year, but something that is often desired and many people may not want to compromise the experience.  This requirement will vary from person to person.   For road trips, vehicle range doesn't need to be over 200 miles if you can "refuel" quickly (sub 5 minutes) and at will (locations to refuel are basically everywhere).   Many older, gas guzzling cars from the 1960s and 1970s barely exceeded 200 miles of range and there was little demand for longer range vehicles.  With EVs, refueling takes time and locations are not ubiquitous.  (I might argue that the number of locations is "getting there" but still has a way to go.) This means that for road trips you need to schedule your breaks in accordance with the EV's needs.  This ease of doing this is actually a function of range itself.  Longer range affords you more options as to when and where to stop, as well as how often.  For road trips, I would argue that a required stop every 5 hours hours (for vehicle requirements) is not a big restriction.  Even if the stop need be as long as 1 hour.  Stopping for human needs (biological reasons) requires similar frequency and duration so you are just coordinating your needs with that of the car.  It is still a restriction, just not a big one.  Reducing the refueling duration and increasing the number of refueling locations would help ease this restriction even more.  But... when producing/selling an EV, perception matters.  So, if customers feel that range is an issue, then it is an issue.  My sense is that with today's number/placement of L3 chargers, 400 miles of range will put customers "anxiety" at bay.  As customers gain experience with EVs I highly suspect that this 400 mile number will drop.  Probably to 300 miles.  Going forward, this requirement may be reduced further as L3 charging locations increase,and charging duration decreases.  Numbers like 600 miles of range are probably not needed for cars (at least not for range itself...  For cars like the Tesla Roadster, this 600 miles of range comes about because the battery needs to be large for power/performance reasons, so long range is really just a consequence of that).

Good points but this misses two important things.  First, you never charge to 100% or run down to 0% (for many reasons).  This means that you are likely to use a *maximum* of 70% of the battery capacity.  A car with a maximum range of 240 miles would have a usable range of around 170 miles (or even less in cold weather or running at high speed on a motorway).  This equates to a maximum of 2-3 hours driving. Secondly, a charging stop will be longer than a normal stop for most people given our awful charging network.  For me, minimum range is 350 miles for a usable, long-range EV.

Interesting point you are making, there is just a few details that I think need to be considered as well:
First let me start with saying that over here on mainland Europe where I live the average speed on a long drive (=outside the city driving) is somewhere around 60-65 mph realistically. I myself am a slow driver, and I get to that value as well. So the range I can make over time is a bit higher than what you are describing, but not much.
Here are the points I would make though:
1) When I drive long range with a patrol car I do stop every 3-5 hours approximately as well, you are right about that. The difference is though that I normally only stop for 10 minutes or so. That's enough time to refuel, take a leak and walk a few steps. With an EV, even if it's a Tesla and you have a Supercharger around, you need to stop much longer to "refuel". That extra time can be problematic, especially if you are traveling with children, and don't have nice places to stop. (Superchargers are not the best areas for children to play... At least the ones I visited so far...)
2) For me the main issue comes not with single drives, but with recharging options. I don't have any chance to recharge at home, and at least one of the places I go to for vacation doesn't offer any kind of power feed either. (In both cases I don't even have access to a household electric plug.) So having the extra range really is givng me flexibility on when I have to bring the car to a charging station. And especially in the vacation scenario, where I have a long drive to get there and still need to ensure that I have enough juice to do the local driving there + get back to the charging point on my way home is quite a challenge. My car does have quite a range, so I can manage, but it is cutting it sort of close.
3) And for the Tesla drivers around there is a third issue to consider: Battery usage without driving. Coming back to my vacation spot: I do not trust the people there, so I would like to use Sentry Mode while my car is parked. Using sentry mode for a week drains a lot of power from the battery. Combined with what I said above about charging stations in the area, this might not be possible to do... And that's a bummer...

Nice break down on EV range.  I agree most people would not need 600 mile range most of the time.  But there are some considerations that mean that it is probably a good idea to have some available long range EV options:
1. The "Audi driver" issue you mentioned.  We need to maximise the number of petrol/diesel car drivers who buy an EV as their next car to make a decent dent in greenhouse gas emissions.
2. Towing.  Towing a decent weight will halve the range of an EV.
3. Uphill driving.  This significantly reduces range.
4. Cold weather.  Again, significantly reduces range.  
5. Charging infrastructure. This might be fine in the UK, but I live in Australia and other than the east coast and a small range around Perth, there are no rapid chargers.  If I want to drive anywhere else, range will be king.  
6. Autopilot. This greatly reduces driver fatigue and should make long driving stretches safer.  
7. Performance.  Having a bigger battery means not only longer range but also better performance.  As a Model 3 Performance owner, I can tell you that the enjoyment of a highly performing car does not get old.

Let's be real: this tendency to make excuses for EVs and telling people they don't need what they think they need needs to stop. No, not everybody *needs* huge range or charging speeds most of the time, but there *are* benefits for them, and there *are* people who do need these capabilities. As for long-distance nonstop driving, that will be moot once we have autonomy, but in the mean time the driver assistance features along with the inherent quietness and smoothness of EVs makes them much less tiring to drive long distance than any ICE vehicle. And it only takes one life-or-death race for time to make that range a necessity rather than a perk.

You can make all the excuses you want, but ultimately EVs have to be just as convenient to use as ICE for people to willingly switch, and that means huge batteries and long range.

You made a good point, and i largely agree, however there are nuances and caveats.
I drive a LEAF30. Its range sucks. My commute is almost all motorway, circa 40miles each way. A good day i sit with the cruise on at 70 for a good chunk of it, and it takes about 45mins. A more typical day is more like an hour. So your average speed isnt far off either. On a good day, the LEAF can probably manage about 80miles. However my SOC when i arrive at work varies between low 30's and mid 50's depending on the weather and traffic density.
So that highlights the first point that you miss. An EV's range is drastically worse in cold wet weather. Living in Scotland this is quite common. My "80mile" EV turns into a "60mile" EV in winter.
Unlike ICE, the range vs speed curve for an EV is also upside down. By that, i mean long, high speed journeys in an EV tend to give poorer range than the mroe typical shorter around town and A-Road journeys, whereas with an ICE you usually get your best economy on a long drive.
Even on the days when my LEAF arrives at work on 50-55% SOC, i ALWAYS plug it in, theres zero chance i'm going to try that return journey with such a tight margin. And this also applies just the same with any other journey. You want some percentage at the bottom for "plan B" and once you've stopped once, you are only ever getting back to 80% or so. Thus your "250" mile EV, in Winter can only do 190miles, and you end up only using 80% of that between stops and now your range is down to 150miles. Again, this generally doesnt happen in an ICE. Your winter range in an ice is effectively the same, and you'll happily run it down to the fuel light because petrol stations are ubiquitous.
Then the part you completely missed out was the actual charging itself. A 250mile EV with a 50 or 60kwh pack, getting charged on a wheezing ecotricity unit spluttering out 35kw will take bloody eons to charge back up again. (and we'll completely ignore broken chargers here...) The charger could also be in use. So you drive your 3 or 4 hours, stop for lunch hoping to fill the car up while your there, and find someone else is taking an hour to fill up their car first... Your now potentially stuck at a service station for HOURS.
Further to that, when you arrive at wherever your going, there may or may not be charging facilities to enable you to fill the battery back up for the return trip. So now your starting your return journey on an empty battery...
All these things together, mean its quite easy to see why Mr Audi Driver, if given a 250mile EV, could actually end up quite pissed off by the end of a long trip, and could quite easily end up wanting more range.
Now, ofcourse, i do largely agree with your point, 600miles is excessive. I'd probably be quite happy with a 60kwh car like the eNiro personally. However i think its also important not to evangalise too much and gloss over the bad things. I find it quite annoying taking my leaf on journeys even around the 80mile range. Where we live, we have various friends and relatives that are all about 40 or so miles away. We do journeys of that length fairly often, and destination charging is almost never available, thus we end up needing to find a charger and top up. Usually thats fine, but theres been days where we've been fairly tight on time, left time in the schedule for charging, then turned up at a bunch of chargers to find a queue, or find someone thats just plugged in etc, and suddenly your having to mess about making alternative plans, and with two young kids, it can be quite frustrating at times. Its very tempting to just fire up the V8 instead!

Strictly speaking - only people who live at petrol stations could do a journey that uses an entire full tank. But in all seriousness- whereas an EV *can* start from home with a 100% full tank, an ICE *cannot* (unless your home is a petrol station). Most ICE drivers will typically start a journey with (on average) around half a tank, and expect to stop off sometime in the first 2 or 3 hours of the journey (not much beyond 150 miles) to top up and take a comfort break/snack (realistically a break that's going to take around 10 minutes, maybe even 15 mins). If you have young kids - it's going to be longer breaks more frequently.
Most EV drivers going on a long journey *will* start from home with a full "tank", and - with a Kona / Niro / Model 3 and similar - easily cover more than that 150  miles initial driving stage (if they want to). Subsequent stages of 2 to 3 hours are also possible in the newest EVs with a 20 minute charge, and soon this will be 15 minutes for road trip junkies. At this point, EVs will realistically be no less convenient for those (occasional, rare) long journeys than an ICE. And better in every other respect.
Having an ICE petrol tank that happens to enable a long range is not there as a optimized design feature, it's there as a side-effect of petrol's energy density AND to compensate for the driver's inability to refill the tank at home. It gives a couple of extra days of commute before that inevitable (and wallet draining) visit to the petrol station.  Small comfort.
