I completely agree with your assessment. Range anxiety certainly exists, but it is pretty much always self inflicted. I can think of 3 specific events over the past 3 years where I got real range anxiety.

I don't ever get range anxiety during my normal commute. All the EVs I've owned had plenty of range for daily commuting. My partner and I just opted for longer range EVs because we do take road trips quite often and don't want to own a separate commuter car and a road trip car. We instead have 2 cars that can easily do commuting and road trips with very little effort or concern required.
First was in my first electric car, a 2017 Kia Soul EV with the 27kwh battery. It had a best case range of about 100 miles, more like 90 in real world. I live at an apartment where we share a couple L2 chargers with the community (not only the apartment but also anyone who happens to drive by, they are put on the street near the apartment). The SOC was at about 50% since I hadn't charged the night before due to both chargers being occupied at the time I parked. So, about 45 miles of range on the GOM. I had about 35 miles of driving I needed to do, so I figured I'd have enough to do everything I needed and charge when I returned. Well, what I hadn't considered (this was only a few months after we first got the car) is that running the AC further reduces the range, as do the hills that are around my apartment. By the time I got back to the charger, it was in full turtle mode with a top speed of about 5 miles an hour. I basically coasted to the charger. At that point, there were no fast chargers anywhere around my apartment, but it was still a totally avoidable situation. Even just charging the car for an hour before I ran my errands would have totally avoided the problem.
2nd time was in my 2019 Chevy Bolt. Again, just recently got the car. It may actually have been my first long trip in it. I was driving a longer stretch on the local interstate and there is a gap of about 50 miles between fast chargers. As I was about to pass the fast charger, I had 70 miles on the GOM and 50 to get to the next charger, which was near my destination, so I skipped the fast charger and kept driving. Well, immediately after that charger, the terrain got hilly and curvy, which I knew but failed to take into account (again). I arrived at the fast charger with no range showing on the GOM and 3% SOC.
3rd time was actually when I was making a video that hasn't been released yet for my upcoming Youtube channel Wrenching Fool. In my 2020 Hyundai Kona EV, I was doing an efficiency test while while fully loaded to test the effect that weight has on efficiency. I got to the fast charger (an Electrify America location) with 33 miles left on the GOM, 12% SOC and all of the chargers were offline except one, which was being blocked by an e-tron that was unoccupied and apparently trying to charge to 100% (probably because it was free for them). There was another fast charge option, but Plugshare listed it as very unreliable. It was about 30 miles to the next major city which has lots of DCFC, but I was a little too close on range to be comfortable. I ended up having to wait about 20 minutes at the first charger before the e-tron owner came back out to their car (shortly after it hit 100%). To be clear, I wasn't out of options, there were plenty of L2 chargers around that I could have used and charged enough to make it to the next DCFC comfortably, it just would have taken longer.
Another instance that happened just recently was not so much range anxiety but more having to overplan my route due to lack of chargers. It was in my 2020 Hyundai Kona EV, and my partner and I wanted to make a trip to the beach. Unfortunately, up until just recently, there were absolutely no fast chargers anywhere on the Oregon coast. There has been one that just recently opened in May. The Kona has enough range for us to drive directly to the closest beach to us and back to the apartment on a single charge (there is a mountain range we have to go over to get there) but it does not have enough range to drive further north or south along the beach and still make it back. We wanted to make a few stops along the way, so in order to do that, we had to go a bit out of the way to make all the stops we wanted plus reroute to the fast charger. We made it there with like 15% in the battery and actually charged more than we needed while eating lunch, but if not for the extra planning and route modification to make it work, it would have been a problem. In Oregon, there are basically no fast chargers anywhere west of the main interstate (I-5).

comments.Comment: I just bought a used Nissan leaf. 8k so mine is really cheap.

Anyone buying a second hand EV, for the first time, will probably need to add on the cost of fitting a wall charger. £600 or more for a decent unit. Possibly well over £1,000 for a fast charging unit. Should such numbers be factored into your figures?
fantastic video and info

Thanks for sharing this information. Most informative. My daughter has just ordered a Tesla 3 on the same basis as you: she is spending £400 pm on fuel. Re depreciation. I've been looking at a 1 year old BMW i3 and the cheapest I've seen is £26k - say £25k after haggling. The purchase price was say £35k (list is £37k+), so £10k depreciation. In 3.5 years it could be £15k, maybe more as there are so many EVs now coming on the market with much better ranges and prices are falling. (e.g. ID.3 44kWh for an expected £27k list in 2021)
Using £15k depreciation and your other costs that means 32.3p/mile and not £13.8p/mile. 
For comparison I've had my Audi A2 for 15.5 years and have all the receipts. It's cost me 30.4p/mile over 77k miles and only a few minor things have gone wrong though I've changed most of the suspension to improve the ride (c£1,200).  My car is still worth £3k (agreed insurance valuation). Like a Tesla and i3 it is aluminium so does not rust and still looks good and modern. Removing the depreciation the cost is 20.1p/mile compared to your 4.1p/mile!!
Conclusion: the riskiest cost with an EV is depreciation, especially if one does below average mileage . The risks reduce with higher mileage as this spreads the depreciation and accrues the cheaper fuel/energy cost. However, higher long distance driving incurs higher costs of using rapid chargers.
As I'm doing less miles now, I don't expect to save with an EV but my next car *will* be an EV for environmental reasons.
I would love to own an electric vehicle, if I could charge at home I would own one, I can't guarantee a parking space

I bought a 2nd hand VW Golf around the same time I'm guessing you got the Leaf, and I've done around the same mileage, so I'm thinking I can probably do a like for like comparison on total costs.

Even if I take out insurance costs, the cost to fix a gearbox, and factor in things like doing the servicing myself, and discounts on diesel, the damage so far has been around £13,000 (£15,500, all in).  That's about half the cost of a new MG EV, on a car that had a sticker price of just over £5000.  The initial savings aren't long in being wiped out...
This guy is the most adorable host on the Internet. I love him!

Here in the USA, gas prices are a lot cheaper., and I'm in one of the cheapest states at $2.25 per US gallon. That would translate to about 48 pence per liter in UK terms. Even still, my Leaf costs almost exactly half as much in electricity compared to an average ICE car in gas for the same distance traveled.
Nissan's servicing costs are ludicrous when you look at what they actually do. I think EV drivers are being used as a source of easy cash in hard times for dealers.

This is a very interesting item,but I only do less than 2000 miles a year in my Ford Fiesta semi automatic,and I've just renewed my car insurance for just over £200 this year,so I would think it's going to be a few more years before the cost of an electric car is going to be worth my time switching.

Excellent points! Love my Leaf, had it for almost 6 years, running costs a fraction of my over Diesel car. Struggling now to justify a replacement for the Leaf, but watching your Vids, will look seriously at Kona 64.

It’s likely that in the next few months I will be asked to join a new
team involving a daily 5 day commute of 35 miles outbound plus 1-20 miles in
the community once at work and then return home.   This is therefore seemingly looking like 3
years of roughly 20k a year including leisure driving, so I need a really
reliable car as mine is now 14 years old. Work is able to pay 40p a mile even for electric cars so it’s the right time to go electric.  There are a number of Tesco supermarkets around with both 7kw and 50kw chargers near the new work.





My budget wont stretch to any new electric cars involving lease or pcp especially with
the high mileage involved so have ignored cars like Ioniq, new leaf, Kia e-niro, and Kona.   My budget is approx. 12K and after bit of research also feel following used examples are not appropriate:




BMW i3                                              too unreliable and complicated

VW Golf GTE plug in                        ditto




This means I need a car that has to be reliable, electric and able to manage the
daily commute with optional rapid charges if need be.  




Potentially I am thinking used 2016 Nissan Leaf 30kw with optional 6.6kw on board charger

that will have covered 20-40k so the majority of the Nissan 80k battery is
still intact and hopefully not have a battery that won’t have lost much battery
health.   As the 30kw seems capable of approx. 100 miles
conservatively average between summer and winter, the onboard charger could be
used to top up the charge for an hour at 7kw (FREE at Tesco’s) to give me the
necessary range to get home as 7kw charges gives 22kw per hour. The optional
6.6 charger is identified using either the weight of the car (1970kg) or the
digital display showing time to 100% charge showing both readings.  




Following advice I am thinking of installing home charger using government grant, advising

DNO, changing electricity tariff suitable for EV’s (Octopus) and making sure
the car comes with locking wheel nuts as well as  the granny and type 2 cables (as the car will
have the optional 6.6kw onboard charger), having telemetrics changed, checking
the sat nav SD card is installed, and getting Connect app.  




Advice on internet suggests that as the daily commute is mostly flat A and B roads,
switching eco off and using B mode for driving including town to yield
potentially 4-5kw economy (I am a very gently driver).   Tyre pressure advice seems to suggest around
38psi which is slightly inflated above normal levels to help economy.  




To preserve the battery state of health I would plan to home charge every night

and use 7kw charge stations to top up and not use the 50kw chargers which are
also available but I believe not good for long term life of the battery. 




Is there anything else I need to consider?
Great video. Owning an EV is a no brainer. I would highly recommend.

You couldn't have explained this simple arguement any clearer. Top video.

I think the hugest caveat is you have to have a charger at home and more than likely live in a house to be able to charge in a garage/on driveway.

There are fast chargers around me but the most stress free way is to park it at home and charge it on economy 7 to get those fantastic less than 10p per kw rates.

When I went to work there, I used to drive from Peterborough to Inverness on a Sunday, which I used to do non-stop. I could manage it on a tank of petrol. Not because it was big or clever, just because I used to enjoy the drive, and never felt the need to stop. I must say, I have driven Saabs for years and they have, in my opinion, the most comfortable seats of any car. It used to take me eight and a half hours, but I never got out of the car feeling tired.

Having said all of that. I would have been quite happy to stop once in a Tesla say around Edinburgh and charged up.

Now that the e-Nero and Kona are around, I think for 80-90% of the population who can afford a £30K car, range just shouldn't be an issue.

Obviously, it will take a while for these cars to filter down to people who can only afford to spend £10K or less, but for 50% of people, a 100 mile range is perfectly acceptable and these are becoming more and more affordable for people on the secondhand market.

Still love Dirty Diesel at this moment as it goes at least three times as far on a tank and is filled in less than three minutes . As for the environment the batteries are made up of materials that used Diesel ,gas and nuclear power to mine ,process ,transport and have a massive carbon footprint. Electricity comes often from burning gas especially on summer evenings when no wind blows and the sun is down . Is this all going to be another fad ?

Like your videos and your enthusiasm to inform on your EV experience. It look like the future but is not for the masses as yet. 
I've been watching a lot of EV YouTube to assess the state on play. The recurring theme is Range, the complexity / irritation of different charging solutions and charging time. How to connect, how to pay, different apps seem like a disaster, why is it not just plug, pay, delay and drive away. Some standardisation is required to effect real change. 
It seems EV drivers are into planning a trip where as fossil drivers don't have to plan that much if at all. In a ICE vehicle you can just go almost anywhere in the UK, possibly with the exception on the highland, with out worries or planning. This is a big issue to overcome because most people are USERS just going from A to B and not interested in overcoming the current technical problems.
Until the infrastructure is in place i.e. readily available, easy to use, recharging is fast (under15 mins) and range is a real world 250 miles+  it won't work for me and most people I've discussed this with. I don't want to add hours hanging about for a charged battery. I have long enough driving days. 
Financially the cost benefit is clear until you run out of electrons. My next step is still Hybrid. But I'll keep watching.

Great video EVM. It is interesting to hear your wife’s perspective and what she considers are the ‘issues’ particularly using the charging network. Public charging really needs sorting out, I am very techy and still think it is too complicated. Good video. My wife is not at all interested in cars and least of all EVs. Without massive improvements on infrastructure, she will not be convinced. She is terrified of being stranded.

Hi Evm, Good description. One good thing to know about PHEV's is they have two batteries. One battery is the big hybrid battery that uses regenerative braking to charge, and it saves you significant gas by using that captured energy in addition to the gas engine.  The hybrid battery is low-energy and specifically for storing and discharging and recapturing small amounts of energy.  The hybrid battery can power the car all-electric for a mile or so. The other battery is a separate lithium battery for electric operation, which is a high energy battery, and adds a high cost to the car. It charges by plugging into an electric outlet and gets no energy from braking.   Your car can be set in an all electric mode that uses only the lithium battery for power but recaptures braking energy to the hybrid battery, or in a hybrid-only mode, or a driving mode that lets it guesstimate when to switch back and forth between electric and hybrid. For example, it might use electric to cruise, and then switch to hybrid/gas when accelerating and braking a lot in able to recharge the hybrid battery, and then actually combine the gas engine and the lithium battery to accelerate quickly. https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/lithium-ion-battery-nickel-metal-hydride-which-better-ricky-leo

When I bought my Rav4 Prime SE I expected to get substantially less than the advertised 42 miles on electric. Part of the reason is because I'm a bit of a lead foot, and because I live in Phoenix, Arizona, the A/C is going to be in constant use (I bought the car in May). Well it turns out that owning a PHEV has moderated my driving somewhat. In particular I brake earlier and more gently. The net result is that I'm averaging 3 miles per kwHr and typical range is 46 miles. So this is pretty remarkable.

The Rav4 Prime, even in EV mode, has plenty of power off the line - the initial torque mitigates the loss of power from the gas motor. Consequently I can accelerate smartish off the line then back-off the acceleration without slowing the pack. Either way, the PHEV is making me a better (urban) driver!

On long distance (over 400 miles)  I am seeing around 39mpg at freeway speeds (for me that's around 80mph) which is not quite as good as the Rav4 Hybrid. However I'm giving away less than I expected.

So overall, PHEV has turned out to be a happy surprise. I can see that electric is the future but for today I'm really happy with my selection.

The problem with PHEV's is they are neither 'fish nor fowl'. I understand they are a stepping stone to a BEV, but they are woefully inefficient. Whichever way you look at it, they are either a ICE vehicle that has to carry around a heavy under ranged battery pack or a short ranged EV that has to carry around a heavy petrol/diesel engine. They only exist to fill a regulatory requirement-and according to the latest info-they do not even do that without fiddling their emissions figures. I also understand that they are a necessary evil until battery prices come down and EV's get cheaper. I think what they should have done with PHEV's is give them a minimum battery range of 70+ miles. I know most PHEV's are based on ICE vehicle chassis, so to do this they should remove the ICE power pack from the engine bay and replace it with a full electric power train and a compact efficient petrol generator unit that can act as a range extender/charger if required. The space created in the engine bay and by the reduction in size of the vehicles fuel tank could then be used for extra batteries and a 7kwh charger unit. I know this is similar to vehicles like the Prius, but that vehicle is still too much of a compromise. The engine is still too big and is sometimes used to drive the vehicles drive train directly. It is far more efficient to have a small generator that runs at a constant rpm to charge the batteries as required and let a fully electric power train propel the vehicle. So in summary make PHEVs  into a true stepping stone to a BEV. A lighter generator instead of a heavy engine, faster charging and a moderately sized battery pack that gives you a reasonable commuting range. You can then run on electric most of time on your average journey, but if your battery range drops below 15 miles on a journey for example the generator could switch on and at least give you the ability to reach a charge point.

My concern about PHEV and the recent review article issue was done with compliance PHEV's that were specifically made for performance and not efficiency.  This is the case with too many PHEV these days that have terrible design.....
1) They are large heavy cars SUV which means the follow apply more.
2) The electric motor is not powerful enough to provide useful driving : and the system is designed to NOT lock out the petrol engine.  Even on a small hill the ICE engine will kick in.
3) Catalytic converters on petrol cars do not work until they reach 200 degC.  This means short bursts of ICE engine for performance reasons will produce a lot of toxic exhaust, including particulates from petrol worse then diesel.  It is normal for a ICE petrol engine to take 5-10 minutes to heat the CAT to working temperature.  For town driving in winter the CAT may NEVER reach operating temperature.
4) Too many PHEV cannot heat/cool the cabin in EV mode, again this is stupid design and common in compliance cars. This forces the driver on a hot/cold day to have to use the ICE engine or freeze/boil.
I agree completely with your presentation, BUT there are too many cars - even the Ionic - that will not lock out the ICE engine in electric mode, avoid these.  Make sure when you buy a PHEV, does the EV lock out the ICE engine under all conditions and is the motor powerful enough (maybe more than 50 kW) to give you town driving that you are happy with. Make sure the PHEV can heat/cool the cabin in EV only mode.  I would recommend you get a PHEV with "hybrid-hold" mode as an option - this allows you to keep battery charge (and run as a normal hybrid) until you reach a town at your destination where you can run in full EV mode.
Example ......
My wife's car (mine is a T-M3) is a Audi A3 etron - a small real car - that has 101 hp electric motor that locks out the ICE engine which certainly enough for town driving - can reach  81 mph (not necessary) and can heat/cool the car on EV mode only.  We get....
60mpg in very long journey 200+ miles
I can get 100-130 mpg on 50 miles, including half on motor ways (my daily commute)
Of course below 25-30 miles we get all EV.
We always charge - no question - it is 1p mile = 10% the cost of an efficient diesel car.
(PS Audi charge ports are utter shite - and audi service is useless)

The petrol engine is basically a range extender for me. The electric network in my area is in it's infancy, so would rather charge at home. Also the electric car technology is in its early stages and improving all the time. Todays electric cars will become terrible old fashioned and low spec compared to electric cars that come out in 5 to 10 years. Put simply PHEVs are better value, you get much more for your money and if you want to go on a long journey and not have to make a long stop say in the Scottish Highlands, a PHEV will manage it. I have a peugeot hybrid.

I've just gone for a BMW 530e. Sorry but I don’t follow the argument. I  chose an Outlander 2nd hand 3 years ago. 70-80% of driving was EV only. Outlander, 2nd hand £15k was an accessible BEV in effect and the ICE barely started in Summer. Unfortunately yes, lots of people use them for the BIk benefits. Since then I've gone full EVM and got an electric car, home solar panels, home batteries, all the automation/gadgets etc a lot of it down to the experience with the PHEV. That said, they need to be dropped at the same time as destination & forecourt charge stations proliferation.

They do not just become a petrol car on long journeys. They become a "self-charging" hybrid. That is what they are - but with a larger battery and the ability to charge while stationary. If your driving pattern is mostly short range you can be fully electric for most of the time. An occasional long journey - no need for range anxiety and with the efficiency of a "self charging" hybrid.
I think most PHEVs are bought by companies, to reduce tax bills and they are used as ICE cars. Never on charge.

I guess servicing for a PHEV will still cost and take a lot longer as they will insist on the usual ICE servicing every year... Also, as you say, if you can charge a plug in a Phev you can plug in a BEV...

6. the Biggest question is Budget?

PHEV have a niche purpose. 
- if tou have too unreliable access to charging for daily commute. 
- to be more comfortable about the odd long trips
- there are sadly not enough pure BEV opinions in all segments. If you have specialised requirements, like towing trailer maybe. There are some options for towing but maybe that car is not suitable for other requirements, or just too expensive up front. 
- it is easier to refuel ICE/PHEV if you run out, but you shouldn't be close anyway. 

But there are reasons to consider BEV to PHEV
- most PHEV  have short EV-range, (except like BMW i3Rex having the same battery size as BEV)
- some PHEV will only provide cabin heat using excess heat from ICE coolant. For the short trips arround your neighbourhood, the coolant barely gets lukewarm providing insignificant heat during winter, but still burning fuel, even if you don't need it for range, effectively banning you from entering EV-mode zone during winter.
- you still get maintenance for the ICE even if you rarely use it.
- parallel hybrid, usually have the electric motor through the transmission, causing slight jumpiness with gear change (even in EV-mode. Serial hybrid rarely have this issue.

I have a 2012 Prius plug in hybrid that is now 9 years old with 78,000 miles. Recording each fill up I have 94 mpg on it. Take for instance in Brighton where I live. There are on street lamp post style charging point, Low power (3KW) but they aren't dedicated charging points, so anyone with a local residents permit can park in the spot.

I think if there is a rational element to the desire for extreme ranges, it is more to do with reducing frequency of charging than long distance endurance driving. Can I go the couple of hundred miles and back again on a single charge or drive there and have some left for exploring, before charging to come back? Most people may never do that or else will only do it once or twice a year (I’m basically describing our typical family holiday). I could make it work in a 150-200 mile range car but it requires a change in behaviour and thinking (as well as faith in the charging network keeping up with demand). I would have to become accustomed to instead charging during a rest stop or something, which is fine but it is a change from the longer range on a single tank thinking of ICEs. And change is often not something that we do well.

What impact is the cost of batteries likely to have on used EV depreciation? Are we ever likely to see an equivalent to the old banger for a few hundred that are common in ICEs? I would think that if a battery with a decent remaining range is worth a few grand then that might set a rough lower limit on the price for a car that still has one. On the flip side, is a car with a truly duff battery likely to just get scrapped as beyond economical repair? I suppose someone with the means might be able to snap one up at a bargain price and fit a newish battery for an overall saving. Maybe I’m overlooking some middle ground with a half dead battery that is still good to somebody. 

I’m just curious how this is going to all look in the future. Retaining value is of course great for those who can afford the initial cost but will the entry price for getting into driving increase beyond the reach of some lower income people? I mean, that few hundred quid banger might cost more in the long term to run and/or may get replaced often but having the money up front or being able to secure credit is still a potential sticking point for many.

I have recently traded my Zoe in for a used 2018 Kia Soul EV. For the three years I had the Zoe, I was leasing the battery. It was a sore point for some of that time but in reality I wouldn't have had an EV as early as I did without that option, so it was a good thing. Then I came to trade it in and I was turned down by many dealers. I could have traded it in at Renault or one of the EV specialists but ended up buying the battery to make life easier. It was a 2014, 22kWh battery and cost me 2200 pounds FYI. I had three options in my price range (I didn't want a Leaf for many reasons, though I'm sure they are worthy cars if they float your boat), a Zoe ZE40 - I would have been very happy to have another Zoe and the range would have been very useful. I found looking at Zoes a chore rather than a pleasure though. It was so hard to pin down what you were looking at, is the battery leased? is it a Q or R motor? It was so difficult to find this sort of vital information easily that it definitely put me off looking at Zoes. Plus, I'd done that! I rarely have the same car twice, even one as nice as the Zoe, so it was probably not destined to be. Next was the BMW i3. This is a really special car. The carbon fibre tub, the driving experience, the efficiency, the rear wheel drive, the insane turning circle, the quirkiness - I loved it all. Downsides? Not quite roomy enough was the crippler but I wouldn't have liked having the badge either, too much snobbiness would have been inferred I fear and it was such a distinctive car that simply putting a Skoda badge on it would not have helped. I plumped for the Soul in the end. All of the three had compromises but the Soul is better to drive than such a bus of a car has any right to be, it certainly highlights how poor a Leaf is in this regard. It is roomy, characterful (Wish I'd found a Smurf, but the silver is still nice), and so efficient. It is bigger and blunter than the Zoe but does around 4.5 miles per kWh compared to less than 4 on the same journeys. The piece de resistance though, and the thing that future proofs it, it has 100kW charging (it's the 30kWh, the 27kWh is 50kW maximum). This is more useful than the Zoes bigger battery, at least it will be when 100kW chargers are installed on the routes that I frequent - Still waiting for the infrastructure to keep up!!!!!

My Octopus GO hasn't gone up yet but my figures are - previous car 27mpg, at £6.50 a gallon is £24,074. The replacement Audi eTron 55 has averaged 2.6miles  per kW over the last 22000 miles (including winter tyres since November) and 10 months with 35% home charging at 4.73p = £673.08, 65% public charging at an average of 35p per kW is £8,750. Also bear in mind that fueling on the motorway, which is, in my opinion, equivalent to public charging, is probably around 12% more than the £6.50 per gallon so, in realty, the difference would be greater. I calculate that home charging off peak, the cost of my EV is around 10% of the previous petrol equivalent and on long trips, charging from home at the start of the journey and then public charging after that, the cost of my EV is just under 30% of the previous petrol equivalent.

Having recently filled my Kia Picanto and rented a Kia e-Niro, I have some useful real-world numbers. The e-Niro was for a London-Edinburgh-London trip to see family over Christmas, so fully laden in cold weather and purely motorway driving using only public chargers. I averaged about 3.6/3.7kWh. My Picanto meanwhile does my usual driving as the car I own. I tend to get around 50-55mpg and can probably eke out 300 miles on a single tank.

I refuelled the Picanto yesterday for £45.41, which works out at 15.14p per mile. With the e-Niro, I charged about 720 miles into the battery at my various stops, for a total cost of £75.80. That works out at 10.53p per mile.

So my tiny efficient Picanto, which never carries passengers, has limited boot space, mixes motorway and urban driving at all times of year, is 5p more expensive per mile than a compact SUV that was full of luggage, presents and other Christmas paraphernalia, doing exclusively motorway miles in a cold December with liberal heating use, and relying entirely on public chargers.

I think that you are right about it being a good time to buy - not compared to 12 months ago but certainly in terms of the near to medium term future.
I reached this conclusion for the following reasons:

1. DEMAND: As you say, demand this year is much greater than before and so the Sellers don't need to offer discounts. This situation isn't likely to change any time soon if at all as we are well on the way to 2030 when ALL new cars will have to be EVs. In fact I think the availability of ICE cars will decrease as the manufacturers switch production towards EVs and the demand will be boosted by the accelerating costs of ICE cars as they are taxed more heavily and the number of petrol/diesel stations decreases. So, demand will shoot up whilst SUPPLY will not be able to cope as we get nearer to 2030.
2. RAW MATERIALS: Not only are the raw materials becoming scarcer but the increased demand for EVs will increase the demand for those raw materials, making the end product more expensive.
3. THE PURCHASE GRANT: In recent times, Central Government has encouraged EV purchases by giving Grants for EV Purchase, making EVs qualify for ZERO road tax (or whatever it's called these days !), Residential Charger installation and even 75% installation grants for Local Authorities (including Parish Councils) to instal community chargers (The ORCS scheme). However, as the number of EVs increases the Government will lose tax revenue and a lot of that money funds other non-transport related expenditures. So, the Grants will be cut back - we have already seen the Purchase Grant reduce and from April the Residential Charger grant will only be available to tenants of apartment blocks. No doubt ORCS will be next. So as a potential buyer of an EV, the "free" money for installing a residential charger or buying a car under £32,000 will soon disappear, making it a no-brainer to buy now.

BUT (and there's always a BUT)

There is a reason why despite the above it MIGHT be sensible to hold off an EV purchase and that is that as more and more EV models are launched it does seem likely that the new models will feature substantially more range than current models.
I constantly read about "battery breakthroughs" that promise 2x, 3x or even more mileage per charge, thereby eliminating 'range anxiety' by exceeding ICE vehicle range many times.
Whether that is a good enough reason for holding off I personally doubt but as you say, DO YOUR OWN RESEARCH !

Key points: there is no such single thing as "the grid". You have: generators, retailers, the NationalGrid (both a company and a network) and the DNOs (UKPN, WPD, SSE etc.)

People think that cables via pylons _are_ the grid. Nope, that's the NationalGrid transmission system and under 3% of all UK power cables. The rest are owned by the DNOs - the Distribution Network Operators, and are usually buried under roads and pavements. So these are not seen.

Alas, we are not out of the woods yet. The DNO 230V networks to your homes - assuming you are not on an estate built to use overnight storage heaters - is good for 1 to 2.4 kW continuous to each home - some slightly more, but usually  not that much margin.

Hm. How many kW do EVs charge at, HPs too? More. The old networks cannot support 100% EV or HP rollout; it was (in the UK) built for "lighting+" duties. It will cope with the occasional peak though, like a shower being taken.

Next up. You've described the communications system which is via your home SMEST2 and travels over a special comms network (look up DCC). This is NOT an Internet of Things / cloud system, which is how most retailers (think Octopus who use Amazon's AWS system) will control your charging. That is, the wonders and security built into DCC is - sidestepped for an overseas IoT service for app control. Hm. Hope that IoT service keeps going OK!

What does this all mean? Today, not much...

The randomised charging is about grid "whole system" frequency stability. And today, local overloads have no explicit control mechanism - as the DNOs (the people who maintain the 97% of wires) do not know who to tell "Turn that overload down!" - the data is not available. Suppose EV charging of 300 kW was on a street with a 230V system good for 200 kW. Who is coordinating this, to stop overloads? Today, no-one. The DNO can't turn that down as they have no idea who to talk to.

Better then to upgrade those cables and local transformers, hidden around corners of estates? Well, there are some plans for that as part of RIIO-ED2 (don't ask). Um, there are about 1/4 million of those guys supplying c. 30 million homes via c. 250,000 km of buried cables. Think about replacing those!

I find a lot of this advice misleading at best, and wrong in at least some cases. The advice about regen is the most obvious, though you're basing your claim on what IMHO is an incorrect and unsubstantiated assertion that careful drivers can't maintain speed properly. More to the point though, if you're a driver who can't maintain speed, use the cruise control. That's what it's there for, and modern adaptive cruise control allows use of the cruise control even in traffic.

Relying on the brake pedal to handle your regen is going to be less efficient, especially for those drivers who aren't careful enough to maintain speed in the first place, because those are also the drivers who won't be able to module the brake pedal carefully enough to ensure they stay within the regen range without engaging the friction brakes. With a higher regen setting, most slowing can be achieved only with the accelerator pedal, without the risk of engaging the friction brakes at all (except on cars with one-pedal driving, which will engage the friction brakes toward the end of a stopping sequence, but even there it's still easier to maintain efficiency with the high regen of the one-pedal driving).

Other things I take issue with:

* The LEAF uphill/downhill test doesn't really demonstrate what you seem to think it does. Specifically, unless you're only driving around 10-15 mph, a lot of the energy used going up the hill is fighting drag (and this is especially true as the speed goes above 25-30 mph), and you need just as much energy going down the hill. So the 7% up/1.5% down doesn't necessarily represent as great an inefficiency of regen as you seem to say. People might look at that and think you're saying that you can only get something like 20% of your energy back with regen, which is far from the actual situation. EV regenerative braking recovers as much as 65-75% of the energy being captured, which frankly is huge and is why hybrid cars were and still are used as a stepping stone to the even better efficiency of EVs.

* A much more minor point is that when you discuss preconditioning the car while it's still plugged in, it's important to understand this doesn't affect the car's energy efficiency, but rather just its range. Because you are still using the energy, this really ought to be accounted for if you want a realistic energy efficiency figure for the use of the car, even though the car itself won't take it into account when displaying its own driving efficiency number.

It's still good advice, because it helps improve range under the same conditions where one often is seeing reduced range (e.g. cooler weather conditions), but you're not getting any energy for free and the actual watt-hour per mile efficiency for the car remains the same whether the energy is pulled from the battery or the charging cable (even though the car itself doesn't admit it).

Regen: Some EVs do not mix regen with the friction brakes ie the brake pedal only engages friction brakes on Teslas. The energy in a body in motion is 1/2MV² so there is exponentially more regen available at higher speeds. There is also exponentially more drag at higher speeds. So if you coast, you get no regen at all and drag uses up your energy. Better to use regen at high speeds. I've not seen any quantitative analysis but I estimate that you can get ~70% of your energy back

Regenerative braking is often quoted at about 80% efficient at recovering lost energy to the battery, and then the car is about 80% efficient at converting battery energy into motion, so in total that is 0.8*0.8 = 0.64. I believe these were numbers quoted by Tesla way back when, I'm sure newer systems are better than that. In other words, if you would use 1 kWh to drive on a flat road at a constant speed of 30mph, you'd instead use about 1.6 kWh if you were to constantly slow down to 25mph and speed up again to 35mph, even if your average speed stays at 30mph over the length of the road.

The other thing to consider is that regen is limited by the power conversion rate of the motor and the battery. Generally speaking, you're on safer ground if you decelerate as rapidly as you accelerate, and no more than that. So driving smoothly and predictably with a good distance in front of you. This is also safer of course!

Something you hinted at in the video but didn't quite 100% clarify -- batteries don't charge at the same speed all the way through the charge. They charge at their fastest when they're close to empty; and the further they get to being full, the slower they charge. This is why on road trips, your trip planning tool will try to keep you at the lower end of the battery charge -- so that you charge faster and spend a lot less time charging. And you'll never charge up to 100% on a road trip (unless you REALLY need it to get to the next stop), you'll typically only be charging up 30% to 50% to get to your next charger

Summary

* kW = the rate at which energy is delivered
* kWh = the total amount of energy delivered / held in a battery
* Cost per kwh x the number of kwh delivered = total cost
* Fast chargers cost more than charging at home
* Miles per kWh is the inverse of kwh (or wh) per mile.
* Electric cars charge fastest between about 5% and 60% full and slow down until full
* Electric cars will only charge as fast as the car can accept OR the charger can deliver -   (whichever is slowest)

In terms of charging etiquette, there's only one situation where you should be obliged to move your car from a rapid.

If your charge is racing along, by all means continue.
If your charge has slowed to a crawl, but there are other units available, feel free to continue
If your charge has slowed to a crawl, all units are being used, but nobody is waiting, feel free to continue.
If however, your charge has slowed to a crawl, no other units are available AND there are people waiting, unplug and move on.

Obviously this is no steadfast rule and you don't have to, but let it be known if you don't move, people are probably gonna call you a selfish tosser.

I remember mentioning on one of your Video tests of a leaf and charging that your battery temps were getting hot. I believe it's an inescapable fact that EVs need good thermal battery management beyond just restricting charge. The temperatures should be controlled by active cooling. This can be done in a complicated way ala BMW with the aircon system, or in a less complicated way by a radiator and simple coolant pump. Nissan really need to adopt some form of good/sufficient active cooling of the pack. 

I drive an i3 (94Ah)and I'm no BMW fan boy, my god they made their own complications in a car that's fantastically expensive to own and run. The one thing it does do well though is manage battery temperatures and charging. I got the Rex variant, because the writing was on the wall for charging an EV away from home to be more expensive than Petrol. We're pretty close now, because when I fill up my little tank with Petrol I can get around 50 mpg and go another 100 miles for a 3 minute fill up rather than a 45 minute charge stop (if you can find a convenient charger). This means a small battery for 98% of my needs and long distance capability without hours spent charging and a pocket full of charge cards and memberships.

Ultimately, the charge network in the UK is poor, the cost of charging is already high and they have a captive audience will be much higher than Petrol ever was...in cars that cost us twice as much!

Many towns and small cities simply don't have the infrastructure to supply that kinda power need without substancial upgrades which will happen as time goes on but we are still very much in the early adopter phase of current EV technology.  

A single 200KW fast charger is going to pull 833 Amps at 240V single phase.  Granted they use 3 phase 480 for most chargers in the US but that is still the eqivalent of nearly 5 mid sized homes if they were ever actually pulling nearly their full service which almost never happens.  Now lets assume you have 2 banks of 2 charging bays each capable of 200KW dc fast charging.  It is entirely conceivable, at certain times to have all four bays being used and pulling 100KW for each vehicle so that means that single set of chargers could consume at one point in time more power than 9-10 households at once if they were nearly maxing their service.

EV charging stations will remain proprietary until/if they can become profitable as a business model separate from the sale of EVs. And this won't happen with the current business model. Tesla doesn't sell cars for profit. It sells cars to be able to sell green credits , which are more profitable. Therefore Tesla won't allow any sub-use of its charging network because the charging network only exists to support the sale of vehicles, which exist to support the sale of green credits. Scratch Tesla from the shared charging station model.

If other EV makers don't follow the same business model, they will not be able to profitably support a charging infrastructure without , ahem, charging more money for the privilege. 
Unless the business model of charing stations becomes profitable it is dead in the water, and the only that may happen is via legislation. It will not happen organically because we already have a complete logistical system set up for long distance refueling, viz the gas and diesel stations. This tells us that the only plausible future for large scale replacement of existing ICEs is with Hybrids, where batteries do the short range work and ICEs do the long range work. EVs are a flawed plan.

The issues at Electrify America are a fairly recent problem: We've been doing multiple multi-thousand mile EV road trips a year since 2019 and we never had any issues charging at EA stations until 2022. There are two key issues at play: 1) The number of non-Tesla EVs being sold is increasing at an exponential rate. and 2) supply chain issues are making it more difficult to obtain the parts needed to keep stations in good repair.

So what you have now is *way* more EVs using the stations which means both more wear and tear on them plus it means that if a stall or two goes down that you now suddenly have queues of cars building up to use the remaining stations, which means wait times for drivers plus even more wear and tear on those remaining stations, etc.

Tesla has a huge advantage here for many reasons: 1) They've been at this long enough that they've been able to streamline the design of their superchargers and they manufacturer their own charging equipment so they aren't as effected by the supply chain issues because they control more of their own supply chain.
2) Their chargers don't need screens or credit card readers which greatly reduces the number of literal "moving/touched parts" or parts that create a single point of failure. It also reduces the software needed because you don't need to design, build, and test a graphical user interface which adds a lot of software complexity.
3) Their chargers only have to work on one brand of vehicle. They don't have to design and test them against other companies vehicles to work out compatibility issues.

Like others have noted: When Tesla originally introduced the SC network it wasn't exactly all smooth sailing at first for them either. It took time to work out the kinks. It took Tesla about 4 years to build out what Electrify America did in 2 years. Tesla just had a 7 year head start. When EA started building their network there wasn't a single manufacturer of DC fast chargers that could supply EA with the number of chargers they needed. So EA had to buy whatever equipment from whatever manufacturer had it leading to a hodge podge of various brands of chargers at different EA sites. This further compounds the parts supply issues because different brands of chargers need different parts so it's harder for EA technicians to have a uniform set of spare parts on hand that work across all their stations.  

EA is already learning some of the same lessons as Tesla: They are working on bringing the charging equipment manufacturing in-house so that they can control more of their own supply chain. Once they get this part of the equation under control I think this will make a huge difference going forward and hopefully they get the kinks worked out soon.

While I think that you point on the lack of charging stations is a fair point to make, HOW you communicate it makes you sound like petulant, spoiled teenagers. Here are some thoughts:

1. OF COURSE Rivian's charger network is not going to be built out yet, they are a brand new company. How you didn't figure that out is just breathtakingly stupid. We are in a construction boom time and even finding contractors and subcontractors to do the work all over the nation will be unbelievably difficult and expensive. As an consulting engineer and project manager, I have managed similar construction projects in different states and it is incredibly challenging and very expensive. Rivian is slated to build 3,500 charging stations. That will take at least 5-10 years, maybe longer. Just permitting each single project in different states an municipalities will take 1-2 years, let alone constructing them.

2. Comparing Rivian, which is a brand new company, with Tesla, which is nearly 20 years old the way you did it makes you look like morons. Think about this point before you even consider arguing. You could have made the point that Rivian is new and they lack many of the advantages of Tesla WITH the qualification that you understand Rivian just got started as a company. 

3. What in the hell did you think would happen if you bought a Rivian? OF COURSE you are not going to have as nice a charging network as Tesla's network. You should have mentioned that if you buy a Rivian, you will have problems finding fast charging stations for it and then provided a couple of examples and dropped it. Instead you repeat the same criticism over and over again ad nauseum. Consider writing out an outline script of your broadcasts.

4. Possibly, Rivian's $5k kitchen option uses less power than standard appliances.  Induction elements are very efficient. That is something you should have checked on. Further, the kitchen option is built for travel and convenience of very high quality materials. These types of options are expensive wherever you find them - like yachts, boats, buses, motor homes, planes, etc. While I agree $5K is expensive, if you are going to do a lot of camping, it is worth it for the convenience.  Using standard electric appliances is cheaper, but chance are they will draw a lot more power. 

5. The Tesla cyber truck won't cost in the $40k range. That would make it as cheap as the Model 3, and that's not going to happen. My guess is that the two motor version will cost $60 -$70k and the three motor version will cost $85k - $100k. I could be wrong, but this would bring it to the same costs as the Ford F-150 Lightning which will START at $40K and go up to about $100K. 

6. The Rivian appears to have a built-in advantage for off-roading and performance over the Tesla Cybertruck in that a computer controls a separate motor for each wheel. This should provide faster accelerate, better traction and better handling than the Cybertruck. The Rivian is also smaller by quite a bit and it should get better range and be much easier to park and drive around town and use with a standard garage. 

Conversely, the cybertruck will have more room, more storage, a larger truck bed, probably more interior room and it will still be very powerful. The acceleration is supposed to be as fast as Rivian's, but we will see. I doubt that the cybertruck will be a nimble and accomplished off-roader as the Rivian because of its large size and because each wheel does not have separate suspension articulation and power control. Rivian's off-road design really is quite brilliant. I will be interested to see how Tesla's truck compares.

7. If you want to go to an area that doesn't have chargers yet, you can store a portable gasoline generator fairly easy in the back of the truck and use it to charge the truck. I know this isn't an elegant solution, but as a temporary measure, it will work. The generator can also power your cooking equipment. It will also provide extra insurance in case you can't get to a charging station. You can buy a very high quality, powerful generator equipped with wheels and a frame for around $2000.00 - $3000.00.  You can get 20,000 watt generators in this price range and that would put out 20.0 KW per hour. If you ran it for 16 hours, you would generate approximately 320 KWh of power - more than enough to charge the truck from zero. It would be noisy, but most of the time you are not going to be with the truck anyway. You can also use an extension cord to locate the generator a 100 feet away from the truck when you sleep. At that range you won't hear  much more than a dull hum. In your case, you could have charged the truck overnight and easily topped off your truck's battery to a full charge in just one night. Plus, you don't have to wait around a charging station when you head home.

Again, this isn't a perfect solution, but it would work if you want to go to remote areas. You would need to carry around 30 gallons of gas, which is easy to do. I would agree that it does defeat the purpose of having an electric truck, but you bought a truck from a manufacturer that doesn't have a mature charging network yet. This would be a fairly cheap stop-gap.

1. Every EV is a giant computer. Maybe a good practice is to perform system updates/restarts before leaving home on long road trips. Well, if you have time to make a 40min video rant for your YouTube viewers - more power to you.
2. Understand charging rate is an agreement between the EV's BMS and the charging station. The final amp charging rate is a decision made by the charge point, not the EV. Problems could definitely be fault of the EV's software, but note #1 above before starting a long road/camping/adventure trip. Also, on long trips, every EV owner should understand Level's/Tiers of charging and route plan accordingly. 
3. Unless using Tesla's charging network, take time to study your EV's recommended charge stops. If you have a copilot, have them Google well ahead of the intended stop to determine quality/status before you arrive. Remember the quality of the charging network = Lots-O-Cash + Lots-O-Time. Still I am planning a 3200 km road trip this summer in my Bolt and I expect it to be an adventure even though I am not going off road or to anywhere remote.  I expect to have some very difficult charging experiences.  I remember driving my first BEV, my 2019 Ioniq, with its 201 km summer range in -25 C blowing snow and having a fully charged starting range of 80 km and finding that the only two fast chargers (25 kW) on the route both unavailable (one broken and one in use by a BMW i3 whose owner said he had to charge to 100% to make it home and so he was going to be there for hours because his batttery was at 10% and you know how slow it can get when you get over 90%.  So I drove to a level 2.  By the time I got to this level 2 I didn't have the range to go anywhere else.  If the level 2 had been down I was calling CAA.  And the isolated parking lot the level 2 was in wasn't even plowed.  I had to drive back and forth to force a path through the snow to get to the charger.  I remember looking at the gas station across the street and seeing the gas cars coming and going freely and thinking that it was like they were in a parallel universe.  They were in the boring universe where life was so easy that people became so lethargic they lost the ability to move and I was Mark Watney alone on Mars.  I was happy to be on Mars.  I always liked adventure. But it was so surreal that this other planet was in the same place and I could see the people on it like they were right there.

There is a lot of misinformation about the 50A service travel trailers use. The 50A service for RVs is exactly the same as the 50A service now required for electric stoves in houses. It has two separate 110v legs that are able to be used together for 220v. This 220v is different from 220v in Europe because of the way that they handle the neutral. When you feed your RV with a 50A service you are providing your RV with two separate 110v legs that are kept separate by the RV unless your RV is set up for only a 30A 110v setup. If you use a 50A to 30A adapter, the 30A adapter only feeds 110v out at an unknown current (likely 30A). On another point, if you slow down to get improved mileage for pulling a trailer you still cannot compare it to the mileage you get without a trailer. Wind resistance varies as a square function. If you double your speed, you essentially quadruple the resistance to air flow. If you drove your EV at a slower speed on the freeway, you could improve your mileage considerably by slowing down with or without a trailer. Thanks for the information... there is a big learning curve to pulling a trailer.  One more thing -- I notice you are using a load leveler system. It basically unloads the rear wheels of the pulling vehicle by adding load to the front wheels. When I pull my trailer with my diesel dually truck, I don't need the load leveler because the truck itself is pretty heavy. I'm anticipating that my cybertruck will not need a leveling system and I would be surprised if there wasn't something in the Rivian that reduces the need for that device as well. EVs are a lot heavier than traditional vehicles so it kind of acts like my heavy ICE truck. Hookups would be far simpler without the load leveler and can be done far faster. You could also speed your hookup time by adding an electric jack in the place of the crank type. (It is also a lot easier on an older person in the heat and humidity we see on the East Coast). About wind resistance. What causes unnecessary extra wind resistance and what doesn't can be counter-intuitive. A striking example: the standard truck with a bed and the tailgate up. It turns out that air tends to start circulating, and the bulk of the air flowing over the cabin goes *over* that circulation, and does not hit the tailgate. Moreover, my understanding is that if the tailgate is lowered that circulation does not happen, and then the air that flows over the cabin makes a sharp turn down, resulting in heavy turbulance, causing *more* air resistance than with the tailgate up

FYI, the 30 amp service at your campsite is 120V (24*120 = 2.88KWh) which results in a charge rate that is twice as fast as a 15 amp (12*120 = 1.44KWh) Level 1 charger.  The best option would be to get a 50 amp service which is at 240V (40*240 = 9.6KWh) resulting in a charge rate a little under 7 times a Level 1 charge rate.

What Jessie had in his hand is what they call a "dog bone" and it converts the NEMA 14-50 power to TT-30 by only passing through one hot leg, one neutral and one ground.  Dog bones are not wired for EVs.  I'm betting that pedestal had two breakers, one 30 amp single and one 15 amp single.

There are three types of loads: 
Inductive: where Voltage lags current:  All those power  tools with motors (corded) AC/DC Brushed Power tools. 

Resistive: Old school Incandescent or Halogen lightbulbs, resistive heaters such as Space Heaters. Dorm Cube Refrigerators, Window Air Conditioners

Capacitive Loads: where current leads the Voltage. AC to DC converters such as the BUILT AC to DC Current converter built into the Tesla (no, it’s not built into the level 1 or 2 AC wall unit, which is why I was rolling on the floor laughing at the both of you as you tried the Rivian plug, as it was bound to fail, as it was still connecting to the same on board AC Charger Built into your Tesla) and power tool chattery chargers.

The little MIG welder works in short circuit mode with a constant voltage power supply. When welding, the wire is directly shorted to ground many times a second and it melts each time that happens. That can cause large (but short) peaks in power use and it looks like the AC inverter protection is fast enough to react to those peaks. You should try one of the inverter stick (SMAW) welders that run on 120V. Those use a constant current power supply that will limit the amount of power used by the welder even when the welding rod is directly shorted to ground.

It is a grounding issue.  One has to resolve what is needed to provide the necessary ground reference.  Common in electronics, where some test equipment has a floating ground.  Since it also defeats some protective circuits one needs to know ground exists to maintain safety, e.g. if polarity gets reversed, high voltage can be on a metal case, and shock one.  But when wired right, one is still protected.

This is a common problem when trying to charge from an inverter. The neutral and ground are not bonded and the evse checks if you have a proper ground. 100% guaranteed that the neutral and ground are not bonded. You can get around this by making a plug with the neutral and ground wires connected together. I do this all the time to charge my nissan leaf and bolt from cheap inverters and it works just fine.

If you buy a Pakayak I highly recommend also dropping some cash on a "kayak sailor" kit so you can sail long distances without getting tired. And if you really want to simplify things I recommend avoiding spending all that money and just getting a $200 inflatable SUP board which you can attach a kayak seat. If Im kayaking short distances and speed isnt a factor or if im just freediving a lake, I go with the inflatable SUP used as a sit down kayak. Theres plenty of room onboard to carry an anchor and all my other freedive gear. If Im traveling farther distances I use a hardshell kayak with the "Kayak sailor" rig.

Protip: Search inflatable SUPs on Amazon. Copy/paste the Amazon item number of each posting to a notepad. Then go to "camelcamelcamel" and search each of those items. CCC shows price history graphs which tell you how low the prices are in the off season. You can set up email notifications for when the price drops back to its historical low. The wide scooter wheel is the perfect shape; thicker in the middle than on the edges. I used to run a flat belt planer in a lumber mill and the belt wheels were all this shape, although they were metal and the belts were rubberized fabric.  This makes the belt self-centered automatically on the wheel.

 That is why the rear triple wheel gave issues and the actual thicker-in-the-middle tire didn't have the belt drift off. 

I would suggest making the middle of the three rear wheels slightly larger than the outer two. Or file some of the material off the outer wheels. Or just use another tire in back.

...just for context.. 
the basic machine used for MIG / ARC-stick / TIG welding is the same.. if you already have a DC stick welding machine, you can easily convert it to TIG welding by using the ground port for the TIG torch & the the other port for the ground.. then using a simple gas power attachment for the argon gas.. then a solenoid for opening the gas.. the switch can be a foot switch 10amps, or a push button on the gun, which is already there when you buy a TIG gun assembly.. 
..if you have a MIG welding, you already have a gas solenoid in the MIG welding machine that you can use for your TIG torch... really dont need to buy a separate TIG welding machine for enthusiast DYIer...

One specific point: When she states that "an electric car needs to drive more than 60,000 km before its lifetime emissions make it cleaner than a car that runs on fossil fuels", she is admitting that BEVs are cleaner, over their lifetime. We can quibble over how many miles must be driven to hit that transition, but 60,000 km is only about 37,000 miles, and cars last far beyond that modest milage number. If she presented evidence that the lifetime emissions of EVs was higher than ICE cars, that would be one thing. However, she admits that EVs are cleaner, on the whole, although it takes 37,000 miles before the break-even point is achieved. 

This does not even take into account the fact that the grid gets cleaner every year, as coal plants close, and more renewable generation comes on line. This is an under-appreciated fact, I believe. An EV can get cleaner and cleaner over time, even as it ages, because its source of electricity gets cleaner. Every time the grid gets cleaner, the entire fleet of BEVs gets cleaner, as a consequence. ICE cars, on the other hand, inevitably get dirtier and dirtier over time, as their engines wear, their milage decreases, and they begin to burn oil. 

Finally, even if there were absolutely no difference between the amount of pollution produced by ICE cars and BEVs, and the only advantage of BEVs was that their pollution was emitted far from population centers, this would still be a HUGE advantage.

Don't forget, burning any kind of fuel in a power plant is way more efficient than burning any kind of fuel in a car engine.  The difference is temperature.  A car engine can't get too hot because it's a safety hazard, and people don't want to wait a long time for their engine to warm up.  A power plant has no such limitations, and can run at a much higher temp.  In thermodynamics, the Carnot efficiency, (the max possible for any heat engine) is proportional to the temp difference between the hot part of the engine, and the cold part.  For cars and power plants the cold part is the same; ambient air.  (Although some plants use river water.)  BTW, this is why cars and power plants are less efficient during heat waves.

I think automation is a great idea and I'm never critical of employing technology to make life better. And I can't blame Zac and Jessie for doing what I'm sure I've done myself in the past.

But the arguments they are presenting for TeslaBot are really just arguments for full or near full-scale automation in general.

And that's fine. But here is the glaring problem most every advocate of full-scale automation is missing:

We first need a largely renewable grid in place to power it. If we put all these robots online with the power grid we have now...where a lot of the heavy lifting goes to non-renewable fossil fuel plants...we will cook the planet, if we are not already there yet. All that automated physical energy needs electricity to power it. It's not like powering a computer or cell phone where you're just altering 1's and 0's on a solid state drive. You are replacing food fueled physical activity with electricity fueled physical activity. 

That is going to be one huge shock to our power grid and a nail in the coffin of our planet if we don't have the clean, renewable energy grid in place beforehand to power such a spike in electrical consumption.

Do Zac and Jessie agree? If not, perhaps you can do a video debunking these concerns?

Random Musings on the Future 

The accelerating advancement of technology indicates that essentially all manual labor jobs can either now or in the near future be replaced by machines. There is already farm machinery that automatically plows, plants, cultivates, and reaps crops (with one operator just along for the ride). Self-driving trains, planes, ships, trucks, and automobiles are not science fiction. They are inevitable. Robots are taking over manufacturing. Teslabot is being developed today to perform the boring, repetitive, and dangerous jobs that are currently done by humans. As this trend continues to its logical end; eventually, there will be no need for the "blue collar working class" as we know it today. The unanswered question is: How is society going to manage the millions of people who will be displaced and replaced by tireless machines? None of the economic systems in the world today adequately address this problem. Capitalism, socialism, and communism all assume there is a huge supply of labor available to perform the vital menial and repetitive jobs. When all those jobs are relegated to specialized machines controlled by Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (as I believe is inevitable), society must find ways to re-purpose the millions of people that will no longer be needed in those jobs. I do not have the answer to this problem, but here are some ideas: 

1) Testing - determine the aptitudes of the displaced workers. 
2) Education - train/re-train people to perform in fields for which they have aptitude and that require the ingenuity, insight, and/or imagination not present in machines (yet). The arts and STEM are potential areas to start, augmented by the feedback from idea 4). 
3) Minimum Standard of Living - Establish a minimum level of income, goods, and services that are provided to everyone and result in an acceptable quality of life for all. 
4) Market Forces - Let the competitive market (supply and demand) determine which job skills are worth more than the minimum standard of living, reward people in those fields according to the value of their skills, and ensure that the desired skill requirements are fed back into idea 2) to maintain the supply of valued skills. 

Idea 3) is akin to socialism and idea 4) is capitalistic. Maybe the future economic system should be called Sociocapitalism. I don't expect this change in the world's economics to happen in my lifetime, but the current trends seem to be heading that way.

When you quantify the value of our annual production/productivity here on Earth, please use "inflation-adjusted" Real GDP, rather than actual dollar GDP; otherwise you are vastly overstating the apparent growth since 1960. Since 1960, inflation has reduced the purchasing power of the U S. Dollar by 10-fold. Thus, $500 Billion in 1960 is equivalent to $5 Trillion today.

To quantify the total annual human production / productivity here on Earth, you might also include an estimate for the value of unpaid household services. In 1960, this value for the U.S. has been estimated at $228.7 Billion; adjusted for inflation since then, by 10-fold, this is equivalent to $2.287 Tillion in today's 2022 (current) dollars. In 2022, the value of these unpaid household services is estimated to be around $6 Trillion (in current 2022 U.S. Dollars).

Hey Zach and Jessie,  I love your show and have been watching it for quite some time, thanks for putting out all this content.  Tesla Bot is cool, but as someone who works in the AI industry, I think you're being overly optimistic on a couple of points.  Mainly onboarding and training costs.  It's not realistic to assume there won't be any such costs for the TeslaBot.  TeslaBot will still have to be trained for every job /  new task it needs to do.  Deep learning models need a lot of data to be effective, and each company will have different processes and thus won't really be able to share data amongst themselves.  Transfer learning will help with basic locomotion and object detection and stuff but training a process of specific actions is really a hard thing to do, just look at self-driving... Companies won't have to solve self-driving but they will have to come up with a large number of training examples (at least a couple hundred for low accuracy models i.e. mediocre bot performance) of their process to train the bot, and this will be a very expensive and challenging endeavor precisely cause it won't be shareable across companies or even across processes in a company.   And the same thing will happen every time you want to change a process, making process change likely more difficult than with humans, cause how are you gonna train the bot on the new process that nobody has ever done/seen before when the bot requires examples of a working process to be trained on?

Eventually, sure Tesla may develop an AGI, or come up with some novel approach to rapid training but nobody, including Tesla, is anywhere near that today, so I don't see TeslaBot being viable in the short term.  I think this is an extremely long-term play and wouldn't expect to see TeslaBot disrupts anything in the next five year, and probably not in the next decade either.  I hope I'm wrong, but I just don't see it happening very soon cause AI technology is far behind what is required here.  Certainly, Tesla is an innovator amongst innovators so if anybody can do it they can, but FSD is an easier problem to solve than rapidly learning any new process by a few orders of magnitude, so given how long they have been working on FSD, you can extrapolate that it'll take quite a while to get TeslaBot up to speed.

The flaw I see in this argument is how much effort will be required to train the bot to do a task.  Tesla is spending gazillion bucks a year working on autonomous driving, and is nowhere near actually making something that can do that single (admittedly complex) task.  Being able to handle unexpected issues while doing even a simple task will require a huge amount of training of the AI.  

AI is great at tasks that have limited deviations and where unrecognized situations are not catastrophic, such as handwriting or speech recognition.  Think how often Alexa doesn't understand a command, or your phone message gets mangled.  If the AI gets a word wrong, the human reading it can figure it out.  If the robot can't figure something out, it either breaks something or it stops and somebody has to go figure out the problem.  If the car can't figure something out,  it either crashes or it stops.  

Each of these 'errors' requires a new scenario to be defined, data collected on various permutations of the scenario, and then the AI retrains on the expanded dataset.  In complex cases this loop may never reach an acceptable level of performance (e.g. FSD), but in general some level of human intervention is required to resolve the remaining issues.  In addition, these tasks may actually have to broken up into separate subtasks and the robot has to stop and reload the next scenario to continue, which in turn may require a whole new logic to determine which scenario to use.  

Thus in addition to spending lots of money and expertise training the bots, for every X bots there needs to be a human 'minder' who may have to have skills much better than the humans who the bot is replacing.

This was a good review of the full value of a fully functional Bot. Non-employers are not aware of the myriad costs and inefficiencies associated with human labor.
That said, there are a few really important points to keep in mind:
1) The revolution is going to take quite a while. Bots are not going to be creating Bots in Gigafactories in a few years. For one, it doesn't even make sense as a use-case. The dumb, stationary robots we use now are more efficient for that. But, moreover, we'd be very lucky if they figure out how to make the mechanical body work well in that time, for general tasks. Just look at Boston Dynamics for an idea of how long that takes, and the limitations.

Then think about how long it's taking to get FSD's AI working. Over a decade, so far. Yes, much of their progress in training the AI, and in navigation, will carry over, but it's still going to take a long time to learn each new task. It's been this long "just" to stop, go, and steer on roads. A very complicated problem, but not compared to mimicking the average day of most workers. Most jobs involve a myriad of tasks, many of which are improv, which is the weak spot for AI. It will take quite a while to train the Bot for each new job they want it to do.

2) It's going to be a VERY long time before they make their way to homes, or other such environments. Supply will be limited for decades, which means they'll go to the highest bidders, which will be corporations, for the reasons laid out in the vid. They will be best at simple, repetitive tasks that are expensive to pay people to do. On both counts, this is the opposite of home chores. Homes will be literally the last place Bots end up, so put your patience cap on.

3) Finally, and most importantly, they will not guarantee any improvement in quality of life for humanity. It's easy to think they will do all the work we don't enjoy and that will leave humans free to pursue whatever we find meaning and happiness in. That is what SHOULD happen, but it will be up to politics whether it does. You have only to look at our current economy. We have the resources now (and for a long time) to increase free-time for everyone who wants it, provide much better compensation for work, and even provide a Universal Basic Income, which has been proven in countless studies to increase overall productivity, as well as health, happiness, and innovation. But, instead, we're still locked into a wage-slavery mindset and quality of life is fairly stagnant. We have more stuff, but not more freedom or happiness, than a century ago. Our productivity continues to skyrocket but it's not making much impact on the fundamentals of our lives. Automation has actually been suppressed, because of our insistence on wage-slavery. We choose to allow poverty, attaching basic needs to formal employment, and this provides a direct reason for workers to oppose automation, as it threatens their life. Innovation is suppressed by poverty. The auto union opposition to EVs is just one example. EVs take less workers to make, so workers try to suppress it. Our economic system is fundamentally self-defeating. Bots are a path to utopia, but we first have to muster the political and moral will to walk that path. Otherwise, we will fork into a dystopia, where people still require formal employment to live, but it's increasingly hard to come by.

I'd like to commend Zac & Jessie's suggestion to buy just one hedge trimmer, lawn mower, stimmer etc & share between neighbours. Not only is it cheaper, it's also much more efficient & easier on the planet's resource demands. If you can't afford any of this equipment, look online to see if there are any neighbourhood equipment sharing schemes in your area. Some of these schemes will offer free equipment loans in return for say, help with gardening or some DIY or maybe, housework; neighbours helping neighbours. Every scheme is slightly different.

A number of companies supplying the professional landscape community have also started to manufacture portable battery charging banks that allow company workers to swap out their batteries, for freshly charged batteries & continue working whilst the depleted battery gets recharged. This system is meant for instances where there isn't a convenient electrical socket available to plug in a charger. The battery charging banks are the ones that get plugged in overnight to charge & are sized in such a way as to make them easily loadable onto the back of a truck or trailer. 
Of course the advent of onboard electrical outlets on Utes might seem to make this equipment unnecessary, but as EV Utes come to the market, users may not wish to deplete their vehicle's battery pack, preferring to preserve range instead.
