I purchased the Ego line multi head power tool with: string trimmer, limb saw, hedge trimmer, extension pole, edger, non Ego brush cutter mod kit for string trimmer, a 5AH and 10AH battery, a backpack to hold heavy battery for long usage, a shoulder strap for multi tool for long usage and a bag to hold and transport most of the equipment easily. So far it all works great and I love it. Though the 5AH battery came with the tool it is no where near enough for me the 10AH battery really seems to be the way to go. The 10AH is not cheap but I will only be buying them in the future as I expand. Ego does sell a much larger backpack only battery but I can't afford that baby. And If I plan on further expanding my Ego line the 10AH batteries will be needed. Like with the snow blower, rider, and push mower equipment. For now I still have gas for those items for I can't afford to switch them yet. And it will take some time to be able to afford to do so working a fast food job. I already spent half my savings on the Ego stuff I have plus the gas backpack electric backpack blower. See comment below why I have to stick with gas for leaf blower for now. Our rider mower isn't just for mowing the lawn it is a work horse around the property we often use it for hauling loads around and up fairly steep hills. plus it is narrower than the big zero turn mowers and can fit down the walk paths. I'd like the Ego zero turn for mowing but for hauling stuff around the yard I'd still need the gas rider we have. The Ego is too wide for general purpose work. I may try and convert the gas rider we have to electric at some point referencing Jessie's walkthrough but I'm not there yet. It takes 8 1/2 hours to mow and trim this property.

As for our chainsaw I did get the Ego 18inch bar electric. I haven't had a chance to use it yet. Again we have a lot of giant old tress on our property and need some serious power to cut them up. I still have our gas chainsaw for now. The bar height is so narrow and the chain teeth are so small and spread out I have doubts It can cut up this larger trees but we will see. For the smaller stuff no question I'll be using the Ego.

For backpack leaf blowers the largest electric I could find were not powerful enough. Basically all the backpack electric I could find are no more powerful than the best handheld leaf blowers and in a few cases handhelds are actually more powerful. The backpack electric right now are mainly just getting the weight out of your hands. For light to moderate blowing they are great. But if you have a lot of yard and a lot of leaves you need more power. I got the HUSQVARNA 580BTS Mark II it is the most powerful I could find on the market at 941 cfm. We have a lot of giant old trees and that is a lot of leaves that require power to move. Plus the driveway is massive and can take a long time to clear off with out power. Now there is no reason why an electric can't be that powerful or more so, it is just that no one is making them that powerful as of yet. I did consider getting an old used one and trying to convert it myself. I hope at some point I will be able to do that with this one. For now It needs to remain gas until I have the time and will to try and figure out how to convert it. We have a handheld electric leaf blower that puts out around 600 cfm. About 4 years ago I bought a Greenworks 80V chainsaw.  The first one was a fail out of the box...wouldn't charge at all.  Exchanged and the second one was a winner.  Came with 2AH battery (3.48lbs).  The power was easily on par with my Stihl gas powered chainsaw.  The weight with this battery was very close to the Stihl.  Quiet...can't emphasize that enough.  Downside - battery died in about 15 minutes of serious bush work.  Sometime in that first year I forgot to charge the battery, went back to it a couple of months later and the battery would not take a charge.  Fast forward 3 years and I decided to buy a new battery...ended up with a 5AH (6lbs).  The saw now lasts about 30 min of serious bush work.  It is way to heavy with this battery but it is still my preference over the gas saw.  (my only other complaints is the safety control that requires the saw to be turned on through pressing a button if not used for X # of seconds...super irritating and of truly questionable value....but no pulling a cord to restart the saw).  On a typical day in the bush I will refill my saw 6 to 8 times depending on how much actual cutting I can do vs moving the wood around.  I would need an equivalent number of batteries to stay in the bush the same length of time. 5AH batteries are ~ $320CDN each, taxes in, plus delivery....so even 4 spares would cost me ~$1300.  It takes 75min to recharge according to the manufacturer (I have never timed it) but to charge all 5 batteries means I would need five chargers or switch batteries every 75min.  I would not recommend this saw for the homeowner....go for a lower voltage unit...and I would not recommend it for a pro for the reasons stated.  Despite the negatives I modified my firewood collection by cutting logs to 4ft in the bush, bringing them back to the yard and using a corded electric chainsaw to cut them into 16" lengths for splitting.  The corded saw is lighter, equally powerful and goes forever with the only maintenance being the same as the cordless - sharpening of the chain, topping up the chain oil and flipping the guide bar until it finally needs to be replaced.  Electric is the way to go...

I think another important point to consider here is how electric lawn care equipment can pair with electric vehicles, specifically most (or all) of the upcoming electric pickup trucks. Most commercial lawn care workers I see in my area use large diesel pickup trucks with trailers, and their equipment fills both the truck bed and the trailer. Most of these electric pickup trucks (and at least one hybrid pickup truck) have at least two standard wall outlets in the bed that can be used to charge spare batteries from the vehicle's larger battery.
At 11:23 Jessie stated that the EGO battery that comes with the EGO LB6003 is 420 Wh (which is EGO's 7.5 Ah battery, their 10 Ah battery is equivalent to 560 Wh), meaning that charging one of these 420 Wh batteries would deplete an F-150 Lightning (est 155 kWh pack, 300-mile range) by 0.27% or ~0.81 miles (1.3 km).
Realistically, even if one was pulling a trailer that decreased range by 50% and drove 100 miles per day, they could still charge almost 62 of those EGO batteries from the truck itself. That's 186 hours of runtime in the blower, or (using the 10 Ah batteries) this same amount of energy could power EGO's 42" Zero Turn Riding Mower for about 23 acres (~93 sq. km).
One could make a battery charger mount that can attach to the side walls of these truck beds and plug into the outlets, or if a product like the previously mentioned EGO riding mower is used, up to six batteries can be put into the mower and charged simultaniously using the mower's own single plug from an outlet. Using these kinds of charging systems within the vehicle could allow workers to put the batteries in their chargers in the bed, then plug the truck in overnight. By morning, they can head to their first job site without ever having to worry about things like "do I need to stop and fill up the truck?" or "are the batteries charged?" or especially "do I need to stop to fill the truck and equipment up with gas?"

Dear Zac, Jesse, and followers, 
great video, especially the health and economic benefits would be tremendous. Some people were asking for numbers, so here are estimations regarding efficiency and V2G compensation:  
Efficiency: American school buses use about 7 miles/gallon and travel 32 miles/day (nrel.gov), = 4.5 gallons/day. 
1 gallon of diesel = 40.7 kwh -> 180 kwh/day. A typical ICE vehicle efficiency is 20%, EVs are above 80%, so an electric school bus would need 45kwh per day, or 1.4 kwh/mile, possibly less as the 4.3 ton iridium electric motorhome uses only about 0.5 kwh/mile. 
Thus, a 100kwh battery (as in model S/X) would be sufficient for 70miles and thus 95% of all school bus routes. 

Regarding grid stabilisation: 1MW capacity is rewarded with about 100.000€/year in Germay. 100kwh batteries can be charged/discharged with about 250kw. Factoring in energy production costs, the fact that busses are not constantly plugged in, management cost, ect., each bus (or tesla) could earn about $10-15.000/year (done by "the mobility house" company in Germany). This requires supercharger-level charging stations, and will increase battery degradation.

Another idea: put solar on the roofs of the busses as well (as done on the Sion electric car). About 4.5kw peak could fit on a type C (most common) school bus. Those would provide almost 60% of the energy needed for the average bus (production about 4500 kwh/year, consumption 8000 kwh (32miles x 1.4kwh/mile x 180 days). Then, busses on shorter routes or in sunnier states would drive energy neutral. 

The high number or identical vehicles and the fact that those can be moved to few centralized factories will significantly reduce electric and solar retrofitting costs.

I must admit, as a holder of two software methodology patents myself, I just don't get the argument as to why software patents should not be allowed. What a patent protects, at the most basic level, is the hard work and resources that go into creating a new idea. Back in the Industrial Age, machines incorporated logic in mechanical workings. Today, that logic is called software and some of the most ingenious advances of the modern world are software advances. If IBM and others (Tibco comes to mind) couldn't protect their ideas around big data analysis, if Oracle couldn't protect ideas around super fast sorting or database mirroring, would they be motivated to pour hundreds of millions of dollars into advancing the state of the art? Not so much if anyone could simply come along and steal those technologies. 

Patents are linear and proportional in their protection of ideas. Consider those who would argue that something like slide to unlock is silly to protect with a patent. That it's an idea that isn't worthy of patent protection. But that's a fallacious argument; if its not worth much, then surely those who would infringe such a patent could simply apply a different method to solve the same problem. If you think a patented idea has no value then you should have no difficulty coming up with an equal or better idea. 

I think someone who sits at a desk and designs a novel software method to, say, vary the timing on an automobile engine, which can make an engine run more efficiently and produce more power without having to redesign the engine should be offered the same protection for her idea as the same person using a CAD program to design a new and novel engine architecture that yields the same efficiency and performance boosts, the only difference being the novel engine design actually gets turned into a physical device (an engine) and therefore satisfies the notion of a utility patent better in the mind of a person who is stuck in the Industrial Age.

Let's look at three scenarios:

Scenario #1: the invention is implemented completely in hardware.

Scenario #2: the invention is not able to be implemented solely in hardware, but requires a software element to control the hardware.

Scenario #3: the invention is implemented completely in software, modifying the timing and control of existing engine components and engine monitoring and control elements that might have been used to adjust the engine's valve timing to yield sport versus economy mode, but never to adjust timing continuously.

Let's just imagine, for the sake of argument, that any of these three means of inventing the first variable valve timing system were all possibilities. Variable valve timing clearly has value; it allows an engine to be more responsive to driver input while operating at higher efficiency.  The patent system exists to reward valuable innovation and invention. What's the argument for not providing those rewards in the second and third scenarios, above?

I've grappled with the dichotomy presented by the need to protect intellectual property versus the scourge that the non-practicing entity lawsuits represent.  

Perhaps the answer is to limit the royalties that can be demanded from patents that are not being applied (non-practicing) versus those that are applied in some product or service.  This would give greater protection and rewards to those who own patents and are using the patented technology in their products, because damage from infringement is higher versus damage to a non-practicing patent holder.  If you've gone through the expense of utilizing a patented process or mechanism, then you should be compensated greater when someone infringes that patent.  But if you haven't, and therefore also haven't brought a new product or service to market that allows society to benefit from the invention, then perhaps you shouldn't receive the same compensation for infringement. 

There's perhaps a bit of precedent here in the  FRAND royalty calculations for patents that are considered standards essential.  The whole notion of SEP is that there's a greater good to society to allow multiple parties to utilize an invention as part of a standard and therefore it should be affordable for all to utilize the patented invention. Same here.  Patented inventions that are sat upon don't benefit society, so there should be incentive to get those inventions into use.  

To give time for a new patent holder to develop products and services around a patented invention, perhaps the first few years after the patent is granted, it can be exempt from the rules I'm suggesting here.  The current status quo would remain in effect.  But after, say, three years, if you haven't shown that the patent is being developed into a product or service, then licensing limitations go into effect so that the amount you may charge for your invention will be limited, ala FRAND-type pricing guidelines.  So, if you don't intend to utilize a patented invention, either accept the lower royalty rates so that others can utilize it, or sell the patent to a company that will utilize it and therefore retain full royalty and infringement power over it.

This guy is great, but the concept behind the patent system is far more useful than its execution. The concept being: if you have an idea, you should be protected from theft of that idea for an amount of time deemed reasonable to take that idea from concept to reality. With perfect execution, this system would actively help the little guy. Since small businesses with a great idea can now be assured that even if their trade secret is leaked, any profit off of it by the thief can be sued for and won. 
In my opinion, the patent office must be funded enough to successfully investigate new patents to ensure they are new inventions. If denied, an inventor can appeal and prove that they invented it before it was brought to market. Experts can be called to verify, etc.
If an idea is sufficiently changed from an existing idea, a new patent may be granted as an improvement. In this way, if you iterate enough on an existing patent you can be reasonably assured that the improvement may also be protected.
Without a patent system, the little guy can be routinely stolen from. Consider the case of an inventor with no means to develop the concept further. With a patent, he can be assured that when he proposes his concept to a large company with the means to produce it, that company cannot steal his idea and produce it anyway.

I am retired now, but starting in 1982 had a small computer graphics hardware company.  One of the things our hardware could do was Exclusive OR (XOR) a byte of data into a video RAM. It's like a normal memory write, except instead of overwriting the stored data with the new, it stores the XOR of the new data with the old data.  XOR is a simpler, more fundamental operation in a CPU than addition.  There had long been computers that would do an add or an increment to memory.  A troll in Santa Clara informed us we had to buy a license from him because he had a patent on doing an XOR to RAM. That's like patenting addition.   I knew there was "prior art" on this, as the patent attorneys call it.  That is, there was commercial hardware predating his patent which also did XOR to RAM.  But the company I knew of was years out of business and I couldn't find any of their documentation.  I couldn't prove it.  Then I realized that Texas Instrument - a huge old Integrated Circuit making company - made graphics chips that did the same thing.  I called them and told them about the troll, figuring T.I,'s legal department would crush this guy.  I found they had paid his license fee! I think it was $25,000 plus an annual fee. For T.I., that was a pittance - much cheaper than taking the guy to court.  For my company at that time  it was very significant.  The trolls are the parasites of the tech business.

The GRID is next to get stranded. 
Our forebears built the grid to distribute power from centralised plants to all around. That is starting to roll back, with Australia and rural communities around the globe as examples. 
As energy is generated locally by solar plants, only 'filler' energy is needed. That lesser 'filler' energy is now transmitted from a far-off plant by long wires. 
Meanwhile, PV and batteries will become even cheaper. So you will also generate the 'filler' energy on your roof, which means that you've become self-contained.
Thus the grid transmits fewer energy units (kWh). But the grid cost remains the same. So each energy unit needs to carry a higher price (to replace the grid). 
Today the cost of replacement is disguised by the grid already being here.
But as the grid ages, we need to maintain and replace sections. At that moment, we calculate if there's still enough energy carried on the line to justify the cost of replacement.  
And so, already today, some transmission cables are not replaced. 
We're at the start of that particular S-curve, but it will soon accelerate. In 10 years, the grid will be unimportant, and in 15 years, it will be gone. And with that, all the power plants (nuclear, coal, gas, wind, solar, hydro) along the line will be stranded.
Mobile phones became accepted within a small group about 25 years ago. How many telephone lines do you still see today? The same will be true of solar panels on roofs and High Voltage transmission lines.
However, one does need to be aware of latitude (how close to the North and South Pole). Closer to the Poles, solar PV is not as effective as it is close to the equator. So wind still makes a lot of sense close to the (Ant-)Arctic. And there, transmission wires continue to make sense. 
But as solar becomes cheaper, wind power will lose importance. And thus the demise of transmission lines.

It appears obvious to me that Ambri's molten metal battery has to be kept hot in order to use it, and maintaining that heat is a cost to the system. What about combining that with molten salt storage for the first kiloWatt in (and last out), and using the molten metal battery for the second and third kiloWatt of storage?

It also strikes me that you wouldn't want to store away power for a rainy, overcast, day in anything that has to be kept molten. The energy to keep it molten is a constant cost, so better to store your rainy-day power in something with minimal maintenance costs. This makes this type of battery great for holding power for overnight loads, where the metal doesn't have to be kept molten for very long before it's used again, but maybe not for longer-duration storage, where it's kept charged.

Although that does bring up a good point. CAN the molten battery be allowed to solidify, with its charge locked-in, and re-melted to access that charge at a later date? If so, you'd need to be able to lock away more charge in the electrical potential than it took to bring it back to a molten state, (minus any power you could then salvage from the heat, once the battery was discharged, possibly to bring the next battery back to a molten state.)

Gravity batteries, including falling water for starters, and maybe those air batteries, make more sense for holding a charge for days, or even months, possibly Summer around to Winter, or from the winds of March around to a calmer, or rather becalmed, month. I suspect a gassed up air tank holds more of a "charge", for a year or better, with the compressors turned off and the valves closed, with fewer losses, than anything you have to keep hot to use. Even vacuum bottles lose heat through thermal bridging eventually.

I'm all for a transition to EVs. But this predicted 'death' of ICE vehicles by 2023, especially ICE trucks, is unrealistic. Here are 4 reasons why...

1) It took MANY DECADES and hundreds of billions of dollars to build the current refueling infrastructure (stations, pipelines). Building an equivalently scaled, standardized recharging infrastructure, plus an enlarged electrical grid, plus widely dispersed recharge stations (even in rural areas), will not occur within 5 years (2023), and certainly not to the scale needed to support ~50 million EVs.

2) Most nations and their citizens simply do not have the financial resources to abruptly (~5 years) transition the bulk of their transport vehicles and infrastructure. This is also true of countries with an aging demographic and citizens with a fixed income.

3) EVs extensively use materials such as Niobium, Lithium, Cobalt, etc. These are not currently produced in sufficient volume to support annual production of many tens of millions of EVs. Some of these are rare earth materials which may NEVER be available in large annual quantities. Limited availability of rare earths may also raise the cost of future EVs beyond what projected 'economies of scale' might otherwise suggest.

4) Truck owners commonly travel much longer distances than commuters/cars. They also tow heavy loads, greatly reducing range before refueling/recharging is required, often ON THE ROAD. Until recharging can be accomplished as quickly (5 minutes, 10 max) and as readily as gas/Diesel stations, this will limit electric truck sales.

Regarding a drop in oil prices, they probably won't be so dramatic. Increasing extraction costs place a 'floor' on the price. This lower limit will automatically reduce production and gluts by closing the wells that aren't profitable.

Another thing not taken into consideration is the aging of the US population. I, for example, owned a sedan from 2005-2015. I now own a small SUV which sits higher off the ground and is much easier to get into and out of. At the tie, hybrid versions were a little out of my price range and there weren't as many choices. In the space of three years, that has changed. There are more hybrid SUV's and I expect the prices to level off and start to drop overall.

Another problem I have is that, where I live, the SUV I own will not fit in my garage. I have to leave it parked outside. So, if I were to buy a plug-in hybrid, I would have to build a shelter for it separate from the house to charge it. . Since the temperature range where I live can be as low as 20F degrees and as high as 97F degrees, the shelter would be mandatory.  I could put solar panels on top of it which would help with the charging (or, for that matter, on top of the house itself), but I would still require a connection to the electricity grid if things failed. 

Which brings me to another worry: The generation and distribution of electricity in the country is not expanding fast enough to meet the rising demand. I have come to the conclusion that the current model of generation and distribution is going to have to change. The current model is based on "stars". You have large generating stations which then distribute the electricity though wires for hundreds of miles. We need to go to a smaller model: You will have more, smaller, generating facilities which are much close to the user and a distribution network which "shares the load" so that the loss of a single station does not result in the loss of power to that region. This kind of system would include generation of electricity at private locations (homes, businesses, etc). 

As a result, the concept of electrical generation and distribution being owned by a single entity will have to cease to exist. There is no other way. 

With all of this, it is simply not enough to start thinking outside the box. We need to realize "There is no box."

Unfortunately, we live in a country in which change occurs only when the crisis is upon us. 

To solve our future problems will require a whole new level of genius from the level of genius it takes to define them.

I think the biggest problem with this is the assumption that everybody wants an EV right now. Ford had a hard time convincing truck buyers that a 6 cylinder turbo engine was ok in a truck instead of a V8 (and they've had to continue offering a traditional V8 because a lot of F150 buyers couldn't be convinced). Chevy still uses big pushrod (read: antiquated) V8s in their trucks and they sell like hot cakes. Do you really think those same truck buyers will be easily convinced that electric is the way to go? I think we're going to see a curve much more similar to the adoption of ICE cars. It's going to take a lot longer than 5 years to convince Joe the plumber to buy an electric truck, especially when gas prices start to plummet.
Furthermore, I don't think the slowing of car sales has nearly as much to do with the EV revolution as it does with shifting consumer preferences. The fact is, there are electric SUVs out there (Tesla Model X and soon the Model Y, and now the Jag I-Pace). If the dip in car sales was due to a looming and dramatic shift to EVs I think we would see it in the SUV market as well. But former car buyers are now simply buying SUVs because they want the high driving position, increased interior space, and "active lifestyle" cool factor. 
Finally, this isn't as big an improvement as cars over horses. ICE cars can still do almost everything EVs can, and they can do it cheaper. There's also an intermediate option (hybrids) that may make the transition slower. A plug in hybrid will probably be a lot more tempting to someone whose skeptical of full electric cars, but will offer a lot of the same advantages. Don't get me wrong, I think the electric revolution is coming, I just think it's a lot more than 5 years off. Probably somewhere between that conservative prediction early in the video and the rapid 5-year prediction.

There seems to be a lot of assumptions with several holes in the article. GM is not just killing off their sedan models. They're also ending EV models due to lack of demand. 15 of the top 20 selling models in the US are trucks, SUV's and crossovers.
Most people in the market for a new vehicle do not wait three years to buy a vehicle. People that wait three years would be in the used market today.
The other hole is that if oil (and gas) continue to be less expensive, the comparative attraction to EV's diminishes.
Yet another hole is ignoring the developing markets in China and India which are continuing to increase their demand for oil.
If we drop back down to $1.50 gas, I'd look for bigger vehicles and more people traveling freely as they'll be less concerned with the cost of transportation.
As to the reversal of oil exports in 2016, fracking. Daily US oil production has doubled since 2012, but natural gas was a bigger driver than oil. Affordable oil makes competing technology less attractive.

Touching on the GM plant closures. In the grand scheme of things, GM is actually having a good run at the moment. They are not closing plants because their vehicles aren't selling, quite the contrary at the moment, they're closing them because they see the shift happening and they're making changes proactively instead of reactively (for once). They're closing plants before the demands for those vehicles drop off at all and they find themselves lagging far behind, hemorrhaging money.

Now, the first part of your video pointed out something about the history of certain technologies on why they took longer to adopt. Specifically, electricity and telephones. Why? You mentioned it; the time it took to fully implement INFRASTRUCTURE. The internet is an exception because at its implementation it largely piggy-backed off existing telephone line infrastructure anyway before broadband became widespread with DSL and cable (and even then, much of that was already existing infrastructure too--the only thing really new was T1/3 lines and fiber--and those most certainly don't go everywhere). Why I believe EV sales won't ramp up as quickly as some proponents like yourselves believe is for that exact same reason. ICE still has a very large convenience factor over BEVs. Honestly, plug in hybrids will make a LOT of sense in this transition period. Plug ins that allow you to do 90-95% of your driving on battery power only, but on the occasion you need to do longer trips, the ICE engine as range extender makes a ton of sense. The maintenance won't be as cheap as a pure BEV, of course, but still, if you can do the vast majority of your daily driving needs on battery power in that vehicle, it will become an attractive package, especially for those who don't or can't own multiple vehicles.

For the people who do long distance driving frequently, ICE will still be king for the convenience/speed factor alone of minimizing time spent stopped refueling/charging. Those people are in the minority, of course, but it's important to allow the market to do what it will in this case as one type of vehicle most definitely does not fit all.

All that having been said, BEVs as it is do make a compelling case just on the cost of operation and lack of required maintenance alone. Once the ranges become long enough and, once again, the infrastructure is in place, EVs will absolutely take over. But do not underestimate the time it takes to beef up the grid for the extra energy demands along with the actual infrastructure of charging stations being plentiful enough for this massive increase in demand. If the infrastructure lags in its expansion/implementation, you will find it slowing down adoption rates, especially if charging stations end up being so in demand that it becomes a challenge to find an open space to charge your vehicle.

Despite the lack of maintenance being a big plus for BEVs in terms of convenience, if the convenience factor in daily use isn't high enough (read: difficult to find charging stations where open slots are not in competition), they won't buy it. At the end of the day, that is what technological advances are for: added convenience.

I have no doubt a breakthrough in battery capacity and charge times will happen that flips my script here, but until that day comes and until the infrastructure is made convenient for the vast majority of vehicle owners out there, you will still find a number of people stubbornly clinging to their internal combustion vehicles. And if the oil prices do indeed drop precipitously as EV use displaces the use of much of the oil, the more efficient internal combustion vehicles may start to come close on the cost per mile of energy basis, which erodes one of BEV's current advantages and thus to some making it a case where ICE still makes sense for their needs (in particular, the long distance drivers).

The next decade of transition will be interesting to watch unfold, that is for sure.

I would say there's a significant flaw in assuming the quick adoption of devices in the 1990s and 2000s equates to people willing to quickly adopt a new kind of powered vehicle. The precedent of quick adoption of things like smartphones, tablets, cameras, etc. needs to take into consideration that the factories, procedures and materials required for building and maintaining them were already scalable and nimble based on the previous technology i.e. you don't have to drastically change supply chain to start making an iTouch after you've been producing iPods for a short amount of time. You don't need to completely rewire all of the continental United States in order to plug in and power your new iTouch while your iPod collects dust. Etc. Etc.

The production and maintenance of vehicles is not as nimble. The factories are probably not as bad to convert since the shell of an electric vs. combustion engine is similar. However, what will slow down the adoption of electric vehicles is the ability for people to conveniently access recharge stations. Recharging these vehicles takes a lot of juice. It's not just building new stations or retrofitting gas stations, you're talking about ensuring that most electric grids connected to the likes of Shell and Circle K can now support these electric cars soaking up hundreds of millions of additional kWh per year (which will increment over time, BTW, as adoption grows). It's that + the idea of these unorganized, enormous corporations being efficient enough to quickly roll out new charging equipment. These are just some of the reasons - I've typed too much already - that I think the transition rate is being blown out of proportion. It will inevitably happen, but I'm not sure how fast. I, personally, don't want two vehicles. This means I will be holding off on an electric vehicle until I can reliably go 300-400 miles at a time in at least an entire State's encompassing border. Just an honest thought :)

That said, the predictions on EVs are accurate, but there's one HUGE caveat - and elephant in the room - which noone's talking about. "Where are you going to get all the extra electricity from?"

To explain: The amount of annual electrical generation required in any given western country (US or Europe, Australia, NZ, etc)  to go to a mostly-electric vehicle fleet is somewhere between 1 and 2 times the amount of electricity those countries were producing in the 2001-2005 years (ON TOP of whatever they were already producing)

IE: We're going to have to double or triple electricity production - and quite simply the infrastructure isn't  in place for that, NOR is sufficient forward planning being applied to deal with the looming issue (It takes decades to build the number of power stations needed). The next big question is "how are we going to fuel that electricity production?"

Even if we go flat out on renewables (wind, solar, hydro and tidal) we could just about match the electricity production levels of 2001-2005 with them (you start running into fundamental limits of what's extractable ) - which means if there's a push to reduce carbon emissions we're stuck between a rock and a hard place - and if we have to eliminate carbon from domestic heating (gas/oil-fired heating systems are likely to end up banned in many places by 2030 due to pollution in large cities - they're responsible for 60% of the NOX in London UK for example), etc that's another multiple of the electricity production requirement. 

You can work on the basis of an increase in requirements of around 8 times 2002 electrical production if you go for a mostly-electric transport fleet (including rail), electric domestic heating and electricity replacing most carbon-consuming industrial processes. Electric aircraft are a non-starter (you can do it for short range hoppers at cost of longer on-ground dwell time, but not for long-haul, which means carbon-neutral fuel production is going to be required)

To compare the adoption chart for EVs to that of telephone, radio, refrigerators, PCs, etc, is absolute NONSENSE.  Why?  BECAUSE THOSE THINGS ENABLED HUMANS TO DO SOMETHING THAT THEY COULD NOT DO BEFORE.  Telephones enabled personal communication across a distance.  Radio enabled wireless audio mass communication, and television enabled video mass communication, neither of which existed before.  Refrigerators enabled people to keep food cold without needing to get ice every day or two.  Digital cameras enabled people to process images without requiring the cost and mess and time necessary for chemical processes.  Desktop computers enabled a single human to have the functionality of a major media corporation of the 1960s.  Mobile phones enabled wireless personal communication.  The internet sped up the delivery of information perhaps a million-fold.

I'm not saying you're wrong in terms of EVs eventually cutting down on the price of oil.  However, you have one major mis-concept-- PEOPLE AREN'T BUYING EVs BECAUSE THEY ARE EVs!  

EVs DO NOT ENABLE HUMANS TO DO ANYTHING SUBSTANTIALLY DIFFERENT THAN ICE VEHICLES.  A vehicle is TRANSPORTATION, with perhaps some element of status involved.  An EV does the exact same thing a car from 1910 did-- it enables the application of torque to rubber wheels to move a passenger compartment along a road.  Press on the accelerator and steer, brake when necessary.  Certain functions are getting automated, but that automation can be employed by ICE vehicles as well.

IT STILL TAKES TIME AND MONEY TO RE-FUEL AN EV.  Heck, the connector even looks just like a gasoline pump nozzle!  Aside from the lack of engine noise, the casual observer couldn't tell the difference between an EV and an ICE vehicle.  EVs aren't going to get you where you want to go any faster, and they aren't going to take you any farther.  Whether they can get you there any cheaper remains to be seen.

THE ONLY WAY THAT EVS WILL TAKE OVER THAT QUICKLY IS IF ICE VEHICLES ARE OUTLAWED OR ELECTRICITY BECOMES AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE CHEAPER.  Otherwise, ICE vehicles will linger in use for a long time.  Unless they become economically undesirable, there will be absolutely no reason for anyone to ditch them, especially if gas goes down in price.  With greater electricity use, electricity rates will necessarily go up.

You missed part of a reason that the truck segment is still doing fine: rural areas.

If you live in, by geography, most of the US, your commute is easily 10x the length of a commute for someone living in a city or suburb.  When you're driving that much, the ability to quickly 'gas up', and the limited charge-cycles of lithium-ion batteries, both matter vastly more.  Current battery and charging technology pose a significant constraint to EV sales in rural areas for that reason.  Even the ability to recharge a car overnight at home may not always be sufficient, particularly as the power grid in more rural areas often goes unfixed after weather events while priority is given to urban areas.  And when you live in an area like that, distance to repair facilities also comes into play; the the sort of Apple model that Tesla practices is far less viable when you're facing a 60+ minute tow to the nearest store v.s. being able to repair it yourself.

I live in the city personally, but even still an EV is not currently a viable option - no way to charge it from my apartment complex, the nearest supercharger is 40 minutes away, and the local chargers are all individual things in bank parking lots that (A) are inconveniently located, and (B) would take an entire day to charge.  Then there's the fact that some people (like myself) rather like long road-trips, and even super-chargers are quite slow at that scale compared to gas.

The other consideration is purely aesthetic; go and find 5 people driving a big pickup truck and show them pictures of the EVs you showed, and ask them if they would rather drive it - 4 of the 5 are going to turn up their nose purely because they like ICE trucks.

In the general direction of the curves I can buy most of that, but the slopes of the curves I question.   EVs have a resistance factor and it is the combination of range and recharge time.   A Chevy Bolt will go 240 miles on a charge but if you run her dead flat and don't have  fast charger, you have to let it charge for 71 hours.   Three days.   That ain't acceptable.   My old sedan goes 250 miles and refuels in three minutes.   That range/recharge limits the EV to the urban commute niche.   that niche has never been profitable for anybody regardless of technology.   If somebody has to cough up $40,000 for a car, it has to be capable of the occasional road trip.   The Bolt does not fit the bill.

Also for general purpose use an EV has to be more comfortable than the Bolt.   It is too cramped to displace the room and utility of either a sedan or a SUV.   Pickups?   I'll reserve judgment.

Also the EV still has to slay its historic dragon:  Poor battery performance.   Who killed the old GM EV-1?   Nobody.   it's crummy lead-acid battery killed it.   The lithium-ion battery offers better performance but heat buildup has caused fires.   Ask Boeing about lithium-ion batteries in 787s.    What is the service life of the battries.   The cars are simple and should last for years if you don't wreck them but the batteries are a huge question mark.

Another thing militating against the EV.   The US is almost at energy autarky.   It has oil and gas enough to last for centuries.   The US DOES NOT have a lot of lithium and cobalt so is back to importing its energy needs.   Bad idea.

So the whole thing isn't the inevitability you claim.   Its like fusion energy.   We know it works but scaling is always an issue in engineering.   We can make craters out of Pacific Islands using fusion but we've been trying to scale fusion down for at least four and a half decades.

The final end point may be accurate but there is a great deal of work that has to be done.

There is another couple of  factors that do not seem to have been taken into account. If you live in a house with a car porch or garage installing a charge point is relatively easy. However if you are on floor 6 of a block of flats (apartment block in the US) dangling a wire out the window is not so practical. Then there is the distribution issue. An electric car uses more than double what a house uses if it is driven 80+ miles per day. The US and UK simply do not have a grid capable of distributing that much power. In fact the UK only has at best 25% reserve capacity on a budget of 7.5kWh per day per household which is less than 2kWh per day. Yes individual houses can take far more than that but the bottom line is the sub stations are 5MW and power up to 1400 homes. That's roughly 10kWh per house per day running at absolute maximum and 7.5kWh per day running normally. There are a number of flaws with this argument. Flaw #1 is the assumption that people will not be buying ICE vehicles because they are waiting for EVs. This at best will probably be a partial truth. Some people will indeed be waiting for them, keeping their old ICE vehicles on the road longer for this reason. But this will almost certainly not be the only reason. Another reason may well be that, just like with houses, we are running short of people who can afford a new vehicle, period. I count myself as one of them. My present ICE truck has been on the road for twenty years and has 300k miles on it. It may well have to do another 100k before I'm able to replace it. And then I may be forced to do without a motor vehicle entirely. Flaw #2 is the assumption that the EVs are a panacea for everyone. Not now and most likely not for a long time. They require very expensive batteries which wear out after a number of years. I do not see myself as being able to afford a vehicle like this ever. Also, except for ones powered by hydrogen fuel cells, they have very hard range limits. Under ideal circumstances, you may be able to get 300 miles between charges. But after that, what then? Suppose I want to drive this thing from Detroit to Florida. I get almost to the Kentucky line then now I have to recharge. How long is that going to take? Most likely hours. I can gas up in a few minutes then be on my way with an ICE vehicle. If I have a buddy driver I can make the trip in maybe 25-30 hours. How long would it take with my new EV? Probably days. If it took me 30 hours to make the trip with my ICE vehicle it would likely take me at least 45 hours, fifteen of those would be waiting for the battery to recharge. Flaw #3 is that motor vehicles are not like tablet computers or even cell phones. With each of those, the switch was easy, optional and relatively cheap. I can do without a  tablet computer. I do not have one now. I made the switch to a cell phone because the operating cost offered to me was actually cheaper than what I was being charged for the old land line. Making the switch from ICE vehicles will be neither. If I buy a used EV, it will likely need a new battery. If I buy a new one, I will have to figure out how I will come up with the $10,000 or more I would need to replace the battery after just 7 years or so. What? A new loan? Even while I'm paying the old one off?  Your adaption curves are very pretty but not very convincing.  Flaw#4 is that you assume that the supposed glut of oil will not move demand in the other direction. Haven't you guys ever heard of an indifference curve? If gasoline suddenly gets cheaper, wouldn't a lot of people be enticed to stick with ICEs? And wouldn't a number of manufacturers be tempted to pump out new ones?

2013... what was I doing in 2013?  I was designing a battery electric race car 😀
March 2014 we were racing, June 2014 set electric record at the Mt. Washington hill climb, September set top speed electric record at Pocono raceway, June 2015 third fastest electric up Pikes Peak, lots of other records since then.  Since 2015 you have Formula E and other electric race cars as well, yet there has been no noticeable shift in the motorsports paradigm away from ICE to electric.  Historically innovation for automobiles comes from motorsport (think supercharging, turbocharging, hydraulic brakes, disc brakes, aerodynamics, electrically adjustable suspension... heck, even rear-view mirrors and seat belts first appeared on race cars) so I don’t think electric drivetrains are going to be any different.  Once Americans see electrics racing NASCAR and at their local circle tracks then they will consider electrics for their daily drivers, but until then I suspect most Americans will see electrics as a “stupid cars for rich left-wing liberal SJWs who like to smell their own farts.” (That’s a quote from a neighbor of mine, regarding my electric race cars).  Personally I liked the electric drivetrain in my race car so much that I traded my Lotus for a Tesla, and one of my drivers (who has a Corvette, Lotus, and Porsche in his driveway) bought a Spark for his daily commute, and another driver (who raced a 600hp Camaro before he joined the team) just bought a Model X.
Don’t misunderstand me, I’m not knocking the idea that electrics will come to dominate the automotive market, but looking at how little electrics have penetrated motorsports and how “what wins on Sunday sells on Monday” still drives the market I think that 5 years is too optimistic a timeline.
Having said that, the point that people are postponing buying a new car until they can replace their ICE car with electric is a really good point.  I have a friend who just two weeks ago explicitly told me that he wants to replace his Camry with an electric, so he will keep his car until such time as I am ready to trade in my Tesla, and he will buy my Tesla.  So, just as stated in the video, an ICE car sale lost, with the matching new electric car sale not happening for two or three more years.

There's a big assumption being made here that deserves to be highlighted.  EV sales by manufacturers other than Tesla are NOT accelerating.  People do not want EVs, they want Teslas.  The challenge for other automakers is to design and build a car as compelling as a Tesla.  It's not just a matter of replacing an ICE/transmission with an electric motor and battery.  Tesla has substantially increased the standard for what constitutes a great car.  Not just for electric cars, but all cars.  Tesla has turned the auto industry business paradigm upside down.  It is not going to be easy for GM, VW, of Toyota to match what Tesla has done.   There are so many cultural, technological, human resource, sales and support, supply chain, and financial barriers that will have to be overcome, and Tesla is already years ahead and growing at an incredible speed.  Thus, the conversion to EVs is going to be very lopsided.  Tesla, if they can manage growth effectively, is going to experience huge market share increases while other automakers will struggle just to survive.  Watch for auto industry consolidations, acquisitions, and bankruptcies to be the big story as 2023 approaches.

Edit:  
I think VW has a better shot at surviving the EV revolution than many other legacy car makers, but it will still be a struggle. Volume is key, and there are too many forces limiting the volume of EVs they can be produced in the next several years. It doesn't matter that VW can produce 11 million ICE vehicles annually today.

In the U.S. VW and other car makers don't have the charging infrastructure that is essential for EV mass sales. Electrify America will help, of course, but the capital commitment so far (penalty for diesel cheating) is inadequate to compete with Tesla's already extensive and still growing Supercharger network.

Battery supplies are also a limiting factor. VW has written contracts for $48 billion of EV batteries through 2025. Depending on the cost of those batteries, say, optimistically, $100/kWh, that's 480 GWh of batteries. That's 12 times the current annual production of Li-ion batteries at Tesla's Gigafactory 1 which currently produces more EV batteries than the rest of the world combined. VW will be competing against Mercedes who just signed contracts for EV batteries worth $20 billion dollars. The competition for EV batteries across the industry will be fierce.

Tesla and Panasonic spent $5B so far on GF1. The huge investment in new battery factories will have to be recovered in the price manufacturers charge for their batteries which will be much higher than Tesla's costs, and supplies will go to the highest bidders. Strained battery supplies and high costs will limit the ability of VW and others to produce EVs at volumes necessary to achieve positive gross margins . It doesn't matter what VW's or Toyota's current ICEV production capacity is. As ICEV sales continue to slump, these factories will become liabilities, not assets. We can expect more factory closings in the future as is already happening in the U.S. under GM and Ford.

The gap and jump to higher sales of EVs than ICE will happen with 2 curves involved - downward pressure on price of EVs (with increasing range above 350 miles), and coming out of a recession.  We're due for a big recession given historical trends.  That tends to really dampen new vehicle sales by individuals as the 2008-11 period shows.   People hang onto what they have until they feel the economy is safe to step into again...

Once things are looking up again and the economy has trimmed out some inefficiencies hanging over, fresh sales will move to the  then more advanced vehicles, which have gotten incrementally better in the intervening recession years...     Range and remoteness/charging issues will keep ICE's viable for a long, long time in certain spaces.   

Also, the rolling fleet is very large and it takes the better part of 2 decades to flush it toward new vehicles - not all new vehicles actually scrap out a prior vehicle... those hangers on find new users.  Because those ICE vehicles will be floating around and crude prices will drop dramatically on lower demand, they'll be more economical to run compared to buying a new EV...which will stall some out longer...

Where I think you'll see fairly high adoption rates will be in light pickups where fleet managers know they have specific range-bound patterns and can justify them on lessened maintenance and fuel charges, mostly in city driving patterns. My wife and I recently moved into a 1970's tract house, which was built with a gas furnace and gas water heater.  We had those replaced with heat pump versions: a Waterfurnace brand "ground-source heat pump" (GSHP) and a Rheem "hybrid" water heater (with an air-source heat pump).  Our back yard was too small for a horizontal layout so they brought in a drilling rig and sank three vertical wells.  We also got a heat-recovery ventilator (HRV) which I highly recommend.  I tell people that while the up-front cost was high, it will pay for itself over time, and our air quality in our house is fantastic.  Also, last year our area had a 100-year heat wave and set the record for the highest temperature ever recorded, and the Waterfurnace had no trouble keeping our home cool, so our quality of life was improved as well.  Zac and Jesse, if you have any questions about our experience with the Waterfurnace or the Rheem water heater heater, let me know and I'll get in touch.

P.S. I know I'm lucky to be able to afford the high up-front cost of this and I wouldn't dream of trying to shame anyone who feels they can't afford the expense of a GSHP installation. EV's have to become much cheaper, batteries have to be sourced, Solar, Wind, Nuclear have to be increased, etc. I am in favor of increasing fossil fuel production and at the same time providing substantial subsidies for clean energy and EVs. Tax oil and gas to help pay for the transition. Thinking that somehow we can flip a switch and make the transition happen is naive. It will take time and a lot of government effort and support. As gas prices rise, lower income families are hurt the most. Not only does the cost of filling our tanks increase but the cost of everything we buy (which must be shipped to us) increases as well. Most people can't afford the payment for an EV. They are stuck with ICE cars for the foreseeable future. We need to bring fuel prices WAY down. At the same time, we need to offer generous incentives to help as many as possible afford EVs. The government is going to have to make substantial commitments to upgrading and fortifying our power grid and greatly expand the existing charging infrastructure. We also have to stop spending money on fuel from overseas. There is plenty of oil and natural gas in the US and those dollars would add, rather than subtract from our GDP. The correct answer is go hard on US energy production with the long-term focus on green energy. It is going to taking tremendous capital investment to get to green. We need a way to pay for it and provide reasonable cost solutions to the consumer until we get there.

New supercharger stations are now under construction in Fargo ND (intersection of I-94 and I-29) and in Drydon and Ignace, Ontario, on the last gap of the Trans-Canada Highway over Lake Superior. However there are still a few other important gaps in the Interstate system that are uncrossable by most Teslas:
I-25: 255 miles from Wheatland, WY, to Sheridan, WY.
I-15: 337 miles from Butte, MT, to Lethbridge, AB.
I-40: 339 miles from Little Rock, AR, to Oklahoma City, OK.
All of these are in very remote, sparsely populated regions, except for the I-40 gap from Little Rock to Oklahoma City. I-40 is a heavily traveled, major conduit connecting the eastern and western halves of the mid-southern portion of the country. It can currently only be traversed by the longest range Model S. It is hard to see how this gap has remained for such a long time. I would hope that this would have the highest priority of the remaining gaps, but it is nice to see that a mere 3 supercharger stations could make the entire US-Interstate and Trans-Canada highway systems entirely traversable by even the shortest range Teslas.

So, while it's become fashionable to find fault with Tesla service, this has not been my experience or the experience of those I know with Teslas. 

First, the cars are super reliable....most reliable car I've ever owned. (Mine is a 2019 DRLM Model 3). But contrary to what seems to be floating around the internet (thanks to Rich Benoit), our service experiences have been simply superb.

For me I've had a couple of problems that were quickly diagnosed remotely (by quickly, I mean within 15 minutes) and were "fixed" via firmware updates. No fuss, no muss. Had these things happened with another brand I would have had to bring the car into the dealer and find that they couldn't find or fix the problem....and waste a whole bunch of my time.

The hardware issues I've had with the car have been a broken windshield (the fault of a rock, not the car), and a collision (the fault of the drivers, not the car). In the case of the windshield I created a service request online, they scheduled it for about a week out, I brought the car in, they gave me an Uber voucher, and I picked the car up later that day. No problems at all...and Tesla's price was the lowest I could find.

In the case of the collision, this happened about 1PM on a Saturday. My car was hit by another car, which in addition to doing some body damage, hit the left front wheel, bending the tie rod and wrecking the steering rack. The car was barely drivable, but I managed to limp into the Tesla Service Center mid-afternoon. Although they were "closed", there were people inside working on cars. One of the folks came out and asked my what had happened. He asked me for the key card and told me they would take care of it.

Monday morning at 8AM I was going to call them, but I noticed that the phone app said my car was already in service mode....so I concluded they found the car. About 15 minutes later I got a call from them asking what had happened and would I authorize 1 hour labor to diagnose the problem. 45 minutes later I got a comprehensive written estimate to replace the rack and the 4 worn out tires. I approved the work and noted that they said the car would be ready by 5:15 THAT DAY. At 1:15 I received another message saying the car was ready to be picked up!

To say that I was impressed is an extreme understatement. 

The only other hardware issue was a clicking sound in the door hold open bars. (a common issue) I created a service request on the app and was offered a slot a few weeks out at the nearest Tesla center or a slot about a week out at a center about 20 miles away. I chose the nearer center as this was not a critical problem. 15 minutes later I received a message saying that this could be fixed at my home and asked me to select a date/time. I did, they came, they fixed the car quickly, and that was that.

To be clear, this level of service is FAR SUPERIOR to anything that I've ever experienced with maybe 20 other new vehicles. As far as I'm concerned Tesla service is simply better than what other manufacturers can offer with their dealer model. 

So, while Rich Benoit puts of videos of sad stories he curated (well, cherry picked), the reality for the vast majority of Tesla owners is far different. Basically, while Tesla service isn't perfect (but then neither is that of BMW, Audi, Mercedes, Porsche, Toyota, Honda, Detroit), in the case of the recent "horror story" videos that have been circulating, I believe them to intentionally misrepresent the reality. They are FUD.

While I really like my Tesla car, I would say that the entire ownership experience, including service, is so much superior to that I've received from any other make, I would be tempted to buy a Tesla vehicle for this reason alone.

A more apples to apples comparison would be to compare the number of moving parts EV and ICE service stations may service in the U.S.

A conservative estimate places the number of moving parts at 20 for EVs and 200 for ICE vehicles. 1.02 million registered EVs as of Y/E 2020 times 20 moving parts divided by 148 Tesla service stations translates to 138,000 moving parts per Tesla service station.

275 million ICE vehicles (your figure) times 200 moving parts divided by 234,000 service stations (your figure) translates to 235,000 moving parts per ICE service station.

The above assumes all 1.02 million EVs are Teslas (they are not), uses a very conservative 200 moving parts for ICE vehicles as opposed to 2,000+, and does not give credit for the service vans.

Not saying your concerns aren't valid but based on the above back of the napkin calculation, Tesla users have a shorter potential wait time than their ICE equivalents already.

Lastly, The Tesla website lists four service stations in your state, is this incorrect? Your video states there are only three and you gave credit for one more due to the service vans.

Dedham
Norwell-98 Accord Park Dr
Peabody-North Shore

I had to use the breaks. the heat was working fine. Other things warnings were coming I don't remember what they were things that you can't turn off just started being turned off. I could punch the accelerator just a little and the car would fish tail around easily in the snow. Finally decided to just call and gave up on the app since there was no way to describe the problem I was having. Talked to someone and they were like "Oh that does not sound good, we can send a tow truck to you right now, but that could be an hour or two can you drive it to service centre?" I was like "I've already driven hours with things being scary so yeah kids are in their car seats and crankiness starting to set in".

I actually remembered seeing a Tesla centre from the highway on the way there to this unfamiliar part of Canada. I used the navigation and it sent me to this really quiet looking industrial area. And it was just after boxing day. I was worried we would get there and there would be no tesla centre, I didn't know how to really confirm so I just did it. Driving down this road surrounded by CLOSED car dealerships I was starting to get really worried. Finally saw the Tesla sign and was super happy. Drove in parked in front the service door. Nothing happened. I went into the showroom in a slight panic. Had ketchup on my shirt. 2 people at desks in this giant room. The usual Tesla centre. Guy comes up to me and engages and I go into the explanation about the car being weird. I did everything I could and I can't really drive this 5 hours home now. After talking to him he eventually says. "oh I'm just a sales guy you have to wait for this guy who is currently on the phone". Remember whole family is out in the car still waiting for me. So I stand there and I just try and look cool. Hotel hair dirty shirt. And it seems like forever but it was probably 10 minutes maybe. Finally he's off the phone and I tell the whole story. He then says "Ok, we'll get you in as soon as possible but that might not be for an hour and your issues sounds like it could take some time to fix". He did some computer search thing. Then I just had to park the car and wait... There was nobody else there.

We ate our lunch in the Tesla waiting room. They got me a nice industrial extension cord so the kids could use the laptop on the kids table. Unloaded the family and we waited. After they realized that my issue was real they were very considerate, but my initial impression was that he thought I was exaggerating. 3 and half hours later. The tech manager came to talk to use about every half hour which was really nice. They offered to somehow give me a loaner car and do the logistics later since I informed them where home was. Problem was.... NO CARS. I said, what ever happens first. Someone returns a loaner car or you fix the problem.

I could see the car being worked on. They come back and tell me that their diagnostic computer tells them that everything is green. His words exactly. But obviously it's not working fine. They are in and out of it, all the doors are open. I'm worried since it's well full of luggage and kids toys and half eaten things of some sort. The front is all removed. Finally it's on a hoist and the tires are all off...

They fix the problem! 

What the tell me was this. A sensor that monitors the wheel rotation in the back was installed at the factory without the little plastic holder that keeps it in place. So it worked it's way out and wasn't sensing the wheel anymore. The computer then went into panic mode. And he summed it up with. "We've never seen this before so we'll make a full and detailed report".

It's been about a month now and of hadn't had a single other issue.

This is why I've said that right now, the fact that Tesla has built all the manufacturing capacity is significant, for now, but people who try to say that Tesla will always be ahead of other companies?  No, absolutely not.  

Everything you've said in this video is something MANY people have talked about, and this leaves a bad taste in people's mouths.  At some point, when there's a lot more competition by the end of the decade, people are going to shop around a lot more and the fanboi thing is going to fade away when every auto company produces EVs.

But, it's a lot more than just that.  It's going to be about how people enjoy the vehicle, and I know there are lots of Tesla fanbois that will talk about how great they are, while ignoring the many thousands of people who've have a different experience.  What is the comfort, how does the vehicle handle, what's the visibility, etc....  They're going to be going against auto makers, that while wrong in thinking they could easily catch up to Tesla, won't be wrong in the long run because it won't be about how many vehicles you produce anymore.  It will be about how people feel about the vehicle and the ownership and this is where other companies have decades of experience, AND the infrastructure in place to deal with problems, because even though you have to completely rip a factory apart and redo it to build a BEV vs. ICE, the same isn't true for service centers, and that's what other companies already have.

The vehicles need to stop having all these little problems.  I constantly hear about issues with Teslas, and the last three 4 vehicles I've owned, all for 120,000 to 140,000 miles, I only had ONE issue where something broke, and I owned a Geo, Kia, Nissan and Toyota.  The only thing any of those vehicles ever needed was maintenance.

Last issue.  Tesla uses Agile as a project management scheme, and that's fine, but eventually that needs to get you to where you release a vehicle, and it doesn't need 100 changes in the manufacturing process or changing a part out with something else.  The other manufacturers are used to producing a vehicle every year, and they don't have to keep changing it, and most never need any recalls.  So, Agile is both good and bad.  It's fine right now while Tesla is figuring out the best way to make a reliable vehicle, but they have about 4 - 5 years to make the 1st vehicle that rolls out of the plant the same as the last one for a given year, and they'll need to follow the model of the other makers, because that's what consumers expect.

I'm rooting for Tesla, really, and I want them to get to where they're releasing vehicles that a middle class family that's making around the median income can afford to buy like what happens in China with BYD and some other companies.  But I see them hyped up so much, with things like them being able to make 20 some odd changes in a week as a good thing, and it is and isn't.  Other companies will put more planning into the design and manufacturing, and they'll make a vehicle people really LIKE to drive, and almost never have issues.  They've been doing it for a long time, and while making a BEV is different, that doesn't negate the experience they have in design and manufacturing.  I would never buy a Tesla in the current config, because if I want service, I want to drive no more than 10 minutes to drop the vehicle off and as I live in a big metroplex with lots of service centers, it's easy.

Yes, Tesla better start making those investments NOW since they're going to be rolling a million+ vehicle off the line this year, and people are going to have a lot more expectations.

Do we need more service centres?  Maybe, but even then it won’t fully address the problem.  Do we need more mobile rangers?  No, I think they have their place (roadside assistance), but travel time is a seriously inefficient overhead for routine service!  Personally I think agreements with existing recovery contractors (RAC or AA in the UK) is a much more efficient use of resources for breakdown situations.

What we need are to give existing Independent garages access to spare parts, manuals and diagnostic software.  My previous ICE cars were all maintained by a local garage no more than 400 metres from my house.  There was no hassle or personal time lost.  Spare parts were delivered same day or next day.  I never took it to a franchised dealer! It was great local service!

Contrast that with my model 3.  My nearest service centre is 40 minutes drive away.  So that’s 2 hours and 40 minutes of driving (including the loaner car).  That’s a lot of hassle for a baseline condition, and that’s mild compared to other residential addresses in the grand scheme of things.

Do I need service?  Yes, eventually!  Just routine things like making sure the brake pads don’t seize onto the calliper, wheel alignment etc….  That stuff is bread and butter for any garage.  But I really hope that I never need anything more than that (regardless of whether it’s covered by warranty or not), because that’s the point where Tesla ownership is dependent on Tesla service.

The next step that will reduce human stress to zero is for all vehicles to be FSD AND be aware of all other vehicle's intentions, the sum of which will entirely eliminate accidents due to driving (but not the irreducible residue due to hardware failures). Networking could either be active, issuing instructions to vehicles or be passive, advising vehicles of all others (and possibly of traffic/road conditions affecting routing). I prefer the latter, because traffic could survive (albeit less efficiently) network failure or even locations having no network.

Should a vehicle experience onboard failures, it could surrender driving to the network as a limp home mode, unless the human wants to undertake the crazy dangerous act of driving manually. If the latter, the network would inform all nearby vehicles to give the human-driven vehicle wide birth to keep the safety margins up.

Perhaps you could do an In Depth episode on the possibilities of networking in the future world of ubiquitous or nearly-ubiquitous FSD. Maybe you could inquire to see if Elon has already envisioned what that world look like. If he develops the network, maybe he could pay for it from the reduction of insurance losses (but don't count on premium reductions!). I happened to work in this industry in the early 1990s when all the oil companies were changing over to double walled tanks.  When the water table is effected there are two problems.  The water soluble compounds transfer to the ground water and the less water soluble compounds stay in the vadose zone.  Instead of excavating and removing the soil (which then needs to be treated) you can treat the undissolved contaminants in place with soil vapor extraction.  Air is pulled from wells the are screened in the nodose zone and then that air is cleaned using activated carbon or thermal/catalytic oxidation.  The contaminants in the water are treated with pump and treat systems that pull water from wells in the effected area and remove the contaminants through activated carbon, or strip them into the air with an air stripper.  Yes, that was normal.  Take the contaminants out of the water and just send them to the atmosphere.

Great series for sure. But at 5:18 you display an image of a metro station. Are you going to say : metro systems are obsolete ? If yes, I would not be so sure : in fact, they may become even more relevant. 

For sure, slow and rare buses in non-dense american cities are gonna be killed by robot-taxis - and these are good news. But in dense East Coast cities, European or Asian cities, not so fast ! Take Paris for instance : the main line (RER A) carries 1,4 millions travellers by day, with a capacity of 100 000 travellers per hour at peak time. The Tesla tunnels with individual cars would never be able to carry more than 1000/hour : is Paris going to dig 100 of them ?  Cheaper to build a good old metro then, especially if tunnel costs go down. And anyway, where would we be going to put all these cars in the narrow streets of a typical European downtown ? No way. So we would need minibuses going through these Boring compagny tunnels.This would be great. But, then, it is what is called a metro, and NYC, Paris, London, Berlin, Madrid, Beijing, Shanghai already have quite efficient ones that cover their downtown quite well...

Let us admit it : for non-American megacities, robottaxis, even going through Boring compagny tunnels, will not be an efficient mean of transportation. If fact, they will probaly be a nuisance : space is scarce, and there is nothing like a metro to transport masses without using much space. 

But the story does not end there : these big cities have less dense suburbs. Where a lot of people live. And robot-taxis have in those places enough capacity. In particular, they will be a very efficient mean to go... to the nearest metro station ! So I would expect the metro systems of big cities to see an increase of traffic. The main reason not to use them ("there is no station near my home") will disappear. Also, metro systems will be cheaper to operate (metro driver is a job that will disappear), have increased speed (automation really makes a difference), and increased capacity (since the interval between two trains will decrease with automation)...

Unpacking Elon's "part ROM, part RAM" comment: "ROM" means "Read-Only Memory".  Once you write to ROM, you cannot write to it again; it's fixed.  "RAM" means "Random Access Memory" but basically it means you can write to it as many times as you want, and each time you write to it, you simply replace whatever used to be there.  Computers use RAM for operations; for example, when you type text into a web browser, whatever you type will be in RAM.

Note: ROM isn't as common as it used to be, because these days we have "flash memory", which holds its value but can be rewritten.  A USB "thumb drive" uses flash memory (and is often called a "USB flash drive").  Flash memory is sometimes called flash RAM because it can be written to.  Anyway, most of the things you could do with ROM, you can now do with flash memory, and then you might be able to download an update and fix a problem.

Many computers now ship with flash memory as their persistent storage, instead of a "hard drive".  But "ROM" does not mean hard drive or flash memory.

Going back to Elon's tweet, Elon is saying that some parts of us are fixed and cannot be changed; other parts of us can be changed.

7:45 well maybe a rating system would help a little, but the problem of fake news is far too complex and nuanced to be solved by a simple popularity contest. The vast majority of people are utterly incompetent at fact checking and just form opinions from their couch.

I'm thinking we need an open source AI  solution built on GPT-3 combined with a weighted vote based rating system.

The ambitious design goal would be a system with precisely one bias: favor things that are actually true.

As a proponent of free speech, I would not want any content to be erased on the basis of being wrong. However, the content could be labeled with it's level of credibility, and readers would be able to filter on this basis.

How do we define "true"? By seeding it with a small number of items that we can't possibly be wrong about, but have a significant opposition following. The algorithm would regard these as "axioms". Two come to mind: the Earth is roughly spherical, and HIV and SARS-CoV-2 are indeed viruses. Nothing more controversial than these (e.g. you can't quite include "vaccines are safe and effective" or "some particular election wasn't stolen", because despite strong evidence these fall slightly short of axiomatic). Generally, since actual conspiracies do indeed happen in the real world, we need to be careful to set the bar for "axioms" extremely high.

I want to stress the distinction between axiomatic and proven. If something is in principle worthy of keeping an eye on evidence, then we should not use it as an axiom. In the above examples, elections and medical data are things that we can acquire a preponderance of evidence in a specific case but which historically have had mixed results in the general case (i.e. other elections have been stolen, and other mainstream medical solutions have gone wrong). So these cases are good targets for practical application of an algorithm, but bad choices for seeding axioms.

Globe Earth is a pretty good case as an effective axiom, as it's pretty safe and there are prenty of flat-earthers generating lots of content.

Given that, we would develop a GPT-3 model as a discriminator for detecting linguistic patterns that correlate with bullshit. The content is quite rich with all manner of fallacies, so it should be a cakewalk for the most part.

Voting would be integrated recursively with credibility. So flat-earthers would find that their voting power decays over time.

Of course the system must be open source. Without transparency and independent verification, there can be no legitimate credibility.

There has long been an argument about whether social media companies are platforms with, essentially the same protections afforded to your telephone company about not being liable for the content (ie what people might say or text on that service); or whether they are publishers with editorial rights to control and affect the promotion of content (such as a newspaper) - in the which case they are liable for the content and need to have the resources to censor it or get sued.

The problem is that right now, they are essentially having editorial control (bias, censorship etc) and still enjoying the government protections afforded to platforms so that they cannot be sued.

Musk's point is essentially stating that these platforms have become the defacto town square: essentially a platform; since there is no other way to get information to the public sphere other than online. The heavy editorialising going on with the Twitter algorithm is not only a threat to free speech, but is also antithetical to the legal protections afforded a platform. Hence the need for something to be done. 

Twitter (and others) need to choose one or the other. The time for keeping  your cake and eating it, is over.
