Regarding the Tesla line - it is a fair concern. Yes, if I were in a super long supercharger line without another charger nearby, I could myself wishing I could hop over to a gas station and fill up in 3 minutes - especially if you are in hurry. Do you care about the environment? Early adopters do, but most folks just want to refill their car and keep moving. Time is money - but you can always make more money. You aren't going to win everyone over on environmental reasons alone. I told someone at work I was getting a Tesla and she was really interested - she is a hard core liberal, vegan and environmentalist - I told her how sometimes you have to stop for charging and that can take 15-20 minutes - she was like no thanks. I tried explaining that this was only needed for road trips, but to no avail.

The reality is that EVs are still in the early adopter phase. They are great and they will eventually win. However, we have to be honest about their downsides so we can mitigate those issues as quickly as possible. Environmental reasons are nice, but EVs just being better overall is what will make them win in the long term - and we aren't there yet. The charging network is still the biggest issue - something the ICE system has had over 100 years to grow into.

Advanced nuclear like liquid salt thorium reactors are completely safe. The fuel is the coolant - no radioactive steam to be vented. No runaway reaction. When the plant is damaged, the fuel drops into collection bins and goes solid. Unlike Uranium, large amounts of thorium together does NOT create a criticality producing a Meltdown... more like a fizzle. 
A source of fast neutrons is needed to produce energy, not a chain reaction. Remove the source Or the fuel and... fizzle. 
These reactors also use the Primary isotope of Thorium as fuel rather than a Rare isotope used in Uranium based fuel (the reason "enrichment" is such a major topic in conventional Uranium reactors). Net effect: 400x the available, minable thorium, so it readily available in far more countries (including the US). 
These reactors use Liquid fuel (typically thorium floride - hence the term "salt" which really means a coumpound with 2 elements - like NaCl - table salt. 

So this thorium flouride salt melts above 400 Celsius. Solid below - This is great even for transport of the liquid as its a solid block when transported - can't be "spilled" at normal temperatures. Heat the container up and its liquid again. 

These molten salt reactors operate quite nicely, producing power until they overheat, then stop cocks melt and the fuel bleeds into catch tanks and the reaction ends. Or you turn off the fast neutron source and the reaction ends. The thorium evolves time into U232 which adds to the neutrons but is present in very small amounts and again, can't go critical until a Large percentage is converted (recall that U235 can't go critical once fuel purity drops below a high percentage (don't know where but more than 70% purity is needed). Here we are talking a few percent after the reactor has been running for a long time (months or more). The fuel can then be pumped out, exchanged and purified Thorium flouride- the U232 along with heavy hydrogen (tritium - worth about $30,000 per gram) and a few other lesser products and the purified fuel can be re-used. 
As an example here - Oakridge Labs ran one of these reactors in 1964-68 without refueling, though the U232 content was starting to get up there. 

In short. If you like a clean future - Liquid Salt Thorium reactors are a great source of Safe, Clean energy. It also produces less than 1% of the radioactive waste, has an abundant fuel source and mainly was shut down way back then because it Couldn't be used as a source of weapons grade plutonium (which we needed for bombs back then). 

China is embracing this tech and a few other countries but not the US. ANY nuclear reactor is still branded as unsafe because... you know Nuclear = Black Magic= politically untouchable. 

There is enough Thorium to power the world for several hundred years (or until Fusion isn't a bad joke... just 50 years away.... 10 if you fudge the math calculating "break even"). 

Note: Many detractors of the tech spread FUD about this by conflating solid fuel Thorium reactors which have Many problems. Even in "scholarly" articles by "experts" they make this mistake... clearly the "experts" are the same schills we see when big oil claims that EVs pollute "more" than ICE with horrendously bad math sourced to "experts". 

More green minded people Really  need to know about this. 

Recommend search terms "thorium" and "molten salt reactor" - Not "thorium reactor" or you will get the other failed solid fuel tech - and many authors conflate the two. 
Kirk Sorenson's videos are a good source of info. Many others.

Great series for sure. But at 5:18 you display an image of a metro station. Are you going to say : metro systems are obsolete ? If yes, I would not be so sure : in fact, they may become even more relevant. 

For sure, slow and rare buses in non-dense american cities are gonna be killed by robot-taxis - and these are good news. But in dense East Coast cities, European or Asian cities, not so fast ! Take Paris for instance : the main line (RER A) carries 1,4 millions travellers by day, with a capacity of 100 000 travellers per hour at peak time. The Tesla tunnels with individual cars would never be able to carry more than 1000/hour : is Paris going to dig 100 of them ?  Cheaper to build a good old metro then, especially if tunnel costs go down. And anyway, where would we be going to put all these cars in the narrow streets of a typical European downtown ? No way. So we would need minibuses going through these Boring compagny tunnels.This would be great. But, then, it is what is called a metro, and NYC, Paris, London, Berlin, Madrid, Beijing, Shanghai already have quite efficient ones that cover their downtown quite well...

Let us admit it : for non-American megacities, robottaxis, even going through Boring compagny tunnels, will not be an efficient mean of transportation. If fact, they will probaly be a nuisance : space is scarce, and there is nothing like a metro to transport masses without using much space. 

But the story does not end there : these big cities have less dense suburbs. Where a lot of people live. And robot-taxis have in those places enough capacity. In particular, they will be a very efficient mean to go... to the nearest metro station ! So I would expect the metro systems of big cities to see an increase of traffic. The main reason not to use them ("there is no station near my home") will disappear. Also, metro systems will be cheaper to operate (metro driver is a job that will disappear), have increased speed (automation really makes a difference), and increased capacity (since the interval between two trains will decrease with automation)...

Whoa, okay. What you said about Atlas V and Delta IV being "50 years old" is very misleading.
Yes, it is true that Atlas' roots date back to the late 50s, but the Atlas V flown today has next to nothing in common with the Atlas rocket that put John Glenn into orbit. Think of it like the Ship of Theseus. Is a rocket, with every component eventually replaced over time, still the same rocket?
Atlas V's engines, main body, fuel pumps, fuel tanks, electronics, and avionics are essentially completely different when compared to the original Atlas ICBM. They share nearly nothing in common anymore.
Same thing with Delta IV. Delta IV is fundamentally different in almost every way from Delta II except in name, and even Delta II was a massive change from the old Thor-Delta rockets from the 60s.

Are Atlas and Delta still expendable? Yes. But (especially Atlas) those rockets are still the most reliable rockets the US has in its arsenal.

To make an accurate comparison, you need to include the energy consumed in mining the rare earths that are mandatory for the current LiPo cells that comprise Tesla's battery systems, and the wind turbines, etc. Yes, that also means you need to factor in the energy needed to mine/refine and shape the steel and other materials to build power plants.

Wind power has proven to not be cost effective so far compared to traditional methods, and then there's the issue of what to do with all the toxic chemicals in the generators and their turbine blades, which are not recyclable with present recycling tech.

Honestly, we'd all be better off perfecting thorium salt reactors as a bridge solution until fusion power becomes commercially feasible. 

I do think having near ubiquitously distributed, medium scale (15-100KWh) backup power sources is a fantastic idea, and I can see that uptake accelerating greatly given the specs touted for solid state batteries - majority composition is silica (glass), minimal use of rare earths, cheaper to manufacture and anywhere from 2-6X storage capacity per lb/kg compared to current LiPo state of the art.

Renewables + Batteries will definitely take over the grid in the next two decades, but your video doesn't paint the current picture very accurately.
Currently, the ~700 mWh or 1000 mWh grid batteries are not cheap enough or big enough to shut down thermal plants.  Solar+storage plants are cheap enough for forward-thinking power companies in good solar regions to build instead of new peaker plants, but battery prices have to drop more to make thermal plants stranded assets.  These new solar+storage plants at best offer maybe four hours of energy in the evening.  They are not big enough to offer significant power 24/7.  
To really make thermal plants obsolete, batteries will have to go below $50/kWh (currently at about $150/kWh) and the battery installations will have to be much bigger than about 1000 mWh, probably more like 10 gWh.  Also, long-term battery storage will be necessary, as in storing solar in the summer and using it in winter.  For the grid to be all renewables, and all gas/coal plants mothballed,  batteries will probably need to be ~ $10/kWh.  That's an order of magnitude cheaper than today's cheapest lithium-ion batteries, and it's not clear that lithium-ion can go that low, because cobalt, nickel, lithium, manganese are all expensive inputs. 
I expect some battery chemistry to achieve $10/kWh, probably some kind of flow battery or something other than lithium-ion, but it may be a decade or more.  In the meantime, lithium-ion and maybe lithium-metal batteries will go below $100/kWh and we'll see bigger and better solar+storage. I was considering buying a model 3 based on assertions about their high residual value.  But I ran some numbers and now I'm not so sure.  When I looked at the history of residual values for Model S and Model X vehicles, one thing is becoming clear:  Out of Warranty repairs on Teslas are **very** expensive.  This in turn can corrode residual values, even if your car still is in warranty.

If a car is built so well, why does the car only have a 50000mile/4 year warranty?  Yes it's 8years/120000miles for the Drivetrain/Battery for the Model 3 LR, but there are a whole heap of repairs that sound like minor things, which would ordinarily cost very little on other cars, but are outrageously expensive on Teslas.  Does $1000 for a failed headlight sound fair?  What about $3000 for a replacement MCU (which commonly happens due to excessive read/writes on flash memory)?  How about $6000 for failed air conditioning?  Suffered a minor bump at 5mph?  That's $110000 to get that dent repaired in the body shop!

What would be helpful is if 3rd party garages can gain access to parts, manuals and drawings.  It can also open up the market for generic parts to be made by manufacturers like Delphi.  I'm a strong believer in the right to repair, but this lockdown on 3rd party repairs will ultimately cause Teslas to depreciate more quickly than they are given credit for right now.

Dealerships are more organic than you think. There is comapny credit, but dealerships are also tied into local banks, who make a lot of the loans. All those hokey Kiwanas Business Lunches in your hometown serve a purpose. It is for the banks to assess actual demand for big ticket items like cars and houses, and banks will afterward tell realtors and dealers how much credit their customers will be getting. This is hyper-local business forecasting, and it is essential if credit and business investment are to be properly allocated. So COMPLAIN all you want about dealerships (and realtors) - they are a lot more powerful than you think.

This is interesting, and Tesla certainly is offering a different experience, but a couple of points.

Before spending between $35,000 and +$100,000 on a car, most people will want to kick the tires and take a test drive. You can schedule a test drive at Tesla's website, but that's not nearly as convenient as just walking into a dealership and asking. They'll need to have some way for people to still do this once their dealerships are gone. Tesla has (I believe) a 7 day no-questions-asked return policy, but who wants to order and put money down on a car, wait months for delivery, only to find out in the first five minutes of driving that, for whatever reason, it's not for you? A test drive saves the consumer a lot of needless grief.

Regarding making money off customers after purchase: Tesla vehicles rely heavily on over-the-air software updates, online features, and connectivity, which is a great innovation, but also puts consumers at the company's mercy. Most of the connected features Tesla used to offer for free are now only available as a Premium Connectivity subscription for $9.99 a month (plus tax if applicable).

I don't like reading comments, so maybe I missed it but I seem to be the only one saying that it is a fallacy that EVs cost manufacturers more to build than ICE cars. Yes, batteries are currently expensive, but the cost to develop and prove a new ICE engine costs a small fortune, especially given their increasing complexity. Then you have all of the tier three supplies you have to buy from, (fuel injectors, sensors, filters. etc.). An 8,9 or 10 speed transmission is expensive to design and prove, (just ask Ford about their recent failed dual clutch trans lawsuit.) Then there's the cost of the extensive tooling for thousands of parts for the powertrain and the army of workers that you have to pay to assemble the parts. So you have thousands and thousands of white collar and blue collar workers that you have to pay, plus pay their expensive benefits. You need floor space, lots of it, energy to heat/cool this floor space lots of machines and energy to run the machines that are building the thousands of parts for a powertrain. How is that cheaper than buying a motor from a third party? And remember, batteries will continue to get better and cheaper.

A note from Teslarati:

The Tesla Cybertruck is, without a doubt, one of the most discussed vehicles in recent memory. The pickup’s polarizing and robust design has vehicle fanatics raving about the possibility of changing the tune of the American truck market today. In a recently published video from The Fast Lane Car YouTube channel, the team discussed why they believe the Cybertruck will fail to be an effective mode of off-road transportation. They highlight its heavy-weight and low-body design as two of the reasons it will fall short of impressively navigating through rocks and trails.

“If you look at what you need for off-road ability, you need ground clearance, you need gearing, you need articulation, you need underbody protection, right?” The trucking experts add, “If you look at the off-road tech, the stuff that you needed back in 1949 is the stuff you still need in 2020-2021.”

Typically, offroading vehicles that find success in challenging terrain have short wheelbase are lightweight and tend to told hold higher-than-normal ground clearances that assist in traveling over sharp crests on trails. TFL’s Tommy Mica highlights these attributes during the video, stating that an offroading vehicle’s biggest enemy is weight.

“Just like on-road, the enemy to off-road is weight. The lighter the weight, the easier it is to crawl up obstacles to maneuver difficult situations. The Cybertruck is going to be huge and is going to be monstrously heavy,” Mica says.

While it is ideal to have a lighter vehicle for offroading situations, that does not mean a heavy car will have issues 100% of the time. In fact, there are many vehicles that hold a weight that is similar to the Cybertruck’s estimated 5,000-6,500 pound curb rating. One is the 2019 Ford F-150 Raptor, a truck that was recognized by Popular Mechanics as one of the top 12 best off-road vehicles available. Weighing in at over 5,500 pounds, the Raptor has been spotted climbing intimidating stretches of steep offroading trails without much of an issue.

Additionally, Mica states that the Cybertruck’s low ground clearance will inhibit the vehicle’s ability to navigate over steep land grades and sharp objects on a trail. However, the Cybertruck’s 16″ ground clearance is higher than the 8.7″ measurement of the top-ranked 2019 Ram 1500 Rebel from Dodge and the previously mentioned F-150 Raptor’s 11.5″ clearance.

TFL tested a Long-Range configuration of the Model X in its off-road tests. Citing a diminished loss of range due to increased power usage, and increased worry over puncturing the vehicles underbody battery pack made their experience not-so-memorable. However, the Model X was never aimed toward off-road performance specifically. While the electric SUV does have traction control capabilities that have performed well on off-road courses in the past, the Model X was not meant for navigating through vicious trails of rocks, branches, and uneven terrain.

Even so, using the Model X’s performance as an off-road vehicle as the basis to prove the Cybertruck’s inability to function on trails just seems silly. The two cars maintain entirely different packages. Comparing a Ford Escape’s off-road performance to the F-150 Raptor’s wouldn’t be justifiable either, as the two vehicles are completely different and aimed toward different functions.

Besides, Tesla CEO Elon Musk has stated that the Cybertruck’s size and dimensions are not finalized. In early December 2019, Musk said the width and length would both be revised to fit inside a residential garage. “We can prob reduce width by an inch & maybe reduce length by 6+ inches without losing on utility or aesthetics,” Musk said.

The Cybertruck’s off-road performance won’t be solidified until the release of its Dual and Tri motor variants in 2021. However, there is plenty of evidence to suggest that the electric truck will be more than capable of holding its own in tight terrain, especially considering its most powerful variant packs a tremendous punch.

Build the Gigafactory in Texas! Somewhere in the triangle of Austin, Corpus Christi and Houston would be perfect. 

The University of Texas is a  huge draw for top students, especially engineering talent. A great deal of battery expertise (John Goodenough and his team) is connected with UT. Stainless steel production/shipment between SpaceX and Gigafactory Texas would be ideal. Material and parts can be easily brought in via air, truck, railroad, and ship (Port of Houston). Texas is already (I'll bet to the surprise of many) a very big producer of clean energy, both solar and wind. The cost of electricity is very low in Texas. The land is inexpensive. Located very close to a huge International market (Mexico) and the Port of Houston for shipment to the East Coast, Central, and South America. The road system goes straight up to Canada branching off to Western and Eastern rural areas and large population markets. Texas is a HUGE pickup truck market. Texas is also huge when it comes to Semi-trucks with a tremendous amount of trade between Mexico, the USA, and Canada, so it's also a natural spot to produce Tesla Semis. Traveling and shipping to Texas by air is also convenient with DFW, Houston, Austin, San Antonio, and Corpus Christi airports in close proximity.

Tesla should be able to leverage a deal with the Texas State government to allow full access to Texas consumers. In 20+ years, the population of Texas will be larger than California - a great market for Tesla to advance. The Texas State government and local governments are very business-friendly. Elon has talked of an  HVAC solution for residential and his Solar roof is about to really expand. (I myself have had Solar City Solar Panels on my home in Texas for 4 years.) 

So let's think big... Batteries, Model Y, Roadster, and future models, Cybertruck, Semi, HVAC, Solar Roof, Power Wall,  Massive Energy Storage Solutions, and whatever else Elon comes up with (my suggestion, is energy-efficient modular homes incorporating all of Tesla's products) can all be produced in Texas and efficiently shipped. There is plenty of land and talented personnel in Texas to do it all, as well as close proximity to hundreds of millions of potential buyers (Domestic and International).

Texans love a challenge - the bigger the better. Our entire country needs a challenge big enough to capture our imagination and bring it to reality. Come on Elon, bring it. Let's get going!

Upon coming home I plugged it in and it would not charge. 

I called the local Hyundai dealer and brought it in. At the same time I asked them to look at the USB connector for Apple CarPlay as it had a hard time connecting, most often never connecting to my iPhone and if it did connect would disconnect after a few km of driving.

It took two weeks to diagnose the issue and get a new part in from Korea. It was the Integrated Charge Controller. That seemed to fix the charging issue. Except for around three months later I go out to drive the Ionic 5 and it does not start again. Once again it was plugged in over night. This time the 12V measured around 5V. I tried jumping it again but got nowhere so I called AA to get a jump start. An hour later the AA guy showed up and jumped the Ioniq 5. It started and and even though it was plugged in overnight it measured only 90% charged. He recommended I keep the car on the charger for another hour. I did that and so far for the last few months it has worked.

The Hyundai dealership shop never looked at the USB/CarPlay issue. When it doesn't connect it comes up with a message stating you need to use a "certified" cable. Hyundai will not sell you a "certified" cable. I've used Apple cables and other brand cables and they all work the same way - they don't work. Hyundai knows it doesn't work properly and they know it's a design/implementation error on their part but will not fix it.

When you pay over $100,000 NZD for a car you expect it to work as advertised. The Ionic 5 does not! Let's do some math, because math doesn't lie.

My TeslaFi data from the last 3 years on my Model Y shows that I've covered 115,926 miles at an average of 283 Wh/mile.  This was achieved in upstate NY and includes at least 2 long distance road trips per year (hot, cold, wind, mountains, valleys, rain, snow, highways, and backroads....you name it).  With a 74kWh battery pack, my car should 'average' about 261 miles on a full charge (when the battery was new).  

According to my data, the best efficiency on a drive greater than 2 hours with less than 100 feet of elevation difference was 214 Wh/mi.  Had I continued at that efficiency, the car would have lasted for 345 miles which is 30 miles above the range that Tesla quoted.  The data shows that the temp was 65 degrees and the air conditioning was not on.

My worst efficiency also took place on the same exact route.  The temperature was -20F and the life support system was working hard.  My car's efficiency for that drive was 457 Wh/mi.  The range for a full battery was only 162 miles.  This data is absolutely true as I remember worrying if I was going to make it to the next DCFC with only 80% charge and 110 miles of distance to cover.  I arrived driving on quarks....whew.

So, if you take my best efficiency, then Tesla has under estimated their range.  If you go by the worst conditions, then Tesla (and likely everyone else) has grossly overestimated their range.

As far as I'm concerned, Tesla is not lying about their range.  It is achievable.  It is not the average, but the average changes greatly depending on the conditions of your particular environment.

LiDAR does not have an advantage over multiple cameras viewing an object from different perspectives when determining the shape of the object. The images produced by two or more cameras viewing an object from different perspectives are different the differences in the images can with simple trigonometry be used to calculate the shape in three dimensions of the objects in view. Tesla use this stereoscopic vision effect (as used by human eyes) to produce an effective LiDAR substitute. This is done within neural networks trained to generate the three dimensional output. It should also be noted that even if only ONE camera is available, provided that camera moves in relation to the object the same can be performed by using the images from successive frames as they will view from differing perspectives just as if you had multiple cameras viewing from different perspectives at the same time...

So let's call it "Partial Self Driving". So what value is that today ? Is it $0 - no. Is it $15,000 - that's up for each individual to decide. It appears from the discussion that a case could be made for deciding its value at the margin ie at the specific point where it avoids an accident ( the guy walking from behind a hedge, or the car going off the road because the driver falls asleep ). Again, it's for each person to decide this "value at the margin". In the first example, where the driver didn't see the pedestrian, an accident would have happened. In the second example, when you're sleepy, you pull over, rest and rehydrate before continuing. So user behaviour avoids the accident. Regarding the potential for your car to earn you money, again paying $15,000 as a "call option" on future revenue of $100,000 is a personal investment decision, including a view of when Tesla will have the feature available, and what the market for robo-taxis will be in the future ( incl. demand levels, insurance availability, wear and tear to the car etc.). But in essence it's semantics. To me it's misleading to call it "Full Self Driving" today when it's patently not that. So "Partial Self Driving" I think would be a better description. Alex's point is spot on, we want AI driving that is BETTER than a human being, not one that can make mistakes LIKE a human being.  NHSTA needs to be more like the NTSB, if the AI screws up the image processing from cameras, there MUST be a failsafe in the form of radar/lidar.

Why Model Y/Model 3 will not become 1000 volt systems based on the 4680 battery cell.  Warning Math.

With 4680 cells in the Model Y,  there was only 828 battery cells that fit. in the Model Y  (9p/92s)  This leads to a  a 386 volt system (max charge will get the voltage a bit closer to 400V).  So what if we try to make the same  828 battery cells to make a 1000 volt system,   The closest you get is a 4p/207s  which will create a  870 Volt battery pack.,  this is close and if we just increase to 860 cells,  now we have a 4p/215s which creates a 905 Volt system.

The problem,  you only have 4 batteries in parallel,  if 1 out of 828 battery fuses blow (Which this will happen),  the other 3 batteries in that single group have to do  33% more work.  This will lead to another fuse blowing. . .Which will ofcourse cripple the car at that time.   

Tesla will need to stay at the 2170 or similar size battery cells if they want to increase the voltage or they risk bricking their cars anytime a single fuse blows . . . Which this happens all the time.

Current 2170 cells,  there are over 40 batteries in parallel,  blowing 2-3 fuses in a single group has minimal impact and the car will drive just fine as is.

With the range: here in Europe, it is not about distance but drive time behind the wheel. After 4.5 hrs you need to break for 15-30min and after 9hrs you have to take a long break. Given that you have an official speed limit of 80kmh for large trucks - which many do not respect though - means you need a 10-80% range (assuming charging over 80% will be slow also at a mega charger and going under 10% is too risky). So first leg is 4.5 x 80kmh = 360km. And per day 720km. Given that a driver will try to minimize the first stop to 15min and also assuming there is not a super fast charger every 350km, I would generously assume a 10min charging which might add 160-166kWh or given the consumption of roughly 900Wh/km it means 180km. For a 80-10% (or 70%) usage covering 360km you need 515km range. BUT then you can only use 6.5hr of your 9hr allowed drive time (4.5 plus 2hr after the high speed 10min charge). Or they need to charge for 25min and then have 4.5hr left ... BUT only if they have a mega charger available... so I would say IF a truck has a real 330mi (515km) range, it can work here. But it is always extra stress to find a charger and only works with 1MW chargers.

So: I think here in Europe we need something with a 800km / 500mi range. Not for every use but for the long hauls. Whether Tesla or someone else is a different story. Despite my handle, I am not a fanboy 😂

I would say that "least reliable EVs in the part 10 years" might go to one of the following before Tesla...

1) Chevy Bolt for having to recall every single Bolt ever made to replace the entire battery pack.
2) Nissan Leaf Gen 1 for having non-active cooled batteries that failed after a few years.
3) Toyota BZ4X (or whatever it's called) for wheels literally falling off.

Also, lets not forget that most other manufacturers were not making EVs for most of the last 10 years.
Finally, they mentioned reliability in the context of their ICE competitors which require significant maintenance (oil changes, engine overhauls, etc.) even when nothing breaks.

Just one thing about the competition and 80% of routes being 250 miles and beyond: while that _is_ true, it is also true that elevations vary -- those are not flat level, constant speed routes at all. Therefore you need more than what is necessary to go 250 miles on a flat road. Not only that, but you want to be able to charge fast enough that you can do several of these routes during your week on the road. Mercedes and Volvo just don't do that. The Semi does.

Another consideration about hills again: I've made the calculus, but for Europe; the amount of power you need to sustain 90 kph carrying 44 tons on a 5% incline is around 700 kW. Mercedes and Volvo don't have that kind of power, they will still be hazards on highways for that reason. The Semi has.

For Europe however, notwithstanding that in its given incarnation it is illegal (too big); the biggest problem to me is that it's not a sleeper cab. There is also the charging network of course, but this will come -- it has to. I do hope that the Semi will come on these shores, and we'll have to see whether Tesla will go with MCS or stick with its own standard... Frankly I'd rather EU picked Tesla, which _is_ the king when it comes to cutting edge technology, and not fall yet again to the NIH (Not Invented Here) syndrome.

Finally, 1 MW peak is all good and well but I also want to see the charging curve... When I get to a charging point for a break which I need to take as an HGV driver and have 30% battery, how much battery will I have when I end my 30 mn break? My 45 mn break? This matters. And note the advantage wrt time: you can have a break while you charge -- you cannot while you refuel.

Regarding needed range for an electric semi, it seems to make sense to start with the highest practical range since there is no fast charging network in place for trucks yet. Also, I have learned as an EV owner and fan that you have to account for things like battery degradation and cold weather while keeping a buffer. As an example, the Nikola Tre 330 mile range could become less than 230 miles in practice assuming 10% battery degradation plus 15% loss in cold weather (yes, cold weather hurts a lot) and a remaining 10% buffer (since you don't want to plan on arriving at 0% state of charge).  On top of that, you may need to consider some range loss due to other factors such as elevation change, head winds and higher freeway speed. Obviously a lower load and a lower speed would increase range. It seems to make sense that the 500 mile range of the Tesla semi will be a huge advantage over the competition.

Based on personal experience with my 2018 Tesla Model 3, here is a smart and easy way to charge your EV when on a long road trip. This is for an EV with a 300 mile or higher rated range. 
1. Start your road trip from home with at least an 85% (255 miles) charge. 
2. Drive 2 to 3 hours until the battery is down to 25% (75 miles) or less. 
3. Plug into a supercharger rated for 250 kW. Charge up to 75% (225 miles). This charging session to add 37 kWh should take no more than 15 minutes. During this short time, you will be wanting to stretch your legs, go to the restroom, and perhaps have a refreshment. A “Pee and a Tea” as the Brits like to say. 
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you reach your destination. 
5. If you plan to stay overnight at your destination, look for a level 2 charger you can inexpensively plug into overnight so you can set out the next day with an 85% charge. 
The key message here is that the fastest supercharging speeds are achieved when the battery is low on charge. The charging speed slows down considerably as the battery charges up. Don’t waste your time trying to fill your battery beyond 75% unless you don’t see another supercharger on your route for more than 150 miles.

The achilles' heel of battery swap in cars is going to be the wait time.  People naively think that it's a shortcut to fast charge times, but that's only the case in low demand situations.  As soon as there's a line, wait times quickly exceeded the time spent plugging in.  At a rate of 3 minutes to process each car, each swap station can only process 20 cars per hour assuming perfect efficiency.  Anyone who has been to a gas station knows that any 'fueling' location needs to be able to handle far more than 20 cars per hour or the user experience quickly suffers.  If you're 5th in line, than means a 15 minute wait just to access the pump.  That's already a comparable time to the charging experience to just plugging in.

The solution then has to be more swap stations.  However, here again is a huge problem.  Swap stations are far more expensive than either gas pumps or HVDC charge points.  That means no company can afford to install enough swap equipment to handle the surges in demand because the majority of the time this very expensive equipment will just be sitting idle.  Economics will force companies to try and maximize utilization, which means lines for the consumer... which translates into a terrible user experience.  (We've already seen this play out with much LESS EXPENSIVE 3rd party HVDC charge points)

Finally, the notion that swap technology will improve so that negates any argument that charging technology will improve.  That's a flawed assumption.  It's undoubtedly true that both the technologies will improve with time, however, the runway to improve dramatically favours charging.  A 50% improvement in charging speeds will dramatically slash charge times.  A 20 minute charge turns into a 10 minute charge.  Whereas a 50% improvement in a 3 minute swap only chops 90 seconds off.

It's simple: Remember Tesla's stated mission? "Accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy."

Your arguments seem to be tied to a few (flawed) assumptions:
1. Tesla's done building superchargers, and their network will stop growing.
2. When Tesla opens its network to other EVs, there will suddenly be a massive influx of other EVs.

But the facts say otherwise.

1. The rate that Tesla is opening new superchargers is actually _increasing_, not decreasing, and the network is projected to triple in size over the next couple of years.
2. In sheer unit volume numbers, there aren't actually that many other BEVs in the US. Tesla continues to dominate the market with over 75% of the BEVs on the roads today being Teslas (Source: Kelly Blue Book). Furthermore, "competitors" such as the Ford F150 Lightning are projected to have production volume numbers to pale in comparison to those of Tesla.

If Tesla chargers a premium to charge other EVs while continuing to rapidly scale their charging network, everyone wins: other brands have at least some hope of delivering compelling EVs without going bankrupt due to lack of charging infrastructure, Tesla gets additional revenue to apply towards building out an even bigger supercharger network, incentives remain for other brands to compete to make decent charging networks of their own, demand for sustainable energy such as solar increases, and the world accelerates its transition to sustainable energy.

If you look at it with ant-brain mentality and see it from the very immediate future, then there's some case to be made for Tesla "screwing all of its customers" but it's incredibly short-sighted, and lacking any real critical thinking.

But you're welcome to think what you want. I challenge you to look back on this a year or two from now though to see how your assumptions pan out.

- the footprint of one battery-swapping station is at least 4 or more equivalent fast-charging stalls
- each manufacturers has different battery size/technology so those swapping stations would need to store a whole lot of different battery sizes (and also adapt their hardware to work with all of those), increasing significantly the already big footprint
- it is not going to scale well
- it doesn't fix the problem of people not having charging stations close by, they would still need to drive to the swapping station
- it is way more expensive to deploy such stations than fast chargers, so that business is never going to be profitable

Six more advantages are these:  1) battery swapping greatly improves resale value and greatly improves the confidence people will have when buying a used electric.  2)  It gets rid of the "osborne" effect where people don't buy electric cars since they are "waiting" for solid state batteries  3)  Battery swapping gets around the "nickel" and raw material problem since the total battery capacity of all cars combined is now less.  You don't have 500 miles of battery range sitting unused in a car driven 10 miles a day.  Less total batteries allows the price of nickel to stay low and be obtainable.  4)  It corrects the "dealership" problem of OEMs since now VW for instance can say, "yeah you won't service electric cars too much but people will come in and want battery upgrades all the time when you lease your battery that is trivial to change".  5) Battery swapping solves the recycle problem since it gives a great time to analyze each battery as they get swapped and mark some for recycling with the customer doing nothing.   6) Battery swapping promotes green energy since any farmer, person with some solar or wind capacity, can volunteer to charge up batteries if delivered to him.

List tự động trên Youtube đưa mình đến bài này. Câu hát đầu vừa cất lên, một cảm xúc kì lạ bỗng dâng trào. Đó là những ngày mình còn đang nghỉ sinh em bé đầu, vốn là một người ít đi xem phim nhưng mình vẫn quyết tâm xem bằng được bộ phim Loving Vincent ấy. 
Những người phải rất yêu, rất thương Vincent mới đủ kiên nhẫn để khắc họa và giải đáp cho câu hỏi "Ông đã sống như thế nào?" qua hàng trăm, hay hàng nghìn bức tranh sơn dầu như vậy. 
Một bài hát nhẹ nhàng như thủ thỉ, không da diết và hẳn cũng không lấy nhiều nước mắt người xem. Phim không kịch tính, không nút thắt. Đơn giản chỉ để có một không gian cho những ai tình cờ thích một vài bức tranh như "Đêm đầy sao" cùng ngồi lại mà thôi. Nhưng xứng đáng.

The thing that scares me is that they always will be people like Vincent (well not exactly like him because everyone is unique but with their own sensitive souls) but not everyone will be remembered like he is. In our world it's hard to be sensitive, it always has been. We can go through life praising Vincent and regretting that none gave him the recognition he deserved but at the same time not notice all the unique and beautiful people around us that would need our help. Or we can be those sensitive souls and go unnoticed. While I'm in no way such a beautiful person as Vincent, I'd like to think I'm sensitive. The problem is that it's hard to find people like you or those who accept you, I feel like a background character in my own life, and the thought of dying and achieving nothing in this world really scares me. It's sad that the example of Vincent didn't teach us all to appreciate the sensitivity because if we don't learn this, there will be always people like Vincent - misunderstood, lonely but beautiful and meaningful that could change the world if only someone let them do it.

I cried so much when listening to this song at the end of the movie. It touched me deeply. I am a person who has struggled with bipolar disorder my whole life. I know  how it feels... 'How you suffered for your sanity. How you tried to set them free." I am also an artist (singer, not professional as I was never properly trained, I never have enough money to pursue music properly) who has always been torn between "bread and roses", of course, I am not a great talent like Vincent, but I know how it feels to use arts to keep you going in life with a mental problem and a deep loneliness and maybe sometimes a doubt of yourself and even your pure excitement at little things in life that people find it hard to understand. You often feel misunderstood, and arts is the only way to express yourself, your soul, and a way for you to be your own best friend, to forgive yourself too. Perhaps, I should learn to sing this song.
